reviews.author: cult_vegetables
reviews.text: There is one mood: Dire, fist-clenching angst. But if Einstürzende Neubauten didn't exist, it might have been necessary to invent them. Their ferocious, industrial maelstrom was literally the sound of The Wall crumbling: power tools, clanging junkyard percussion, bass, and at center, Blixa Bargeld's cathartic wail. It's a humorless concoction, but Ishii was the perfect conduit to capture their theatricality, matching the band's raw, vital immediacy with his camera, even including a horror-tinged video amidst the live destruction.

reviews.text: I have no clue if this succeeds as a concert film or a narrative film, but it sure as hell succeeds as an industrial moodpiece. If only it could be seen in better quality than 240p on YouTube... ah well, still great. I've been digging backwards through Einstürzende Neubauten's discography and been loving their later material recently, where they became a bizarro ballad-cum-ambient act, and I was steeled for something much more aggressive than this was- this is just some particularly clattery post-punk! Harmless! Hell, I bet these folks could write a pop song with those chainsaws with barely any work. More concert movies need piles of televisions, flames and architecture.

reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: Director Jang Joon-hwan (Save the Green Planet) looks at the June Democratic Uprising - in which demonstrations forced the South Korean military regime to implement democratic reforms leading to the current, Sixth Republic. 1987: When the Day Comes frames these events between two student deaths. Bak Jong-cheol passed away January 14, 1987 as a result of torture while being interrogated - information that was initial suppressed. The attempts by the perpetrators to derail the investigation, and public outcry over it, makes up the bulk of the film - concluding with the national funeral for protestor Lee Han-yeol on July 9th, 1987.

reviews.text: The true essence of loneliness is not felt when you're alone, but when you're surrounded by people you can't connect with. No one captures a mood quite like Wong Kar Wai, the narration and the cigarette smoke crawling in slow motion, opening and closing of doors, we are all under his spell, his mercy. Tony Leung, with or without the mustache, is always pleasant to watch. Faye Wong channeled a new level of energy with two different performances. (I Fell in Love with An Android, but That's OK) Maggie Cheung seemed to be centuries away, but her shadow is ever-present. I expected -- wanted -- in the mood for love 2. (or 3. What's the order of this trilogy again?) Turns out Wong Kar Wai's never contented with making the same thing twice. Still awesome.

I may not always rate these films as highly as my favourite films, but they are more important to the world. The purity of art's inner intention matters, at least to me. 37 Seconds is exactly the kind of special movie I have nothing but respect for.

reviews.text: A reliable comfort watch for me. As much fun as PIECES is, I revisit this Calum Waddell-directed documentary housed on disc 2 of the Grindhouse Releasing edition way more often. reviews.author: Flynch
reviews.text: ABCˋs movies of the week sind so eine kleine Fundgrube für kuriose Filme. Was sie nicht mit Aufwand, Sex, Gewalt oder dergleichen zeigen können bzw. dürfen, machen sie zum Teil mit einfallsreichen Geschichten wieder wett.DER EISKALTE TOD fühlt sich wie eine kleine Nebengeschichte von THE THING an. Das gleiche Setting, die Paranoia, die Monotonie und das Misstrauen setzen Robert Culp und Eli Wallach in diesem Kammerspiel gehörig zu. Mit seinen knapp 70 Minuten Laufzeit verzichtet der Film auf unnötige Nebenplots und kommt zwar gemächlich, aber ungeheuer atmosphärisch und rätselhaft zum Punkt. Diesen feinen eiskalten Mysteriethriller sollte man sich am besten ohne Vorkenntnisse zu Gemüte führen, denn der Zuseher weiss gerade so viel wie die beiden Protagonisten und auch wenn vielleicht der eine oder andere des Rätsels Lösung bereits erahnt, zaubert einem der schräge Schlußtwist dennoch ein kleines Grinsen ins Gesicht. Creepy !Für Fans von rätselhaften Kammerspielen und Freunden von bitterkalten Angelegenheiten.

However, those began in the middle of the 1960’s and from then until about 2000 they were a regular staple on all the major broadcast networks; they were treated seriously and some were even noteworthy, such as Carpenter’s Elvis, The Day After or Spielberg’s Duel. Its first half an hour is a confusing mess of flashbacks and a constant stream of new characters (the hysterically bad subs didn't help matters... I laughed pretty hard every time Simon Yam was referred to as someone's 'sister-in-law'), but its lengthy final act is pure, unhinged CAT III goodness as ex-soldiers storm a small village to take vicious revenge for the death of a friend's wife. reviews.text: The beauty of 90s Hong Kong Cat III films is that their "everythimg goes" nature allows them to do things conventional films wouldn't dare. This film is a mix of crime thriller, silly erotica, soap opera melodrama and a psychological exploration of a damaged man. Goes without saying that it is very rough around the edges, yet somehow it works. It has the sleaze but it also manages to be quite engaging, certainly more than other exploitation vehicles of the time.

So, he’s kinda saying it without saying it – there’s going to be a battle to the death in this house. And if you’ve seen any gialli before, you KNOW what people will do for money.

reviews.author: Mike Marsbergen
reviews.text: A... FOR ASSASSIN was released in July 1966 and is typically cited as a "proto-giallo," when really it's a fantastically twist-laden, highly cynical murder mystery. Every character is a suspect, and each of them is morally repugnant in their own way. I'd say it has more in common with a krimi than a giallo. It's mostly a melodrama, where the characters' motivations are basic, self-centred, and highly emotional. Then there are occasional moments of amusement where the inspector comically mimes the act of slashing one's throat.

reviews.author: Hungkat
reviews.text: It's always heartbreaking to watch someone who makes a minor blunder that undoes everything they’ve done right up to that point. A seemingly basic premise quickly devolves into something far more complex. A Hero expertly examines society's construction of a model, carved out by social expectations and the media, whose ethics and morality are publicly scrutinized at every step he takes. Farhadi asks a lot of questions yet offers very few to no answers. It's a film of truths, half-truths, and little lies that resides in the ocean of grey, and it's within this zone lies its emotional core. It's hard to judge who's right and who isn't. There is no winner. But losers, there might be a few.

reviews.author: nick
reviews.text: A Hero is not on the same level as A Separation, or even The Past, but it's still a rather important entry in Asghar Farhadi's glorious filmography. Arguably Farhadi's most outwardly political output to date, A Hero repeats Farhadi's winning formula of everyday moral dilemmas, this time in the social media era.

reviews.author: BananaPudding
reviews.text: Dishonesty is a malady that burns like a forest fire and manufactured empathy is the fuel that further scorch the searing flame. At the risk of sounding awfully similar to an Ehrlich one-liner - Asghar Farhadi's UNCUT GEMS.

reviews.author: Sam Jalali
reviews.text: Given that this is a further refinement of Asghar Farhadi’s career-long obsession with the architecture of moral debt, A Hero feels like a perfect proving ground for his sensibilities in exploring how a singular act of perceived "goodness" can be dismantled by the bureaucratic and social machinery of modern Iran. And as expected from Farhadi, he is always in line with the ways that the economic and institutional pressures of the regime have built impossible expectations for what we perceive as integrity.

reviews.author: Michael James
reviews.text: The master storyteller in Asghar Farhadi returns with yet another powerful and immersive human drama, that’s deceptively simple yet complexly layered. He takes up relatable everyday characters, throws them in significant situations and explores the complicated moral psyche of human minds, through his well written conversational dialogues and terrific character developments. It captures and reflects the contemporary Iranian society mindset effectively, and further keeps the slow burn drama engaging with solid plot twists. A compelling watch.

reviews.text: This honestly feels like a film made purely so Paul Newman and Joanne Woodward could mess around and enjoy themselves for the entire runtime. It’s a silly little goose of a film, nothing particularly groundbreaking in its narrative, but the charm sits squarely in the performances and all the visual trimmings. The plot is basically Newman’s reporter mistaking Woodward’s fashion-family heiress for a high-priced prostitute, though that premise fades into the background pretty quickly because the real highlight is their breezy, joyful chemistry. There’s something refreshingly unpretentious about how the film jumps straight into its playful mood and never pretends to be anything else.

Because on one hand it’s so painfully misogynistic and super phony, but then it has Joanne Woodward playing this super relatable lead who has to choose between joining up in the god awful 60s gender roles or being supremely lonely for the rest of her life. And it’s…. understandable! Woodward is so genuine through this whole thing, it’s sort of amazing how she manages to pull it off considering like literally everything else. And then Newman’s such an awful cad but you also kinda get her attraction because he represents total freedom— she so clearly wants to be him as much as she wants to kiss him. …

Giuliano Gemma is absolutely great in the central role - providing a likable and entertaining centrepiece for the rest of the film to revolve around. The film moves quite slowly, but the central plot is interesting and there's plenty of interplay between the supporting characters. The film doesn't have the bite of later genre entries, but it makes up…

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: A Pistol for Ringo opens with two men approaching one another and facing off in the viscerally familiar pose of gunfighters: shoulders slightly tensed to pull their arms out from their bodies, ready to raise a gun at the slightest twitch from the man they face. Then their postures relax, and the men shake hands and exchange Christmas greetings. With this introduction to Ringo's world, it's no surprise when our first sight of him is of feet on a hopscotch board (court?!), or that the first time we hear his voice, he's arguing with children about hopscotch rules they claim he's violated.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Fans of 2015’s winsome “Shaun the Sheep Movie” would be forgiven for worrying that its sequel might betray the simple pleasures of the original (and the long-running TV series that inspired it). After all, the previous film was about a mischievous sheep traveling to the big city in order to find his missing farmer, and the new one is subtitled “Farmageddon.” But anyone bracing for the stop-motion equivalent of a Michael Bay movie — anyone convinced that Aardman Animations has abandoned the workaday joys of “Wallace and Gromit” in order to chase the hectic spectacle of most contemporary kids’ cinema — has had the wool pulled over their eyes.

But if I stick to the way the tiger becomes a motif in this film, it's something close to an irreducible life-force, a life-force that cannot be denied, a life force that persists against all odds.

Hwang Jung-min is our titular felon, with Gang Dong-won is his reluctant assistant. The other principles include Lee Sung-min as the slimy politician who framed Hwang, and Park Sung-woong as a former colleague who will be responsible for a retrial. His debut would be an interesting double-bill with Salo, his last film; watch as the little, despairing allusions to fascism and forced labour in Accattone become all-consuming terrors.

reviews.author: Edgar Cochran ✝️🍋
reviews.text: An audacious, controversial auteur from the very beginning, providing Bertolucci his first film industry participation as an assistant director, I thought, with all the naivety in the world, that this being Pasolini's debut and an early 60s film, there would be more air to breath and more compassion. Naturally, I was proven wrong, as the auteur explored, since he ever grabbed a camera, the darkest corners of humanity. The film is endlessly depressing, partially derivative from the works and themes of the Italian fathers of Neorealism, but more exploitative from the viewpoint of a morally degraded Rome, relentless towards its characters, in a world where true friendships do not exist and where tragedies are expressed through Bach's music.

reviews.author: Sam Jalali
reviews.text: Although technically the first feature film directed by Pier Paolo Pasolini, Accattone set the foundation for everything that we have come to love most in his provocative and legendary body of work. We nonetheless still recognize it as the definitive blueprint for his cinematic identity. Being his directorial debut, adapted from his own literary explorations of the Roman underworld, Accattone not only has not aged a single day in time but, like all of the most vital works of Italian cinema, its message is one that still resonates with the way the disenfranchised are treated in our world today. Above all, the relentless honesty that Pasolini creates within such a desolate setting results in one of the most hauntingly beautiful…

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: Bound by the life he has been given, Accattone is a saint of circumstance. He is caught in that most vicious cycle of all: poverty, and therefore makes decisions based on where he has found himself. When we first meet him, he is living the high life; wearing a fresh white sweater, a gold chain and a smile. As the picture progresses, he finds his luck slowly beginning to dwindle, but it begs the question: did he ever have any luck to begin with? Or was he placed on this planet to suffer?

reviews.author: Alice
reviews.text: I get it, it's realism, life for poor people was awful in post WWII in Italy. But I can't bring myself to feel anything for the main character, who is effectively a pimp who abuses his poor prostitute and leaves her in the hands of people who beat her up. And yet the focus is on the poor pimp, who we are meant to sympathise with. Yeah, I'm sure life was awful for poor men in post WWII Italy. But it was much much worse for poor women. Pasolini was too complex a person to be addressed in a short Letterboxd review, and I understand you can't read everything through a feminist reading, but I personally find it very hard not to. That being said, from an Italian perspective, it does feel very real and authentic. Unfortunately for Pasolini, sexism has always been intrinsic into Italian culture.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Fellini removing his name from any attachment to this film out of distaste for its script is a bit rich as this really just delivers the coup de grâce on neorealism's best and worst traits after the likes of Rossellini, De Sica and Fellini himself had already dealt mortal blows to the genre. Like Buñuel's Los Olvidados, this punctures neorealism's sanctimony regarding the suffering poor, depicting the people being left out by Italy's postwar recovery as reduced to bestial survivalism, but Pasolini nonetheless approaches this with an empathy that renders its protagonist's vulgar spiral as a kind of passion play, immediately nailing the sacred and profane provocation that would make Pasolini such a lightning rod for the rest of his…

Story wise, it's a predictable assassin for hire revenge thriller, but the execution makes it engaging. Scott Adkins shines in the lead role with his screen presence and action sequences. The hand to hand combat and stunt sequences are the film’s biggest strengths as they were very well choreographed. The brutal fight scenes and dark humour scenes are neatly balanced. The visuals and editing gives the movie a comic book vibe. Background music and screenplay support the fast paced action well. Overall, it’s an entertaining watch.

reviews.text: Fair warning: The dog dies in Peter Flinth’s “Against the Ice,” a turgid survival drama based on the true account of two Danish explorers’ punishing 1909 trek to the north-eastern tip of Greenland. In fact, all of them do — not just Bjørn, the adorable sled puppy who plummets to his doom at the bottom of an Arctic crevice just a few short minutes after fresh-faced engineer Iver Iversen (Joe Cole) makes the mistake of bonding with him by name. The situation later becomes so grim that Iver begins to shoot the weakest dogs and feed their meat to the stronger ones, who will soon be eaten themselves.

reviews.text: When writer-director Nadav Lapid was doing press for his Berlinale-winning “Synonyms” in 2019, he told a funny story about his conflicted approach to the Israeli notions of masculinity and national identity that rage across his films: When his sister-in-law had a baby boy, she asked him for advice as to whether or not they should circumcise the child. “I totally understand if you don’t want your son to be Israeli,” Lapid told her, channeling his late mother’s lifelong hope that her children would leave the country behind. “But if you’re staying in Israel, then be Israeli.”

His formal strengths remain clear, particularly his facility to find a physical dimension to his discontent and there's much to admire in his disposition to keep going way past the point being made. The movie is jusst impossible to separate from his alienated fuck up feelings and the discomfort gives it a stronger dimension.

Der flüssige Animationsstil zeichnet ein dreckiges Science-Fiction-Setting mit futuristischen Elementen zur Erweiterung unseres Daseins. Letzter Punkt kommt in Altered Carbon: Resleeved auf Storybasis aber sichtbar zu kurz und wird kaum ausgebaut. Die Welt dient als optisch grandioses Szenario für einen Sci-Fi-Thriller mit aufregenden und brutalen Action-Sequenzen, lässt durch die flache Charakterzeichnung und mäßige Krimigeschichte sein grundlegendes Potenzial jedoch liegen. reviews.author: JakubM
reviews.text: Altered Carbon, the series, works best when it combines small-scale storytelling with intricate world building. Unfortunately, each of its two seasons stays on that path for maybe a couple episodes before weaving in centuries-old grudges and placing its main characters at the centre of every single person’s existence. The joys of watching a weirdo hard-boiled detective solve murders in this universe are drowned out by an endless raising of stakes. Resleeved tacks the opposite way, thrusting its characters into a minor squabble between yakuza families and ignoring pretty much everything else. It’s exactly what I wanted from the show. But because it’s anime, the whole thing just ends up feeling like an excuse for sick ninja fights. Character quirks and the mystery elements go right out the window. Moral of the story: I’m a miserable grump and impossible to please?

Leider fehlt es dem Film inhaltlich an Biss und war somit für mich nicht mehr als seichte Unterhaltung während meines Trainings am Fahrrad. Die Actionszenen sind gut und vor allem blutig inszeniert, was den Spaßfaktor erheblich steigert, jedoch letzten Endes als größter Pluspunkt nicht genügt um den Film als gut zu bezeichnen. Der Look ist wirklich ansehnlich und besonders die Neonfarben erinnern gelegentlich stark an "Blade Runner 2049". An den Animationsstil muss man sich gewöhnen und ich denke er ist nicht vollkommen optimal umgesetzt, schlecht…

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Let's begin with the costumes: the brides of Christ wear outfits like blood-soaked bandages, with the most imminent red like a menstrual stain. Alucarda is draped in funerary black, while Justina and the other girls are more colorful. The doctor is also an imposing, gaunt blackclad figure. He is serious and somber, unlike the strange Roma-caricatures (in greens and other bright colors, typically). It's easy coding for the most part, but the nuns especially stand out. Those costumes suggest so much, from their medical allusions to their distinct evocation of femininity and the mixed symbolism of menses--blessing or curse, female empowerment or fertility, depending on who is reading or writing it.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: A body horror in which all of the horrifying transformations take place in the psyche of the protagonist. The act of watching and being watched. The male gaze and the constant threat of sex and violence it implies. An exploration of purely cinematic means to communicate the five senses. These ideas could be treated dryly or academically, but here they are communicated through the cinematic language of Italian thrillers of the late 60s and 70s. The movie equivalent of a reduction in cooking, most of the narrative and character detail is stripped away, leaving only the sensual "essence," the most lurid uses of color, sound, music, imagery, and editing employed during that era. It's not the most accessible movie, but I'm still confounded as to why so many genre fans wrote this off as boring or too arty. I find it thrilling and insightful.

reviews.author: Willow Maclay
reviews.text: Cinema of bodies and eyes. Constant male gaze runs throughout commodifying the female body. The lead's sexual awakening and guilt brings notice to the world around her that's watching always. There's pure horror in the nature of the male gaze through the power dynamics at hand, but she reshifts this power finding strength in her own body. Hélène Cattet, Bruno Forzani's homage to giallo pictures of the seventies is experimental in nature. It is broken up into three vignettes of womanhood and finds it's power in images that are constantly shifting and playful in their diversity. It's almost Denis-like in how brilliantly they shoot around bodies in ways both sensual and terrifying. Some of the images are a little unsubtle in their meaning, but the film is so beautiful I'm hard pressed to actually care when everything is this beautiful and consistently engaging.

Kazan's exploration of his own family's culture and how it blends together with that of America's is what makes this a particularly fascinating one to watch. Every lead is rather fine with what material they are given, although the supporting cast could be somewhat better. At times one can already admit that the film is a little bit too long for its own good but Kazan still manages to successfully create an engaging story with the material at hand.

I think the pride comes from how impossible it all seems, but the reason you’re here is because someone did it. You hear the stories from your parents and you can’t believe anyone would do what they did for anything. But you can’t believe it because you’ve never lived in the conditions they lived in. I know America is terrible, but as Kazan later said when defending the film: “To oppressed people, America is still a dream.”

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: I don't know that I've ever seen a film that operates like this? Formally details the psychology of serial murder in uncompromising and unbearably close proximity; documenting this unhinged psychosis with an unpredictable camera that straps itself to the killer's headspace (and body), craning and lurching as it bleeds between the reasoned justifications, erotic impulses, and physical logistics of his decision-making. The ease with which this floats from his mundane inner voice—frequently detailing a history of slights that have inspired his sadism—to his completely clumsy, primal violence with minute awareness of space and procedure is horrifying. Not sure I'll ever watch it again, or ultimately what value it even has with regard to its subject, but it's certainly something to behold.

reviews.text: A dynamic camera that is much lauded mixed with a simmering, ambient score from Klaus Schulze, krautrock god, creates a film at conflict with itself. The soundtrack is haunting, beautiful, and creepy all at once, while the camera work is jarring, abrasive, and intense. The voiceover monologue (think The Cremator) is rambling, but not incoherent, just erratic. This is a skilled crafting of what the urge to kill must be like for the mentally ill afflicted with such a compulsion. Whether it is accurate, I thankfully cannot say, but it is an affecting film.

reviews.text: #SlasherSaturdayMy turn in the rotation to pick the slasher of the week, I went with this Meta-slasher, for it’s eye violence, movie theater setting, movie-within-a-movie narrative, and the iconic Zelda Rubinstein. And I loved it for all of the above reasons even if it’s not the best slasher flick, per se. It’s definitely a little disorienting at first as there isn’t a clear delineation between the film’s narrative and the nested film’s narrative. The blurring seems intentional, though, and once you kind of get your bearings, everything starts to fall into place. A couple of friends are at the local cinema watching The Mommy, where Zelda Rubinstein has tasked her son with collecting people’s eyeballs from….the local cinema. But as…

reviews.author: MJsays
reviews.text: Now this is what I call finding a diamond in the rough. What a brilliantly-crafted, vicious little nightmare. Its narrative structure is unconventional to say in the least, but Anguish is made with so much stylistic gusto it doesn’t even matter if you don’t get what the hell is going on. It literally hypnotises you from the opening scene and pulses through your veins until the beguiling finale. On that note, it also happens to feature one of my new favorite hypnosis sequences EVER. I’m actually baffled that this doesn’t have more of a reputation, especially with genre fans. Honestly, horror films this imaginative and with a subversive flair like this don’t come along very often, so seek it out if you haven’t already. You’ll be thankful. If you don’t, I’m sure Zelda Rubinstein’s ghost will happily haunt you until you change your mind.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Her squirming endears her to the audience. Vulnerability makes her immediately relatable, a viewer of a horror movie as the proxy for the audience viewing a horror movie. She squirms as we squirm at the sight of eyeballs being plucked from skulls, at the metronomic tick, at the quasi-incestuous undertones. She squirms and we squirm. Nearby audience members show her kindness, and it renders both her and them more sympathetic. From this connection, the film blends several narratives and keeps track of them through our avatar on the screen. We watch people watch a film in which someone watches a film in which someone watches a film, but it never feels convoluted. Instead, the impossible loop of narrative only serves…

The twist of the movie is surprising, but ineffective, and it provided no definite justification on why it is the way it is. The film presented us with a muddled reasoning of its creation: multiple extreme racists wants to live in the 1800s for no apparent reason besides being racist…

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: You can tell that something is “off” about the world of Gerard Bush and Christopher Renz’s artful and harrowing but frustratingly half-baked “Antebellum” from the very first shot. An exorcism thriller about the moral inertia of a country that refuses to give up its ghosts, this provocative debut opens with a five-minute oner that wends through a Louisiana plantation with a supernatural grace, as if the slaves, jailers, and soldiers who drift through the frame aren’t going about their lives so much as they’re performing a choreographed roleplay of America’s original sin, like robots following their loops in a horribly problematic new amusement park from the company behind “Westworld.”

reviews.author: Cole Duffy
reviews.text: Brutal. Arctic’s greatest strength is its realism: the survivors aren’t superpowered beings who can overcome anything or sleep in the corpse of a bison, but rather normal people, and it sucks us into the ice-cold world the film presents us with. There’s no tragic backstory, no lengthy exposition, just two people desperately trying to survive. Leading actor Mads Mikkelsen has never been this good before; it’s easily the best performance of his career, all in his eyes and the way he drags his unconscious costar along in a sled. It’s also shot beautifully, letting the beauty of the harsh Arctic come across as alien and barren. What we have here is a solid survival film with some great acting, and it’s a highlight of the calendar year so far.

reviews.text: Arkansas is a rural neo-noir crime thriller that's mellow, quirky, and satisfying. It stars Liam Hemsworth and Clark Duke as Kyle and Swin, two small-time drug dealers who were caught in a drug-deal-gone-wrong situation, with one bad decision after another, they find themselves at the crosshair of a mysterious kingpin, Frog, played by Vince Vaughn. The film has a natural southern charm. Performances included supporting cast John Malkovich, Michael K. Williams, Vivica Fox, all were fantastic. There were 5 chapters, I think it could have been tightening up, the last chapter was drawn out. But I was happy with how it concluded. It's a great directorial debut from actor Clark Duke.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: At 148 minutes, Army of Dead does drag on a bit too long. When it finally arrives at its climax, its deliberate pace vanishes for a frantic, messy finale that isn’t quite as satisfying as it could be. Overall though, this is easily Snyder’s best movie in at least a decade. When Ward fights back tears as he tries to apologize to his daughter for all of the problems he’s caused, one senses that Snyder is pouring his guts out in a much more metaphorical way than is typical of zombie movies. It’s clear we won’t need a Snyder Cut of Army of the Dead. This is a Zack Snyder movie through and through.

reviews.author: Cinema_Strikes
reviews.text: As always, Larry Cohen is the king of the high concept - here, what if you let somebody borrow your insurance and identity to get hospital treatment and they died, turning a little mild insurance fraud into something else. Of course, the plot turns out to be much twistier than that. This is one of Cohen’s last films, and the dialogue is just not there, nor are the Skinemax production values (this feels a bit like an erotic thriller minus the nudity and sex). Not can Crystal Bernard (of Wings) really pull off the lead - she always seems more petulant than desperate. But Judge Reinhold and Traci Lords are fun in supporting roles.

reviews.author: Joe
reviews.text: Written and directed by Larry Cohen, but other than a couple of moments of oddball humor you probably wouldn't know it until the last couple scenes, which finally kick it into a level of sinister energy that it unfortunately lacks before then. The climax, which involves the bad guy being incapacitated with a cloud of the cremated remains of one of his victims, is one for the sizzle reel. If this were a forgotten product of 1940s RKO instead of 1990s USA, it would probably be one of the best ways in the known universe to kill an hour, but this version has Judge Reinhold.

Cohen manejó como nadie el perfil bajo de sus producciones, el aire desenfadado, la autoparodia y la sencillez del que hacía películas para y sobre el ciudadano medio en un Hollywood que entonces estaba obsesionado en reconquistar el mundo con un retorno frankensteiniano del cine épico, de los grandes héroes y los biopics de personajes históricos. reviews.text: One of the most well rounded films I've ever seen. That this was barred from America for having the potential to 'spark race riots' is such a red herring–this shit was barred because it's such a sympathetic and full portrait of Afro-Jamacian life in '80s Brixton. With some really nuanced and fantastic character writing and acting, this really puts you in the shoes of its main character. It flips the script by showing the full and diverse world of the black community–from work, music, different churches, family life, and even some of the ugly side with a scene about gay bullying or implied violence towards women–while the outsiders (white people) are shown strictly as the unpredictable spikes of fringe violence.…

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Rooted to the bloody tissue of real life and enameled with traces of early Jane Campion, “Babyteeth” is the kind of soft-hearted tearjerker that does everything in its power to rescue beauty from pain; the kind that feels like it would lose its balance and tip right off the screen if it stopped being able to walk the line between the two. And yet, despite a handful of shaky moments and a story that sounds like a supercut of all the worst tropes in contemporary independent cinema, Shannon Murphy’s primal and surefooted debut never falls into either mawkishness or sadism. It keeps you on your toes from the moment it starts, brings together a winsome but wounded group of people who are all struggling to slay the “tiny gods” in their heads, and then forces them through an ordeal that might just break their hearts. And yours.

reviews.text: The terminal romance genre is a genre so often occupied by manipulative and schmaltzy trash; however, with Babyteeth, you’ll find a refreshing, wonderfully quirky and heartbreaking teen cancer-romance that isn’t afraid to find comedy amidst tragedy. It’s a film that is wholly honest in its portrayal of a dysfunctional family in constant worry of what the future holds, with Shannon Murphy capturing those feelings in a way that never feel patronizing or manufactured. This is an incredibly unique and tender debut feature that shows what a bright future Murphy has ahead of her. I can’t wait to watch whatever she’ll be doing next!

Aquela pequena casa, recheada de objetos, recortes e fotos, guarda não apenas o segredo da trama de "Bacurau", o filme, mas um aspecto essencial ao espírito do povo que vive na comunidade que o batiza (fictícia, mas muito próxima do real). Aqui, por mais que a embalagem seja o cinema de gênero, a base é bastante autêntica: a identidade do nordestino, o nordestino do interior, das pequenas cidades e povoados. E tudo no filme é de verdade: as estradas, o verde, as pessoas, as crianças, o sotaque,…

reviews.text: In some respects, Kleber Mendonça Filho’s “Bacurau” can be seen as a logical continuation of the Brazilian critic-turned-auteur’s two previous features. Much like 2012’s revelatory “Neighboring Sounds,” for example, “Bacurau” is a patient and sprawling portrait of a Brazilian community as it struggles to defend itself against the dark specter of modernity. And much like 2016’s unshakeable “Aquarius,” “Bacurau” hinges on an immovably stubborn woman who refuses to relinquish her place in the world — who won’t allow our blind lust for the future to bury her meaningful ties to the past.

reviews.text: A completely bonkers movie that begins as a Brazilian social drama, observing the townspeople's cultural rituals and impoverished conditions at the hand of a corrupt mayor with an almost western-inflected sense of community. Beautiful desert and mountain vistas interrupted by small character interactions and location detail that carry a sense of local history as well as their procedures for everyday resistance. But then a shift occurs. There are a few off-kilter tonal and formal details that signal it; a split diopter here, a wild zoom there, but the shift is sudden nonetheless (if you don't want to know more I would suggest not reading further), and by the end, this has somehow transitioned into a full-blown spaghetti western splatter comedy…

reviews.text: What defines a “Bad Boys” movie? It’s been 17 years since the last sequel came out, but some of the key elements are still easy to pin down: You need Will Smith as flashy Detective Sergeant Michael “Mike” Lowery, and Martin Lawrence as his slightly more sedate platonic life partner Detective Sergeant Marcus Burnett. You need Miami in all of its hyper-saturated splendor — nuclear orange skies, bikinis on the boardwalk, and a bass so thick that it seems to bounce the entire city. And you need an unfiltered mega-dose of whatever mutant testosterone has been oozing out of Michael Bay’s every pore since he first hit puberty. We’re talking all three of the big Gs: guns, gangsters, and gay…

reviews.text: One of the best comedic satires of the century, in my book. Kitao Sakurai and Eric André's Cabin Boy. An absurdly hysterical social and filmic commentary created through inconceivable but perfect methods of cinematic magic. Structure and form as spy cameras capturing reactions and moving the characters, or personas, forward. Security images as propellers which drive the roles to their ridiculous "finish." Really though, the film has no beginning or end (in the same sense of the slick transitions between the cameras, tones, etc. used to distinguish multiple aesthetic realities). It amalgamates flawlessly, ultimately existing in the faction of our subconscious aching to see an amusing interruption or disturbance from the colorless status quo.

reviews.text: Bong Joon-ho's most underrated as far as I'm concerned, and his most successful in portraying the absurdity of poverty. Though his films always have a strong political penchant here it manages to be woven at its least-conspicuous but no less is it any pronounced, various depictions of class and its struggles forefronted in its central narrative pull that render the myriad of lower-class responses to their circumstance evident and as such attaining a political comprehension. Whatever absurdity of the upper-class exist, they are de-prioritized in not being depicted; the only existences that matter here are those awaiting false promises to trickle down. In the meantime they bark and bite amongst each other to be the top dog in the bottom rung.

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Bong Joon-ho's debut feature, Barking Dogs Never Bite, is darkly comic but very amusing. As a comedy-drama about killing dogs, I should probably have to hand in my vegan card for enjoying it so much. However it is so compelling and enjoyable and Bong was clearly talented from the outset of his career. There's loud music and fun camerawork, and the plot is both funny and weirdly moving. Bong's usual undercurrent of socially conscious themes is present here, through depictions of poverty and the corruption of academia. There are also ideas about gender, as one man is emasculated and a pregnant woman faces discrimination. Barking Dogs Never Bite is not as refined and as sharply intelligent as Bong Joon-ho's later films, but it is nevertheless an intriguing and entertaining piece.

reviews.author: Matheus Fiore
reviews.text: Eu tenho pra mim que o Bressane, junto de caras como Nelson Pereira dos Santos, Jorge Ben, Nelson Rodrigues e Zagallo, entendeu o Brasil como eu jamais vou conseguir. E o Bressane fez isso justamente na época em que as características definidoras do nosso povo e da nossa nação pairavam no ar, até o momento em que tudo ganhou forma pelo futebol barroco da Seleção de 70. Em Olavo tá tudo lá, cidade e campo, afeto e ódio, violência e paz, as contradições sociais e culturais dando vida a todos os espaços filmados.

reviews.author: igor nolasco
reviews.text: Os últimos dez minutos desse filme são uma preciosidade. O cinéma vérité antropofágico, um cinema hermético que não se restringe à uma masturbação intelectual e envereda-se pelas ruas e pelo povo. É Helena Ignez em seu vestido de bolinhas chocando as senhorinhas de Copacabana, é um grupo de criancinhas que sorri e acena para a câmera enquanto o texto é recitado em tela, é o caos urbano mostrado de forma propriamente caótica - como deve ser - em detrimento de uma falsa realidade maquilada e ensaiada. O experimentalismo de Bressane, de Sganzerla, da Bel Air, é fascinante.

reviews.author: SeanAloysius
reviews.text: Com Bressane passamos a ter certeza de que a "pequena forma" engloba - e, portanto, contém - a "grande". A partir disso, que é o mesmo que dizer "a partir de determinado ponto entre o final dos anos 60 e o começo dos 70", os filmes de Bressane passaram a ser o lugar ideal (o lugar livre) para armazenagem e eternização dos maiores sons de cinema: grunhidos, sons de vento, repetições de frases soltas, músicas de filmes esquecidos, músicas de filmes bastante lembrados, Roberto Carlos "lado b", Rádio Nacional, boleros retirados dos discos de vinil de um morto, todos lançados sobre as imagens, contraindo ou estendendo o escopo. Este inventário - que aqui está mais para "arsenal" - é o centro nervoso destes trabalhos: são esses sons - e talvez apenas eles - que podem nos fazer entender, ter um lampejo ou ver flanando diluído na luz o sentido do que é montagem.

reviews.text: And here I thought the budget for Robot Holocaust was bottom of the barrel. This is a movie that knows it has absolutely nothing in its hand and still decides to go all in anyway. From the endless supply of terrible miniatures, reject Gamorrean guards, Mad Max wannabes and the cutest lil' stop-motion octopus grasshopper monster, Galaxy aka Galaxy Destroyer aka Battle for the Lost Planet plays out like a cheap student film you once made with your friends over a couple weekends. If you go in with that mindset, it makes for an extremely amusing watch, though be warned: there are frequent dull lulls which may test your patience before something stupid happens and it becomes interesting again.

It's interesting to note the different feel between a little film like this reaching for the stars and its sequel which feels impoverished because it got more money behind it. Someone else said this feels like an adaptation of a HEAVY METAL comic and that's perfect.

reviews.text: Es geht ja also doch. Nicht nur in Italien wurden in den siebziger Jahren Actionthriller-Reißer produziert, sondern eine Handvoll auch in Deutschland. Dieser Streifen, der wohl als besondere Rarität anzusehen ist, hat alles was man sich für dieses Genre wünscht: Spannung, Action, kurzweiliger Aufbau. Entstanden 1973 unter der Regie von Jürgen Roland, fühlt man sich direkt von Beginn an in die damalige Zeit versetzt. Wohl kaum ein anderer Hamburg-Film ist so lebhaft actionreich in Szene gesetzt, wie "Zinksärge für die Goldjungen". Aber der Filmintellektuellen, der es ab den 70ern geschafft hat, der deutschen Filmindustrie die Daumenschrauben anzulegen und damit eine gesunde Entwicklung zu stolzen deutschen Genrestoff verhinderte, würde ich gerne mit den beiden "Profis aus Fernost" in einen Raum einsperren.

reviews.author: Björn Becher
reviews.text: Starker deutsch-italienischer Poliziotteschi. Henry Silva spielt einen italienisch-amerikanischen Gangsterboss, der mit seiner Gang (darunter auch – einfach nur für etwas Abwechslung bei der Action - zwei asiatische Kampfsportler) in Hamburg einfällt, um sich die Stadt unter den Nagel zu reißen und die lokale Gangstergröße Otto Westermann und dessen „Kegelclub“ zu vertreiben. Dazu kommt aber noch ein bisschen „Romeo und Julia“, weil sich die Tochter des Amerikaners und einer der Söhne des Deutschen (Horst Janson eher flach als blonder Schönling), die beide mit den krummen Geschäften ihres Vaters nichts zu tun haben wollen, ineinander verlieben.

reviews.author: Dmitry_Karpyuk
reviews.text: История борьбы жабы с гадюкой, немца с внешностью Дмитрия Быкова и итальянца (Генри Силва) за власть в Гамбурге. Параллельно с мафиозными разборками развивается романтическая линия их детей, своего рода версия "Ромео и Джульетты", причем сынка играет будущий Капитан Кронос, который выйдет уже на следующий год. Несколько трэшово и с обилием тёрок в интерьерах, но всё равно динамично, а погоня на катерах в финале даже впечатляет. Снято немцем и существует ещё и немецкая версия, сильнее отцензурированная и с другой музыкой — спасибо, нам это не надо.

reviews.author: Dirk Senger
reviews.text: Jürgen Roland haut hier einen astreinen Pulp-Streifen auf Groschenroman-Niveau raus, der zwar in Hamburg spielt, aber dort leider größtenteils an den falschen Schauplätzen. Es ist schon ein Unterschied, ob in einem Gangsterfilm ein Auto in den Straßenschluchten von New York hochgejagt wird oder in der Nähe der Barmer Ersatzkasse und einem Spar-Supermarkt in der Perle des Nordens. Immerhin sind die Auto- und Motorbootstunts ziemlich geil und Henry Silvas Hackfresse ist immer gerne gesehen. Eher zum piepen ist Horst Janson, der wohl direkt vom "Der Bastian"-Dreh rübergekommen ist, selbstredend in Jeans-Buxe und -Hemd. Ihm wird auch die Eigensynchro gegönnt, während alle anderen Nebenfiguren übelst von anderen Sprechern übertont werden. Der Score steht dem in nichts nach und hört sich nach grausamen Hintergrundsgedudel aus dem Zirkus Krone an.Trotz und wegen der Unzulänglichkeiten aber eine Spaßkanone erster Kajüte. Wann sieht man schon eine Hauptdarstellerin in einem kanariengelben Overall, der so eng getragen ist, dass sich im Schritt ein Cameltoe bildet ?

reviews.text: This film is cited (on Wikipedia and elsewhere) as influencing German hip hop culture, which is surprising for several reasons. The first is quite simply that, growing up with an American view of hip hop, the idea of European hip hop culture is always surprising. Though of course America's pop culture saturates the entire world, the idea of art like hip hop having an impact back in 1984 suggests a pace of saturation far faster than expected. Besides, hip hop is as American as, uh, I dunno, all the rest of pop music.

reviews.author: Quiller
reviews.text: Fresh! How else to describe this hip-hop musical, set and filmed in New York City’s outer boroughs just as hip-hop’s wider culture was beginning to spread globally? (Beat Street was one of several movies released internationally in 1983 and ‘84 that incorporated breakdancing into their choreography.) The story is slight, and the acting occasionally amateurish. But the film’s heart is in the right place. Director Stan Lathan and producer Harry Belafonte make an effort to understand hip-hop on its own terms instead of shoehorning it insistently into existing pop narratives. When the film shows us the social milieu of its South Bronx setting, it feels very authentic. As a time capsule that captures some early hip-hop artists’ misgivings about the…

It's also worthwhile for a rare Duane Jones role. Not the meatiest of parts, but given how few movies he did, it's always nice to see him.

Soon, he realises not just that strings are being pulled around him, but that he, too, can pull strings - something he does rather shamelessly to ensure his girlfriend Betty (Vera Miles) gets top billing in a music show. reviews.text: A delightful film in which Bob Hope provides a loose portrayal of colorful New York City Mayor, Jimmy Walker. He presents a sympathetic image, often showing him as in tune with the needs of the average voter. One great scene has him attending a banquet, where the audience is of an unknown ethnic origin. An introduction in a language he doesn't recognize provides no help, so he keeps dropping the names of ethnic heroes until he finally stumbles upon the right community and the audience applauds in approval. Pretty good script with some raw political realities between the wisecracks. Recommended.

reviews.text: A massive hit in its native Korea, “Believer” is a wild and boisterous crime drama that’s evenly split between romanticizing the back-and-forth between cops and robbers, and lamenting the pointlessness of that endless pursuit. Directed by Lee Hae-young, a rising talent whose distaste for half-measures was already on full display in his previous work (e.g. 2015’s “The Silenced”), the film espouses a violent commitment to both sides of that coin — the fun of the chase, and the hollow pain that someone feels when it finally catches up to them.

reviews.author: WraithApe
reviews.text: The synopsis I read likened Believer to Oldboy, but that's a lazy comparison at best. There's an element of revenge but nothing like the highly stylized carnage Chan-wook Park offers up. Instead, it's a subterfuge-fuelled, darkly humorous police procedural - an undercover cop in pursuit of an elusive drugs kingpin. The twist is telegraphed from some way off, but it's not really about that anyway; it's more of a slowly dawning realization that Won-ho (Jin-woong Cho) has been barking up the wrong tree the whole time.

A kinetic blast of jazzy goodness and some rollicking good tunes, especially one raucous duet between two pirate skeletons that had me rolling. It goes without saying anymore that Deaf Crocodile curates the absolute best in animation from around the globe. This has to be my new favorite! If you have ANY interest in animation, you owe it to yourself to see this one.

reviews.text: It's so refreshing to dive into something I have zero knowledge on - this is so kaleidoscopic and joyful and vibrant! Anthony White's review really hits the nail on its head; Benny's Bathtub is a perfect distillation of all the wonderful insanity you can only achieve through animated filmmaking. Not only through its creative techniques - the use of photo backgrounds, the painted textures, the constant morphing / use of visual metaphor - but in its content. It's a film where a Norm MacLaren-style tangent can coexist with Woody Woodpecker and a pedo ornithologist. To directors Jannik Hastrup and Flemming Quist Møller, everything is equal in their cartoon melting pot - it's a beautiful kind of maximalism.

reviews.text: I have not sought out information on this film, but every bit I've ever heard/read focused on two things: the length of it and the epilogue's sharp turn into madness. What I had not heard before (and what I suspect is bandied about in more in-depth reviews that I just hadn't read) is that this is Fassbinder at his visual best. It's wrapped in shadows, tilted and framed through bars, around corners, and beneath its subjects. It captures the bleak beauty of Berlin in the throes of depression and nascent fascism. Had it been a shorter film, I would have screencapped it.

reviews.author: Will Steele
reviews.text: Rainer Werner Fassbinder’s magnum opus is anything but easy viewing. Despite its appearance on the Sight & Sound Top 250, the broad runtime and episodic chapters firmly situate Berlin Alexanderplatz as an early example of auteurist television. Cinema is not the medium through which this vast story could or should be told, but that didn’t stop Fassbinder delivering a cinematic statement within a televisual format just as potent as his other great works.

reviews.text: In the mediocre production scene of the late 1950s, Big Deal on Madonna Street has the merit of demonstrating that even in Italy it is possible a cinema that goes beyond dialectal sketching, entertaining with intelligence and good taste. The result of the thematic, stylistic and professional maturity acquired by Mario Monicelli with some previous works, the film tells the hilarious story of a gang of petty thieves who decide to organize in a meticulous way a big "scientific heist". The director, here also a screenwriter together with Age & Scarpelli and Suso Cecchi D'Amico, relies on a very fast pace and a barrage of irresistible gimmicks, but his work goes far beyond the farcical reinterpretation of some famous caper movies…

reviews.text: Anti-Rififi.* You know that one scene in The Nice Guys, when Ryan Gosling’s private detective tries to break into a building? The savvy professional wraps his hand in a protective napkin and goes to punch through a window, and in doing so he slices an artery in his wrist - the film then cuts to him struggling in an ambulance, bleeding profusely, hooked up to a ventilator about to pass out. Always loved that joke. How it plays with our expectations, knowing full well that we’ve seen similar break-in scenes a million times in a million other flicks. Big Deal on Madonna Street is basically a full-length movie version of that joke. And it’s goddamn brilliant.

reviews.text: "Big Man on Campus" is a 1989 comedy directed by Jeremy Kagan. In an absurdist retelling of Victor Hugo's 1931 novel "The Hunchback of Notre-Dame", the film centers around a hunchbacked character named Bob Maloogaloogaloogaloogalooga (one "Malooga" and four "loogas" as he puts it) who inhabits a tower on the UCLA college campus. While Hugo's story is far more the dramatic formulation, "Big Man on Campus" is an ironic college comedy that essentially turns its character into a caveman or a missing link for study.

reviews.text: Well...wow! What a documentary! Billie Eilish: The World’s A Little Blurry is absolutely stunning. The documentary showcases her life and outstanding abilities perfectly, delving deep into her mind, creating one of the most grounded and intimate documents of a celebrity I’ve ever seen. Her bond with her family (especially Finneas O'Connell) is admirable and the way director R. J. Cutler pieces it all together, splicing monologues alongside her songs, truly allows for a transfixing watch for its entirety. The documentary as a whole feels so personal, so meaningful and is executed in such a brilliant way that I was left stunned. I honestly wasn’t prepared to like this as much as I did but it truly is a great documentary and dare I say it... one of the best I’ve ever seen. 2021 Releases Ranked

reviews.author: RanchoTuVu
reviews.text: "Black Heat" aka "The Murder Gang" is a sleazy 70s crime drama set in Las Vegas directed by Al Adamson. It features Russ Tamblyn in a nasty role as Ziggy, the criminally mean leader of a criminal gang. Aside from a few scenes of the Strip everything is sleazy hotel rooms and tacky apartments peppered with distasteful acts of violence. There's a couple of private card games tucked away in cheap apartments and you know those gambling debts gotta be repaid one way or another. Four sevens beats three aces and two jacks. The writing is mostly bad so I guess that would have a deleterious effect on the acting, but it doesn't change the basic fact that "Black Heat" still drags you into the sleaze as well as any movie can.

His body is claimed by a woman named Mrs Gorgandy, who wants to keep the corpse in prime condition in order to sell it to a local surgeon (there’s good money in a cadaver, you see; it’s “how she…

reviews.text: An odd, long forgotten entry in the filmography of Ken Loach, whose movie career sadly didn't exactly take off straight away after the masterpiece that was Kes. A children's period adventure film based on a novel by Leon Garfield, at first glance this isn't exactly in line with Loach's more socially conscious work but just like the aforementioned Kes it is told from a child's perspective with attention to realism, employing an unfussy, docu-style approach to storytelling that meanders and often lingers on the more ordinary details of 18th century Yorkshire life.

reviews.text: I'm a huge fan of Ken Loach but this adaptation of an 18th century children's adventure/first love story really shows the lack of time and budget he had to make this film.It's quite an endearing story but Loach's signature 'authentic naturalistic performances from non-professionals' doesn't really work here and the whole thing just looks amateurish. The picture is dark, and the sound is muddy, and the titular Jack is a minor character who is French with very little English - a change from the book that seems to have been made because some of the funding came from France.I was still interested in the story of Tolly and Belle, but the film reminded me of the Children's Film Unit productions that used to be shown on Channel 4 in the eighties.

reviews.text: Ken Loach's third film for cinema release is a near forgotten feature based on a Leon Garfield book his children had enjoyed. It's an unusual project for Loach (certainly in light of his later works we have come to know and love) it's inception seems to stem from two things; the first being that following the success of the previous film, 1971's Family Life, across Europe, producer Tony Garnett secured funding for the National Film Finance Corporation by making Black Jack a co-production with France (this also led to Jean Franval's casting as the titular Jack, changing the character's nationality to French) The second being the fact that Kes had delighted and spoken to working class children everywhere. As such…

reviews.author: ciaran_vallely
reviews.text: While at first glance Black Jack would seem a bit of an outlier in Loach's career, there are definitely connections to his wider filmography. A focus on the powerless, especially their struggle against the establishment. A natural, hyper realistic style. Loach continually walks that line between having his movies play out in a conventional/traditional style, and seemingly just letting his camera wander through a scene that he has come across by accident. And his preoccupation with putting "non-actors" at the centre of his movies, and still getting good performances from them are all on display here.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: A strange children's picaresque that at first seems such a departure for Loach, but his realist framing occasionally takes on borderline magical whimsy, while the frequent refrains of poor hustlers and image-conscious landed gentry dancing around each other warily fits this strange departure into his wheelhouse (and even makes for some pitch-black comedy). It's not particularly surprising, but on the strength of this, Loach could be a fine interpreter of Dickens.

reviews.author: Dennis Vehlen
reviews.text: 'Black Jack' (though I prefere the more exploitive German title 'On Your Knees Django, and Lick my Boots') is a mean spaghetti western that gets pretty much everything right. The direction and camera work are on point, the soundtrack is great and the violence is brutal and sadistic. I especially like how the revenge is executed in a more personal way, paying the villains back the same things they did before. Though villains is a strong word here, because almost every character in this movie is a hateful bastard to begin with and Robert Woods is hardly playing a hero either.It's probably my favorite western performance by Woods so far. He fully uses his Giuliano Gemma & George Hilton -esque screen presence as the anti-hero who is out for revenge after his men cripple him and rape & kill his sister - his manic laughter and menacing slow walk with a stick make him one of the more memorable spaghetti avgengers.

reviews.author: Chris Hughes
reviews.text: Roy Williams Neil’s voodoo horror film Black Moon is well made, but it’s saggy. The plot revolves around Juanita (Dorothy Burgess) who is the daughter of white colonialists who were killed on a Caribbean island by the natives. Years later she’s compelled to return to the island with her daughter and their nanny Gail (Fay Wray.) Concerned about the whole situation, Juanita’s husband Stephen (Jack Holt) sets off for the islands to bring his wife and daughter back. But he’s too late. Juanita has come under the spell of voodoo and is involved in the sacrifice of a native woman.

reviews.text: BLACK MOON contains elements of WHITE ZOMBIE, I WALKED WITH A ZOMBIE and NIGHT OF THE EAGLE. And, not unlike most movies that have voodoo as part of the plot, it is rife with suggestions that "practitioners" are ignorant.

Basically, Dorothy Burgess responds to a trauma in her own past by embracing voodoo and rejecting the white middle class values of her husband, Jack Holt. If you squint hard enough, maybe you can read the film against the grain and identify with Burgess and the natives staging a rebellion against the island’s racist planters, at least until things go off the rails at the end.

Blind Beast shares similarities with The Laughing Woman, but it amps up the depravity significantly (in true Japanese genre cinema fashion). The ending is really the stuff of nightmares and the only way this kinky torture drama could have concluded.

reviews.author: V. Lepistö
reviews.text: Starts out as thriller but suddenly takes unexpected paths and becomes one of the greatest pieces of sexual horror ever in silver screen. Like with Red Angel, Masumura slowly strips the characters naked. Stuck in a cave of grotesque fantasies, the twisted play takes stage. It is sexual nightmare, horror film, twisted tale of love, commentary on sexual obsession which I suspect isn't that alien theme to Japanese society... The idea of "touching as art" also provides some very dark humor. It doesn't follow any rules because rules are our invention. It simply follows obsession which leads to the point of no return, point that we all are afraid to admit that is there; our inner bestiality.

reviews.author: Rafael "Mister Movie" Jovine
reviews.text: For some reason, I thought coming in this was going to be a yakuza movie, but it ended up being more like an artsy erotic movie where our two protagonists start rambling a lot about art, life, and sex. Our titular character is also horny AF and spends most of the film touching the woman’s boobs. And from time to time, the dude’s noisy mom pops up here and there as the creepy momma she is. I did like the ending though; I really loved how Masumura used the power of suggestion to make the scene even more effective, making me look away. Also, the production design and the cinematography are hands-down the greatest aspects of the film.

reviews.text: Marginally interesting in the first act as this sort of transgressive horror/thrillerish study of art vs morality, then becomes pretty enveloping as an Oedipal thing, but by that third act I was totally exhausted and pretty much checked out of the whole sadopsycho deal. If these masochists are content to fuck, bite, beat, stab and dismember themselves to death, why should I give a shit?? Not that it never happens (e.g see: In the Realm of the Senses) but it’s incredibly hard to get me to care about these kinds of stories and people; and the film doesn’t do all that much to try and convince me to, as it is much more focused on the-ultimate-climax-agony/ecstacy-oblivion-of-psychosexual-debauchery blah blah blah stuff…

The Oedipal complex is complementary, but not unnecessary, as it is seen during the last unforgettable chapters.

reviews.text: The eyes are the window to the soul and the means of experiencing the outside world. Yasuzō Masumura's Blind Beast takes us on a depraved journey into pure self indulgence; touch and personal sensation the only route to individual pleasure. The film takes a real minimalist approach - just three characters, a mostly single location and clear presentation of the central themes. This is juxtaposed against some truly surreal and ornate set design - the titular character's world populated by giant fleshy sculptures dedicated to the female form. A tribute to a world that he cannot fully experience. Art his only release. The drama between the three characters and exploration of the central themes makes up the backbone of the…

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Blind Beast" is a 1969 Japanese Pinku film from director Yasuzō Masumura. Still within the first wave of the pinku films movement, "Blind Beast" holds a close perceptional build with late 60's arthouse energy, as this was within a time when the genre was also an insertion point of film that was driven for a niche group but mirrored the major genre movements of the time. Many pinku films easily have an appearance that would match of other works but be uniquely unto themselves, as "Blind Beast" is securely one that does this. Before seeing this film, I had only seen Masumura's "Giants and Toys" (1958) which I wholeheartedly love in my viewing experience of blending commercialism and western commerce…

reviews.text: The most evocative moments of this film are the beginning, just after our lead wakes up in the blind man's studio and finds herself surrounded by eyes, breasts, and other stone body parts protruding from the wall, and at the end, as everything falls apart, so to speak. In between, we have a psychological drama/horror that sees our heroine attempt some cunning escape plans and experience bizarre, artful torments. It's got a few questionable moments (and one huge one), but it is a disturbing and effective film.

reviews.author: CinemaSerf
reviews.text: Set during the Grand Inquisition, this is actually quite an entertaining little bit of Peplum. The Doge of Venice (Feodor Chaliapin Jr) has a handsome young son "Sandrigo" (Lex Barker) who has managed to irritate the Inquisitor "Zeno" (Guy Madison). The latter decides to frame the former for treason, and now it falls to Barker to save both himself and his father, whilst still keeping hold of his lady love "Leonora" (Alessandra Panaro). Luigi Capuano has packed quite a lot into ninety minutes here. The production standards are actually quite high, there is bundles of intrigue and swordplay, a soupçon of romance and Madison plays well as the baddie. The plot is pretty processional, the ending is never in doubt - but this is still quite a watchable action adventure that looks good and flows well.

reviews.author: Weirdlingwolf
reviews.text: Ahoy, matey's!!! Expect far more than the ship's mainbrace to get spliced on this ill-fated pleasure cruise to Hawaii! There's titillating T & A and hot snatches of gore, in Frank Mitchel's cult 70s psycho slasher 'Blood Voyage'. The 1st seafaring slasher has groovy-looking 70s chicks, hirsute alpha dudes, soapy Agatha Crispy theatrics, and salty seamen! Forget about turgid landlubber, Mike Myers, this sinisterly ship-stalking shipmate is where its at! With the directors hand's rock steady at the tiller, this bracingly brine-lashed, bikini-splashed blood-spiller is a killer diller! Not one for the anchors that poo-poo vintage Grindhouse goodness, as 'Blood Voyage' is a yacht better B-slasher than the neg-heads would have you believe.

reviews.text: This is reality fabricated to brilliant effect. reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: One of the preeminent works of the Hong Kong New Wave, Boat People is a shattering look at the circumstances that drove hundreds of thousands of Vietnamese refugees to flee their homeland in the wake of the Vietnam War, told through images of haunting, unforgettable power. Three years after the Communist takeover, a Japanese photojournalist (George Lam) travels to Vietnam to document the country’s seemingly triumphant rebirth. When he befriends a teenage girl (Season Ma) and her destitute family, however, he begins to discover what the government doesn’t want him to see: the brutal, often shocking reality of life in a country where political repression and poverty have forced many to resort to desperate measures in order to survive.

reviews.author: ablackie
reviews.text: The story behind Boat People is fascinating: it was shot in Hainan, becoming the first Hong Kong production to film in mainland China, with the permission of a PRC government that had recently fought a war with Vietnam, and was therefore eager to capitalise on anti-Vietnamese propaganda. It's a reconstructed vision of the country in 1978, based on refugee accounts and comprehended through the eyes of an outsider, both literally and figuratively - the protagonist, a Japanese photographer, is an obvious stand-in for director Ann Hui, and it takes time to adjust to the strangeness of the cast speaking Cantonese as a substitute for Vietnamese. A thoughtful exercise in comprehending a then-unknown and closed society entirely through second-hand accounts, but ultimately there is something inescapably artificial and contrived about its construction and execution.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: One of the more blunt and brutal depictions of forced migration and post-war reconstruction I think I've ever seen. A work of clear-eyed and empathetic misery grounded in the perspective of a foreign photojournalist in order to give an observational naturalism and realism to the more viscerally disturbing details here: the usual poverty, corruption, prostitution, police brutality/executions of a movie like this joined by grenade/mine-exploded children and labor camp massacres, and a last-minute immolation for good measure (Sequences so upsetting to watch they immediately resulted in accusations of tasteless propaganda-driven exaggeration even at the time.) But even more fascinating is how that same perspective allows her to mirror her own complicated artistic role in developing a meticulously researched and yet…

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: The contrast between the freshly painted, not lavish but nonetheless clean and statically filmed interiors of officials and the rawer shooting of areas still marked by a half-century of war and destitution hints at how hastily the facade of normalcy has been erected, which the photographer Akutagawa notices quickly. It's easy to suggest that the film is anti-communist (though how people have managed to juggle the idea that it's both anti-communist and pro-1980s China is beyond me), but it seems more accurate to say that because Hui remains so resolutely within the POV of her foreigner protagonist, the increasing horror he witnesses is less particular to a system than the accumulation of a long and harrowing history. As Nguyen, one…

The US had previously offered financial support for France during the First Indochina War; France wishing to reclaim its former colonies lost to Japan and the US seeking to contain the spread of communism in South East Asia a la domino theory. The liberation of Saigon on April 30, 1975 and subsequent reunification of Vietnam was met with great hostility by the US, who proceeded to impose harsh sanctions and cut all diplomatic ties against a newly-independent, war-torn country dealing with infrastructural devastation,…

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: This one was almost too tragic for me. It's about how Vietnam struggled to get back on its feet after the Vietnam War, a dark but sympathetic struggle, but it's also about how the battered and broken Vietnam government oppressed both refugees and its own citizens during this slow recovery, raising itself by climbing the wreckage of its own desperation and perching atop a growing pile of corpses, building the foundation of its new society from the suffering of its own people. It's not just about a particular historical victim but also about how victims defer their victimization when they're backed into a corner, spreading it like a plague, salting their own fields.

reviews.author: Sean Fennessey
reviews.text: The Not-So-Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie. It occurred to me as I was watching again for the first time in a while that I’m now the same age as Robert Culp’s character, a privileged self-serious sophisticate living comfortably in Los Angeles with his urbane wife and high-toned friends as they acclimate to their Esalen-learned emotional elevation/hoodoo. The New Hollywood classics hit different the older you get. I adore Dyan Cannon in this, it’s amazing to think this is her first big film role and the first thing she did professionally after divorcing Cary Grant (33 years her senior). Mazursky’s balance between unease and enlightenment is so graceful but fearless, I really admire what he was up to at this time—none of the self-flagellating psychological violence that his peers were after. It’s all grounded dramedy, realistic but heightened, sexy but ordinary, full of broken characters gluing themselves back together.

Steckler's character is private detective Charles Smith, hired to locate a cat burglar played by Carolyn Brandt who stole a stash of heroin from Big Mack, a pusher. reviews.author: FakeVoorhees
reviews.text: While I enjoy Mystery Science Theater 3000, I think there are a number of films that have had their reputation unfairly tainted by being featured on it. First, there's the general assumption that any movie done by MST3K is a bad movie. The films featured are guilty by association. Then, there's the edits made for content and time to fit MST3K's format that alter the original movie. And, of course, there's the riffing throughout the movie. This all makes it difficult to accurately judge a movie based solely on its MST3K version. When watched separately and judged on their own merits, many of these movies really are not that bad.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: A thoroughly Barthelmean romp. Chefs-knife satire that piles on the ironies and sociological vitriol; viewing trauma, cultural programming, bigotry, secrets-and-lies-based genteelism, etc. via an audacious wit and transgressive scathe, complete with those sudden bursts of violence and fanaticism Cohen would go on to make his bread ‘n butter. But it all feels more urgent here, much moreso than in later works. With timeless relevance and an ingenious final sequence, few film show the perturbingly bizarre, hypocritical and deeply troubled, deluded mechanisms of the USA in all their incongruous absurdity quite like Bone does. As American as apple pie.

Black man Bone appears at this couple’s poolside in mere flashes of a second as they desperately hang on to hear if the exterminator picks up on the other end. Our disheveled anti-hero simply reaches in and pulls the rat out, only to then terrorize the couple for their wealth. Lines of questioning bring the couple sudden anxiety of…

reviews.text: A faint call to prayer, intensifying. Glimpses of future and past - grave digger's skull, a vulture perching among shards of glass, the drowned body of yourself, as you were and may be again. Cranial eclipse and volcanic spume draw a father's son back to a forgotten, primordial battleground. Djinns take shape, Shaytans lurk; the deformed dwarf and the old man of the caves, omnipresent fire-breathing master, a conflagration to be doused with music, fighting fire with flute. Tiered salt pools reflect the chimerical light, scene of original sin; a curse, birthed moth-like, maggot-swamped and blood-encrusted, overseen by the great, ghostly baboon. The dreamer awakens, to claim his birthright.

There's a djinn in there too, and snake handcuffs, and somebody gives birth to a giant moth, maybe.

Of the three, this is the most impenetrable -- less narrative-heavy than the Friedkin and far more restrained than the Kuei, using the gorgeous Turkish landscapes and flute score to sketch out its strange, impressionistic nightmare story. I don't think I've ever seen a Charlie Daniels Band music video quite like it.

reviews.author: Sam Van Hallgren
reviews.text: In Chuck Klosterman's new book (But What If We're Wrong), he talks about how films inevitably reveal more about when they were made as opposed to the time they were made about. So true with this one. In 1989, Vietnam was still The Last War; and as the Cold War, too, was coming to and end, audiences at the time could be forgiven for believing that Vietnam might just be the LAST war. Because lessons were learned. And there is no better illustration of that belief than the final minutes of this film - a celebration of the anti-war movement's taking part in the 1976 Democratic convention. 17 years and a couple of wars later it seems a confoundingly anti-climactic…

The film was always going to live or die based on how everything came together and sadly too little is explained, making this another thriller with a WTF ending but with no real satisfaction. With non-existent production values, poor picture quality and bad makeup effects, it's hard to recommend Breathing Room to even the die hard fans of one-room thrillers (of which I am one).

reviews.text: Bruce Springsteen might never get old, but he sure as hell isn’t getting any younger. Seventy-one this past September and fresh off a sublime Broadway run that saw him burnish his own myth by stepping out of its shadow, the Boss still looks like he’s 45, reflects on the past like he’s 90, and plays the guitar like he’s immortal. And yet time is catching up with him all the same, if only through his friends. E Street Band co-founder Danny Federici died in 2008, followed by saxophonist Clarence Clemons in 2011; when former Castiles legend George Theiss succumbed to lung cancer in 2018, Springsteen became the last surviving member of his first band.

reviews.text: Many of the features you'd expect to see in a blaxploitation film are present in Arthur Marks' film. Characters that feel like anti-heroes in many ways, cinematography with distinct tones, and a fantastic soundtrack all contribute to this film's success. But, in my opinion, what makes this film so unique is the way it subverts itself, making you assume it will go in one direction and criticize something just to wind up with a completely different film in the second half. The concept of "abuse of authority" and "corruption of power" prevails, but the setting is not the one we were presented with.

reviews.author: teamgal
reviews.text: Director Arthur Marks has a great eye and the ability to work very economically. In his film's opening minutes, he manages to remind audiences of IN THE HEAT OF THE NIGHT, immediately letting us know we're in a town knee deep in racism. What's great about the script here is that we get the opportunity to watch two revenge films for the price of one. The entire cycle of oppression and wrong-doing, followed by violent comeuppance, is fully played out twice. As a matter of fact, the film's first 45 minutes (which follows the narrative one expects — corrupt white cops abusing the African-American citizenry) moves at such a break-neck pace that it's exhilarating. The film's second act (blacks take the place of the dead white pigs, and are just as cut-throat) swaps out racism for capitalist-critique.
