reviews.text: Man, this is a really fun one. A spooky and somewhat campy supernatural house movie that serves as a very obvious inspiration for The Shining and slow burns itself into a haunting stasis before nosediving out the window with a ludicrous ending courtesy of Karen Black doing her absolute darnedest. Oliver Reed and Bette Davis are great, too. I’ve seen it portrayed as a commentary on materialism destroying the American family, but I prefer it to just be a kooky forgotten pulp magazine story whose foreboding atmosphere signals the start of Fall. A perfect movie to watch with the windows open and the brisk air whistling as the leaves swirl and change color.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Burnt Offerings is a haunted house movie with a difference, given there's no ghost as such. The title doesn't give much away, and indeed the film doesn't either as it slowly builds towards the conclusion. The film was clearly an influence on The Shining as it shares so much in common. Burnt Offerings is perhaps a little slow and subtle and that's probably why it never found itself with true classic status. There's a lot going for it, however. The atmosphere is heavy and foreboding and the film is always interesting and mysterious, even when there isn't much happening. The central cast is great, with Oliver Reed, Karen Black and Bette Davis. Reed in particular is surprisingly suttle in the central role. The conclusion is very well done and worth the wait. I wish a bit more had been made of the house itself but still; this is an effective horror film and worth seeing.

reviews.text: Tadashi Imai's Bushido: The Cruel Code of the Samurai is perhaps one of the most direct takedown of the myth of Bushido. It covers 350 years of Japanese history and spans seven generations of a single family. It starts out in modern day Japan and concerns a young salaryman named Iikura (Kinnosuke Nakamura). His fiance has tried to commit suicide by taking sleeping pills (for a reason unknown to the audience) and he is beside himself. He seems to feel guilty about something he did and to take his mind off the situation he reads his family records that have been discovered at a temple. Each entry he reads is depicted as a short vignette with Nakamura playing the role…

reviews.author: Chevalier
reviews.text: One of the greatest most underrated masterpieces of japanese cinema. Brutal, and depressing as hell, like other samurai films of the 60s this one holds nothing against an inhuman code of rituals that still lives in modern Japan. The film goes the extra step by having the final segment taking place in contemporary Japan, where loyalty to the emperor, and to the feudal lords of the past has been replaced with loyalty to companies. Stomping over human pride and emotions. Relentless and sharp in it's critique of the japanese mentality of sacrifice for the sake of others. At one point one character more or less admits, in clear defeat, that he's not in control of his own life. More people need to see this one.

reviews.text: This is the only world we have, I wonder why it has slowed down, just for us to suffer with these unbearable feelings of love that can’t last or perhaps were never meant to. The agony of knowing you are the author of your own misery and choosing to keep writing the story is something I find in all of us. We are cursed with the exquisite pain of a love that never arrives whole, intensified by its incompleteness. We are the architects of our own emptiness, building monuments to people who have already abandoned us, always wandering open spaces that circle back to the same sorrow we’ve carried for so damn long.

reviews.author: MichailBetter
reviews.text: I was absolutely convinced I'd like this film, but I really didn't expect this execution, which reminded me of Yi Yi in some scenes. The switches between color and black & white scenes were reminiscent of Tarkovsky's Nostalghia, and the portrayal of the love scenes was like something out of a sad novel, a few hundred years old. And in fact, if I'm not mistaken, that's exactly how it was meant to be. The guy never really did anything wrong, and yet he's still only disappointed in the end. I find these kinds of themes very interesting. He was always there for the women, but for some reason, it never worked out. And those reasons were never unjustified in the end. The fortune teller was right, man... love and all that. Shit sucks.

reviews.text: 拥有着强大作者欲的处女长片，像一曲风格化浓烈的柔板布吉舞曲，城市景观外化了角色心境，在迷人的感性与理性中不断飞越，光线和时间在连绵的跳切镜头中得到延宕，空间也在此刻软化成了一个变形的晶体，由无数情感的流线构成，但这些流线并非致密的，而是松散的，随着情感的渐变而逐渐消亡。今晨，我与我的爱人在首尔海底相拥，她凝望着我，我们面面相觑，爱就在一瞬间，可是说不出口，只留下一片蓝色的空白。接近完美的处女作，但《黑色咖啡店》以后再无郑圣一。

reviews.text: From the title alone, you'd already know that Lino Brocka isn't going to aim for subtlety, especially with a Bible parallel both in the name and the story that he's telling. But I think that how the familiar tale translates itself to a setting in the Philippines under Martial Law only makes Cain & Abel come off so angry - and that's where the power of Lino Brocka's film has come about. It's a very simple premise, but I think that Brocka imbues this Biblical tale with a sense of class consciousness that doesn't remain so simplistic, especially when knowing Brocka's strong opposition to the Ferdinand Marcos regime.

reviews.author: Brandon Streussnig
reviews.text: Familial melodrama as a microcosm for life under a brutal dictatorship. A mother pitting sons against one another, everyone in their orbit just endless collateral damage. And so it goes, on and on. An astonishing, precise work. Many films map society or community onto one, singular group of people, shrinking larger conflicts down to their basest level but what Brocka does here is so urgent, so devastating. All the while, crafting a bleakly satisfying revenge thriller on top of it all. A masterpiece that exceeds its more famous inspirations.

reviews.text: Narratively speaking, Calamity of Snakes has potential. But instead, we're just presented with a grotesque exercise in animal cruelty with barely any artistic merit. Being a category III film, I expected this to be transgressive in some capacity. Likewise, being no stranger to exploitation cinema, there's not much I haven't seen in terms of animal exploitation. In my past reviews, I've refrained from commenting too much on animal cruelty as to not practice moral hypocrisy. However now that I'm vegan, I feel morally obligated to openly condemn it.

reviews.author: Eli Hayes
reviews.text: Clinical experimentation, which is what I should have expected from Trank — a filmmaker clearly not being given enough credit — at this point, but it caught me off guard nonetheless. The comparisons to Gotti (of which this is essentially an opposite), et cetera, simply had me prepared for an entirely different, and altogether much more by-the-books experience. I was not expecting a bizarro, fractured, absurd, genuinely terrifying, purposefully off-putting and deeply, deeply sad study of a haunted psyche.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Credit has to be given to Trank here for the deeply uncommercial premise of taking a mythic figure who inspired an entire genre of film for a century and tackling the ugliest, most unglamorous, and pitiable period of his life. He commits to it well enough but unfortunately, he doesn't quite have the filmmaking chops yet to get this to the next level it needed to go imo. The whole thing is a bit too dry and literal (a lot of time is taken up by vague expository gestures towards a lost son, hired goons, buried money, police surveillance, etc) when it should be more psychologically unhinged and swept up in the atmosphere/paranoia. It's also not particularly visually imaginative work…

reviews.author: davidehrlich

But while both films offer a bleak look at the final chapter of a fabled rock star’s life, this one has the chutzpah to be so much bleaker; if Van Sant’s movie was strung out, Trank’s is utterly zombified.

reviews.text: A strange biographical crime drama that is unfocused and misleading. Stars Tom Hardy as the title character Capone. After 10 years in prison, he’s home, suffering from dementia and harrowing memories of his violent past. I like Hardy, but this was weird. He plays a caricature who’s senile, hacking, coughing, spitting, and can't seem to hold his bowels. The raspy voice and slurring were hard to understand. I had to watch this with subtitles. Some of the flashbacks or hallucinations were interesting, but it meanders. And I'm not sure what the tone they were going for. It’s dramatic and bizarre but feels like a parody at times. This could have been any decrepit old man. I looked up director Josh Trank after watching Chronicle, which was a highly underrated film. reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: I'd be curious to see Ferrara's original cut, but honestly I can't imagine it having much more personality than this version. Production value almost doesn't suit him, with the hard-boiled Leonard dialogue preventing the pockets of air that give Ferrara's actors their breakthrough moments of frightening reality, while his endless pans around gaudy stucco lack any and all of the roughshod, brutal autocritique of his best work. The '80s seemed to be a bad time for Ferrara, filled with futile attempts for mainstream style; thankfully his early, independent streak would come roaring back in the next decade.

Karate versus bull, muscle bound motel fight, international spies, a secret formula, neo-nazis, mad scientist murder, CIA man whore, motorbike nonsense, tons of random pedestrians looking directly into the camera, awful dubbing, a nearly incomprehensible plot, and motherfuckin' Bolo Yeung. reviews.author: Holerbot6000
reviews.text: A bit dry but informative documentary that not only chronicles Coco Chanel's life and career but examines the immortal question - what makes Chanel Chanel? According to Karl Lagerfeld and others, she wasn't particularly original or visionary and often incorporated other people's ideas into her work. What made her Chanel though was a knack for picking just the right elements and turning them into a trend that her army of followers rabidly consumed. Most fascinating of all is that she completely left the industry and then came back in her 70's and that is when she did her most iconic work. I'm starting to get up there myself, so it's very life affirming to see a story about any artist who still has game in their twilight years. Proof positive that just because your name is Coco, you don't have to be a stripper either. Not that there's anything wrong with that!

reviews.author: anna nomaly
reviews.text: The carnage quotient is low, but that's okay: from the outset, it's leaning toward character study rather than traditional slasher fare, more Schrader than schlock. Brandon Maggart's sensitive, implosive performance is fascinating, holding everything together when the director is unable to. Lewis Jackson's filmmaking is largely flat and low-energy, and he makes the fatal mistake of rarely going in for closeups once Maggart's face is obscured by his costume. The eyes are the window to the soul, but you have to be able to see them! All that said, yes, the finale absolutely destroys, and it made me wish the rest of it was better, weirder, or both.

reviews.text: Disaster / Action from Alvin Rakoff. A bitter ex-employee sabotages an oil refinery, triggering a large blaze which spreads throughout a city. Curse those pesky kids with their cigarettes! Silly, cheesy and melodramatic. Boasting a stellar cast, including the likes of Henry Fonda, Leslie Nielsen, Ava Gardner, Barry Newman and Shelley Winters (she's great!). The performances are satisfactory for the most part, though the characters are generally dull or unlikable. Tonally messy - the fairly straight direction clashes with the increasingly ludicrous aspects of the script. There is some production value - with some good stunts, impressive fiery set pieces and laughably dated vfx… but it’s all a bit forgettable and daft.

reviews.text: Legend has it this was at some point intended to be a fourth DIRTY HARRY movie, but Clint rejected it. Too bad (not that SUDDEN IMPACT isn't terrific), because even though it's derivative of previous Callahan outings, Eastwood would have certainly injected some much needed humanity into this story of corrupt lifer cops and their community of rotten professionals. Unfortunately we get charisma vacuum Chuck Norris, one of two robots prominently featured in this film, and this turns into a pretty perfunctory (if adequately satisfying) lone wolf thing. Thankfully local boy Andy Davis does a fine job allowing terrific location work and a roster of actual Chicago cops to color outside the lines and lend this some distinctive and much needed atmosphere along with his simple formal economy.

reviews.text: really really scary stuff. i’m not talking about the fire incident, which is a tragedy for sure, but i’m talking about the romanian politicians and others involved that have this audacious greed and corruption where they choose to prioritize money over the lives of civilians that have their trust. while the discourse in political science the documentary covers can feel a bit excessive for those who lack interest in that area, there is no denying that it’s overall effective in painting the clearest picture of a stagnant aftermath caused not by the indifference of the people but by the resistance from those in control — despite being fully aware of the vile crimes they committed. the editing in particular immaculately articulates this notion in a hard-hitting but intentional way.

reviews.text: Feels like it'd do really well if watched back to back with Spike Lee's Bamboozled, especially when you're coming to consider the ways in which Marlon Riggs is interrogating the ways in which African-American portrayals in media have been sanitized for the sake of the appeal of a white audience when you're coming to consider the standards that were set by most shows that were at the peak of their prime as shown in here. But what makes Marlon Riggs's perspective so special especially in the case of Color Adjustment comes clear from how it engages with the way black audiences have seen themselves on screen, and how it forms what Riggs shows here.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: Although not as engaging or all-encompassing as Ethnic Notions, Color Adjustment is just as informative. This time, Marlon Riggs specifically examines the ways in which Black people have been portrayed on television since it’s inception in the early 1950’s. One thing I have noticed as I make my way through Riggs’ body of work is how ahead of his time he was, and how much his works hold up today. In this case, this fact can be attributed to the unfortunately slow progress of racial depictions in media, as well as the political and social ideals attributed to Black people in America overall. Here, Riggs shows the lack of proper representation of Black life in media through a series of close…

reviews.author: theironcupcake
reviews.text: Like Ethnic Notions before it, Color Adjustment is another of Marlon Riggs' striking studies of Black images in American media, this time specifically observing the previous forty-plus years of Black performers and characters seen on television. Narrated by Ruby Dee, Riggs' film chronicles the cultural impact of numerous shows and mini-series, including Amos 'n' Andy, Beulah, The Nat King Cole Show, East Side/West Side, I Spy, Julia, All in the Family, Good Times, The Jeffersons, Roots, The Cosby Show and the short-lived dramedy Frank's Place, the analysis of which is supported by such commentators as Henry Louis Gates Jr., Esther Rolle, Diahann Carroll, Norman Lear, Steven Bochco and Sheldon Leonard. As with the aforementioned earlier documentary, I admire Riggs' unwavering…

reviews.author: Paul Thomas
reviews.text: This documentary came out in 1992, yet the trend has only continued. The way African Americans are represented on TV has progressed, and the film gives credit to these steps forward, yet there's always little things in it to keep it from moving forward at the rate it should. The unconscious bias of white producers usually anchors too much progression. Whether it's Good Times needing to show a goofy buffoon stereotype with certain characters to soften the blow of respect demanded from white audiences of poorer black characters, to the Cosbys only getting the respect deserved when a black family is shown to fulfill the American dream and buy into Reaganism 100%, Color Adjustment is a very enlightening film that could have come out today and hold the same point.

reviews.author: Stephen Gillespie
reviews.text: A follow-up work to Ethnic Notions. This is a narrower work, also, Its focus is on televisual representation and it charts a thorough history of it. The focus is always on the issue of narrow representation: when Black individuals are so few and far between on TV, each role takes on an unfair weight. This opens up a lot of perceptive and fair criticism, and this documentary makes us reflect intelligently on what each representation means and what drives it.

reviews.author: Zoë 🐛
reviews.text: Loved this - especially as someone very interested in media in the 20th century, and as someone who knows very little about television beyond just knowing the names of the most popular shows of the past. So insightful and really exposes how American television as a medium truly is defined by and beholden to capitalism and conservatism, even more than American film. I definitely want to see Ethnic Notions now.

reviews.text: A companion piece to Ethnic Notions, again using a combination of talking heads and manipulated archival footage to examine the evolution of black representation on television. As with the earlier film, this largely resembles a 'neutral' PBS documentary in form and tone, though Riggs' anger, intelligence, and personality are still visibly present throughout.

reviews.author: Movie Good or Movie Bad?
reviews.text: A really great sequel/spiritual successor to Ethnic Notions. Exploring what Black representation was at this time is really incredible, especially in the nuanced way that Riggs explores it and his willingness to critique someone as big as Bill Cosby for the time. I do think this central critique leads the way for a lot of Black television and film to change and I almost wish Riggs could have seen that change with time.

reviews.author: Christian Ha
reviews.text: Confession of Murder was a big letdown for me. I went in hoping for a tense, gripping thriller, but what I got instead was a wildly uneven film with bizarre tonal shifts and some downright goofy action sequences. The movie tries to balance serious emotional weight with over-the-top set pieces, but the result feels disjointed and unintentionally silly. There are moments where it seems like the film wants to be taken seriously, but then it immediately undercuts itself with absurd stunts or melodramatic twists. I just couldn’t get into it. The pacing felt off, the characters didn’t really grab me, and the whole thing came across as too chaotic for my taste. It’s simply not my style, and despite a few interesting ideas, the execution felt all over the place.

reviews.author: Jenna Ipcar
reviews.text: Do yourself a favor and watch this awesome little made for TV movie instead of Sorkin’s big wankfest of liberal rewriting. Not only is this just as engaging without leaning on big name casting as a shortcut for empathy (not that there aren’t recognizable faces but), but it’s far more accurate to the politics these defendants actually held and represented. Even better, this movie doesn’t try to recreate jack shit, not only do they use actual footage when necessary but it inter-splices actual interviews with the defendants giving their retellings and reactions.

reviews.author: Dawson Joyce
reviews.text: Superbly cast, sticking dead-on to the facts, and expertly paced from start to finish, HBO's Conspiracy: The Trial of the Chicago 8 is not only a fantastic recount of famous events but also an inventively experimental blend of documentary-like realism and film-like dramatization, from its clever utilization of archive footage and interviews during recreations to its mix of televisual camerawork with cinematic lighting.

But this one, I’m afraid, was pretty boring most of the time. It gets a bit more exciting in the second half and the ending was actually quite impressive. Shooting on actual location is a production value that should never be underestimated. And speaking of production values, Julie Ege and Marcia Fox are definitely the highlights here and very easy to look at. Even at a slow pace, they keep the movie watchable.

I don’t know that that is a good way to start a review of the film, but it’s truly the most important way to start a review. The film makes no sense, and it is frustrating trying to understand it. reviews.author: cult_vegetables
reviews.text: An ex-con and a crisis of conscience: Classic L.A. pulp, the ink still bleeding off the page. The tabloid heat is tempered with chilly moral ambiguity, constantly challenging the credibility gap, and that's just the point. Bad decisions set the gears in motion, and all wounds are self-inflicted, a fantastical inversion that sets this film apart. In stark, minimalist B&W, the flamboyant Sterling Hayden is a highlight: a boorish, trash-talking detective who stops just short of being the Glendale Gestapo. And he's the hero!

reviews.author: The Film Foundation
reviews.text: Born on May 15th in Makó, Austria-Hungary (with his sun in Taurus and moon in Virgo) Andre de Toth came to Hollywood in 1942 after a short stint directing Hungarian films and working under fellow Hungarian émigré Alexander Korda in England. He was known for his fierce independent spirit and for making westerns, crime pictures, and HOUSE OF WAX, the first color 3D feature film released by a studio. In 1953 de Toth made CRIME WAVE, a tour-de-force film noir starring Sterling Hayden. The head honchos at Warner Brothers didn't want Hayden though, they told de Toth to cast Humphrey Bogart. When de Toth refused, they cut his shooting schedule down to 14 days. But de Toth got what he…

reviews.text: Quick, cinephiles, what’s Doris Day’s greatest film? No. No. No. It’s Andre de Toth’s Crime Wave. What? You don’t remember DoDa in that film? Well, who’s that singing “S’Wonderful” on the radio in Dub Taylor’s service station at the beginning of the film?

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: Man alive does this movie look good. Noirs that use light as well as they do shadow are rarer than you’d think, but it’s the brightness of DeToth’s film that is its most striking feature. In the daylight — as with the climax of the film — LA is on display in all of its grungy glory, with the sun glinting off of the myriad cars and shop windows, and the sky a big, open fronteir. At night, the black is deep and dark, but it’s interrupted by splotches of brilliant light: diners, shop windows, apartments.

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: I feel like I often use the term 'documentary-like' to describe some of these black & white crime films from the 40's and 50's, but "Crime Wave" truly earns that descriptor: the story feels stripped bare of anything but the most essential facts, I don't recall any nondiegetic music after the opening credits, and scenes like a crowded police station are packed full of background actors you see once and never again, as well as ambient noise like dry-coughs and passing traffic, all there just to add a sense of realism. Somehow director André De Toth released five films in the year of 1953, but this one is not to be missed by fans of noir and crime pictures.

reviews.text: "Crucible of Terror" is a 1972 film directed by Ted Hooker. An interesting narrative concept, the film centers around a mad artist who has a devious obsession with turning people into bronze statues. This awful and interesting method marks for the film to pick up just enough speed to be interesting, but begins to become further scrambled with elements of possession, a cult, and a kimono. In full honesty, its a case of interest in the beginning of the film, followed by dry slow progression in the middle. The end of the film doubles down on the madness and pays off those who stayed in attendance, but still isn't worth the middle of the film. Just another example of British horror obscura that has sat on the lower shelf within its own genre.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Spike lee does The Treasure of the Sierra Madre as men-on-a-mission, hangout/heist picture through black history and Vietnam only instead of being slowly corrupted by greed Lee wrestles with how we are already corrupted and haunted by imperialism, whether we understand exactly how or why or the all-consuming depth of it or not. Delroy Lindo gives one of the most brutally sad, destructive performances in a Lee joint (no small feat, especially considering his own in Crooklyn) playing a man whose seething rage, political contradictions, and emotional complexities are as direct a counter-point to retroactively trying to "win" this conflict through cinema as there's ever been. Nothing easy or fair or righteous about the application of violence or the allocation of resources as dictated from the top down so if you manage to survive the senseless carnage on the ground you might as well take what you can and give to the cause.

reviews.author: Nathaniel Thompson
reviews.text: Tragically underseen, this Italian occult shocker riding the success of The Omen features the spookiest use of Venice since Don't Look Now, one of Pino Donaggio's greatest scores, and a climax featuring a still-shocking moment of taboo violence that can clear a room. Gorgeous, haunting, and filled with surreal imagery, it's the story of a boy named Mark whose blindness means (a) he should probably be living in a much safer city that isn't filled with canals, and (b) he can experience visions of violence and the impending arrival of the Antichrist courtesy of his sister's pregnancy. A real gem that's still crying out for a decent home video release.

reviews.text: The sympathy this shows for Bubba is far more than many films show neurodivergent people, and the agency it gives him as he gets his revenge more, too, than you usually see. I'm not saying this somewhat grim rednexploitation-slasher film is enlightened exactly, but it avoids pitfalls you would expect and has a sense of... justice. That's the difference from a mean-spirited horror movie: it sacrifices that sense of terror you would get from sympathizing with the victims of the killer by making them horrible people, targets of justified vengeance. It's possible (very possible) to tap into that kind of fear for sympathetic victims, but it's also very easy to fall into the trap of just making something nihilistic and…

reviews.text: One of, if not THE first movie to feature a killer scarecrow, and it's absolutely spectacular! And the ending fucking SLAPS! Definitely one of the best horror movie endings for sure! Only issue I really had is that the scarecrow isn't really onscreen a whole lot. I get that was on purpose to add to the creepiness, but since this is called "Dark Night of the Scarecrow," I feel like we should've seen him more. But other than that, this movie was great! reviews.author: Disgustipated
reviews.text: When Delphine Seyrig appeared in that two-tone silver dress, outlining her figure as though each bedazzling sequin were pasted directly onto her skin, she was incredibly stunning. The brilliance of her presence could not be contained by the camera, sequins flared like supernovae across the lens, and I could not look at her for too long in the same way that one cannot stare too long at the sun. Delphine Seyrig is the purring evil at the centre of this film, and when combined with the stunning cinematography this really is a masterpiece of euro-horror. I am glad I have finally been able to catch up with it.

As others have noted, this is the kind of thing that’s just begging for the neo-Hitchcockian stylistic excess of a De Palma to match its absurd energy, but honestly it settles well enough with Branagh whose penchant for self-serious operatics (and lack of tonal control of them) sort of works in the materials favor… By the time he’s doing some baroque Edgar Allen Poe murderous generational melodrama insanity in the Long Goodbye tower apartment and Wayne Knight shows up with a pizza right before an experimental art coffee table is used as a weapon it was hard to argue against the weird, silly fun of it all.

reviews.author: Edgar Cochran ✝️🍋
reviews.text: Very loosely based on a true story about a Japanese-born Korean student who raped and killed two girls in 1958 and was given death sencence by hanging five years later, Kôshikei is Ôshima's personal transformation of an ordinary execution story into an expertly directed satirical dark comedy with important undertones of criticism against capital punishment, the Japanese nationalist anti-Korean sentiment and the blood-soaked Japanese imperialism, all through a scope that intents on the ridicule of the nationalist (Minister of Education), political (Public Prosecutors), religious (Priest) and legal (District Attorney) authorities. With a stunning ability to intertwine both the comically absurd and dramatic glimpses of powerful ideas about the contradictions found in the definitions of "human justice", Ôshima challenges prejudices and societal xenophobia, and invites to reflection for his time and for the times of today.

reviews.text: Brechtian in style and form, Death by Hanging is stratified absurdity-theatre from pioneering Japanese filmmaker Nagisa Ōshima. Richly profound regarding its thematic presentation, there are a plethora of difficult topics being explored throughout the film such as race, class, guilt, identity, nationalism, bureaucracy, power, existentialism and, most of all, capital punishment—death, but specifically, the law vs. morality paradox that exists between the legal execution of a prisoner and subsequent governmental body carrying out this execution, with an act of murder committed by a citizen upon another. Where is the line drawn? Do we determine what is right or wrong by legality or morality? I believe the film is about this very quandary. Equally so, it is about race and, in…

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: A unique and odd film, Dementia is a silent work from the 1950s, playing with mundane surrealism in a way that feels proto-Lynchian. This is a creeping film of shadows, gazing men, and words that follow you. The world is populated with mysterious strangers and the topics dealt with (death, domestic abuse, murder) are heavy. Music seems to be a key part of the film, from its jazzy latter stages to the wailing sounds in the middle. Dementia has so many images that stand out, like its possible class connotations and the endless hands that reach out. It's the ghouls of insanity, the spotlight of the accused, and a home amongst the dead. Shame about the undercutting ending. Still, Dementia is a darkly magical descent into the laughter of the surreal.

reviews.text: A through-line exists between the work of Ed Wood and David Lynch, and it's called DAUGHTER OF HORROR. A dramatization of a dream that was experienced by star Adrienne Barrett, this is an experimental D.I.Y. passion project from one-time feature filmmaker John Parker. Originally released as DEMENTIA, the haunting movie tiptoes between horror and film noir; dreams and reality; life and death. This is an intersection between ERASERHEAD, CARNIVAL OF SOULS, and PLAN 9 FROM OUTER SPACE that I love with all of my heart. (Joseph A. Ziemba)

reviews.text: Then-present-tense cyberpunk, Demonlover is forever frozen upon the cusp of a lost futurism already lapsing into a decadent kitsch. The flows and tentacles of capital, all periphery and no center, shells within shells, without flags or loyalties. A Venn Diagram of exploitation with too many circles, relationships impossible to plot. 9/11 rendered this frictionless world of jet lag and instantaneous document transfer as unreachable as the Austro-Hungarian Empire after World War One. The brief glimpse of Bush II on hotel tv is shocking enough, but he is talking about energy companies, not yet a 'war-time president', but the spectre of the torture dungeon lurks here too: before it was policy, it was just business.

reviews.author: viewer 🛸
reviews.text: Prurient, horrific, dreamlike cyberpunk espionage. George W. Bush, Suicide Club, and pixelated porn on the TV. Darkthrone on the soundtrack. Rain on the window; reflections and hazy light and color everywhere. Terror more palpable than Videodrome arises when the capitalist rabbithole leads to the (NØ LØV∑) deep web. Mind and body are hostage to the darkest and most depraved back alleyways of internet mercantilism. Characters whose soul has all but vanished are nonetheless fascinating; Demonlover is a nightmare labyrinth where 'humanity' is all but gone, butchered, wasted, yet it's full of beautiful images and even moments of strangely delicate and always fleeting intimacy. Got the best rip I could find over on karagarga and this is one of those films…

reviews.text: Would've watched this sooner if I had known it was Assayas' sleek, upsetting spiritual sequel to Ferrara's New Rose Hotel; sharing with that film an effectively oblique, elliptical style and lo-fi postmodern cyberpunk/corporate espionage milieu of screens and transactions and despairing industrial weaponization of sex/violence. Parts of it recall Mulholland Drive/Inland Empire era lynch in its depiction of women nightmarishly pursuing and being trapped in and consumed by a depraved industry of fantasy, others parts more the perverted voyeur techno-horror of Videodrome, but it is ultimately this ambiguous, off-brand arthouse William Gibson taken to desensitized, internet-age exploitation extremes that really makes it stand out.

reviews.author: Betamax Jones
reviews.text: If there is something that the social media age has done it’s this illusion of perfection many people strive for. “Here’s my meal”, “Look at the weather my perfect family and I are enjoying”, “Look how cute my dog is”. What these images don’t tell us about is the forgotten sun tan lotion, the dog relieving itself on the rug or the slightly funny taste to the potatoes. It sells us this image of perfection that many aspire to, but that image is a lie, a perfect snapshot of an otherwise ordinary world, one filled with strife, things we will never truly understand ourselves until we have walked a mile in those shoes.

reviews.text: There were two reasons why I watched Doctor Chance. 1) Apparently, people classify the films of F.J. Ossang as punk cinema. 2) Joe Strummer. It was the second reason that made my head turn though. And sadly, he couldn't save this dank, monotonous, experimental crime thriller. Whilst watching Doctor Chance, I felt that a collection of cool elements does not always make for a cool movie, especially in Ossang's context of abrupt circle transitions, characters talking nonsense, and the cinematography looking like the D.O.P. hit the incorrect white balance setting on the camera.

reviews.text: A brilliantly baffling film: one of the most striking and experimental uses of colour I have seen (as pregnant with meaning as Barry Lyndon, as passionately surreal as anything by Anger, as anti-sculptural (i.e. Baroque, according to Wölfflin’s terminology) as Moby-Dick by Huston was sculptural (i.e. Classic) thanks to the dye transfer technique used) in narrative (?) film, a crazy assemblage of quotations filmic and otherwise (Film Noir, Burroughs, Road Movie, Kokoschka, Murnau, Georg Trakl, Dumas (Milady) etc), filled with insanely corny (B-movie) dialogue collaged with lines of surrealist poetry, this is a film that baffles and blinds my desire for interpretation but it has so many moments of pure strangeness that perhaps only multiple viewings will allow me to…

reviews.text: At some point during a ‘free Superchannel weekend’ back in the late 80’s, my family taped this on a blank VHS. Therefore, parts of this movie are super-nostalgic because of the sheer number of times I’ve seen them (particularly the ‘eating dog food’ scene, and the first video montage the son makes…because there are boobs in it). But the rest of the movie is just as nostalgic due to the sheer amount of pastel colours blanketing the house interiors (honestly, I’m very much pro pastel furniture and gold-plated faucets, so I’m all set for this look to make a comeback).

Easy to see why this became a hit and even spawned a TV series (swiftly canceled though it was, like all too-soon small-screen spinoffs of '80s movies).

reviews.text: Nominated for the Best First Screenplay and Best Female Lead (for Hong Chau) at the 35th Film Independent Spirit Awards, Driveways is a skillfully constructed and well-calibrated drama from director Andrew Ahn which discovers a pensive sadness in daily mundanity. Collaboratively written by Hannah Bos and Paul Thureen, who have previously written together for television, it's both seductive and spellbinding. It displays their attention to dialogue as well as their talent for allowing moments to evolve patiently, and the cinematography of Ki Jin Kim is graceful in conveying their sentimentalities.

reviews.author: Matt Singer
reviews.text: I will never watch any kind of making-of documentary or behind-the-scenes featurette about Denis Villeneuve’s Dune. I don’t want to know how this film was made. I prefer to believe the extremely convincing illusion that Villeneuve somehow traveled to the year 10,191 and documented the strange civilization he encountered. Dune is full of stylization and visual artistry, but the future it conjures feel so complete and tactile that some segments play like a documentary of the world to come — which is an especially impressive feat since that world involves giant sandworms that consume everything that passes through their sphincter-like maws.

reviews.text: much like the other Dunkirk this covers a few stories that has a fun British cast that captured a lot of different opinions on the war as it was really just starting to crystalize in the civilians lives and what it means. Lots of dynamic narratives that pollinate the fracturing of a European landscape that felt heartbreaking at times really the dread of being stuck on that beach as these soldiers had to endure constant bombing with nowhere to hide felt nightmarish. They captured the tragedy but also the humanistic spirit with these boats bringing some but not all of these soldiers home. Really gut punching material but one that you could see as a unifier cause really this was not the end just the end of the beginning.

reviews.author: Sophie Farrell
reviews.text: Widely considered to be one of the essential British war films, 1958's Dunkirk is a film that I knew very little about apart from the fact that it is about one of the key turning points of the Second World War. It is a film that I have been interested in checking out for ages as I've always found how this period in history has been presented in film, especially in the years that immediately followed the end of the conflict, to be incredibly interesting. I did have high expectations for Dunkirk and while it didn't necessarily blow me away, I still found it to be a very interesting film.

reviews.text: Has any other filmmaker displayed Rossellini's ability to consistently capture miracles? EUROPE '51 starts with the nominal language of melodrama before a shock ruptures the formalism and unleashes something else upon the world. And I mean "world" not in its artistic conception of a work's diegetic reality but in the actual sense of the world around us, of a separate but connected web of people who share a moral responsibility toward one another. The tragedy that befalls Bergman in the first act might have been the cruel punishment to end most films, but by positioning it so early, Rossellini forces a confrontation with the world that opens up the frame (and deftly critiques communism's myopic materialism in favor of a…

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: The Italian government heavily censored this neorealist movie upon its limited release for being too radical in its social and moral implications. It is directed by Roberto Rossellini and is a condemnation of consumerism and selfish values following WWII. It follows Irene Girard (Ingrid Bergman) who's proclaimed mentally ill after becoming obsessed with humanitarianism following her son's suicide. This is a remarkably rich and affecting work, accentuated by an extraordinary performance by Bergman and beautifully conveys the apprehensions and the search for aspirations in a post-war Europe.

reviews.text: Like efficient railroads or universal healthcare, the annual Eurovision Song Contest is one of those international phenomena that most Americans refuse to acknowledge. Conceived in the 1950s as a way of bringing Europe together through the magical power of “light entertainment” and copious hairspray, Eurovision has basically evolved into the Olympics of pop music. But despite the fact that the competition has served as a launching pad for global superstars like Abba and Celine Dion, the average American couldn’t seem to care about it any less — we live in the imperialistic bubble of our own cultural-industrial complex, and even in the BTS era it’s hard to remain optimistic about a country that made Three Doors Down into platinum-selling artists…

reviews.text: From the first time I saw this, it quickly became one of my all-time favourites. This film is possibly the funniest and most nihilistic black comedy out there. Filled with utterly deplorable characters in the slums of Ostend, Belgium living out their horrendous lives. The movie pulls no punches, yet it doesn't seem like it deliberately sets out to just be as offensive as possible. All of the depravity has a sense of realism to it. Though the film itself definitely explores some surreal territory including a man who lives upside down in his apartment, and a woman who loses her hair after seeing her son masturbate. There are also various creative elements to the storytelling, embodying some metafictive elements.…

reviews.author: kat🕷
reviews.text: "Ex Drummer" is a pseudo milieu study about psychological and moral abysses in the interpersonal ghettos of Ostende, exaggerated with a liberally applied filter of dirt and disgust. The visuals and soundscape are definitely great. Whether the movie really wants to denounce any grievances or simply break taboos and celebrate an aesthetic of disgust dripping with piss as an anti-cultural counterprogram remains a big secret. But I can't deny a certain fascination for this movie. The sometimes comic like, bizarre narrative helps to endure the spectacle of this absurdity without sinking too deeply into the swamp of social voyeurism. I still felt kind of bad when I watched it.

reviews.text: As Jean Douchet put Le Testament du Docteur Cordelier makes for a fine dialetical duo with Picnic on the Grass, both taking most of the same subjects (the fate of the European upper classes at the start of the European community experiment and how it relates to post war scientific nature), but while the previous film, a lovely color theatrical pastoral, concentrated on Renoir's more upbeat tendencies, this black and white TV horror comedy goes for all his destructive ones. Their relationship tells more about the contradictions of Renoir`s artistic sensibility than any other of his films. It is a diquieting film using our familiarity with Stevenson's story as jumping off point and growing more and more troubling the more Renoir's dissection goes. Jean-Louis Barrault performance is one of the great ones, particular when he plays Opale as cinema's beloved tramp going into its pure anarchic rage most movies must keep repressed.

reviews.text: Jean Renoir's TV movie take on Stevenson's Jekyll & Hyde, or in this case 'Strange Case of Docteur Cordelier and Monsieur Opale'.Despite being moved from 19th century London (which itself was a stand-in for Stevenson's Edinburgh) to contempory 1950s Paris, this version is far more faithful to the book than any of the Hollywood versions.We know it's directed by Renoir because he introduces the film in a weird 'Jean Renoir Presents' scene at the beginning, shot in a TV studio.Despite some theatrical overacting and poorly staged fight scenes (at one point I thought this must be a parody) I really enjoyed this, and particularly the performance of mime artist Jean-Louis Barrault in the dual role.And there are some fantastic street scenes of Paris to feast your eyes on, but I did start to feel a little nauseous watching so much puffing on cigarettes.

reviews.text: Como sólo antes la misteriosa La Nuit du carrefour (1932), Cordelier es insólita en la carrera de Renoir por su carácter precipitado y fulgurante. Más sombría de lo habitual, pero no exenta de comicidad, se benefició de la libertad que le confería una idea luego muy copiada: rodar una película con procedimientos - economía, rapidez y varias cámaras - televisivos. No se tema por ello una improvisación caprichosa; de hecho, es la más fiel a Stevenson, pese a actualizarla y trasponerla de Londres a París, de las muchas versiones cinematográficas de la novela breve The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll & Mr. Hyde. Está verdaderamente adaptada, en la medida en que son otros los conocimientos científicos y psicológicos, otras las creencias…

reviews.author: gaia
reviews.text: Clearly made for tv and that weighs quality and rhythm down. Still, despite being unlicensed and modernized, it remains the most faithful adaptation of the novella. Cordelier/Opale's characterization is clear: they are precisely the same person, only Opale doesn't have Cordelier's appearance to hold him back. The doctor feels no remorse, so of course his alter-ego doesn't. And this is a doctor who has been corrupt for a long, long time, a hypocrite rapist protected by a facade. He is not betrayed by himself. It's protective, affectionate Joly/Utterson who's betrayed, whose friendship Cordelier/Jekyll doesn't deserve; here he is finally given space as the "main character", the eyes through which we see the story, and also as his friend's lifeline ("The pain caused by your anger gives me hope"). He's the emotional center of the story as he originally was.Plus, Barrault was truly giving his all and he carried the whole thing with his extraordinary mimic; he elevates the movie.

reviews.author: Collin Brinkmann
reviews.text: Feels like a parallel to the Psycho of Hitchcock -- who like Renoir made his first film in 1925 -- and who 35 years later knowingly downshifted into surface level B-horror black-and-white aesthetics with the full knowledge that what exploitation filmmakers had been doing to get across cheap thrills & violence & titillation, he could do fifty times better. Renoir does something similar here with the horror / monster / mad scientist template, and like Hitchcock takes the thirty-five years of artistic experience & proven mastery under his belt and imbues the project ("elevates" it, if you want to use that word) with a deeper plunge into moral, psychological, near-religious territory that lesser filmmakers, or at least those with less cultural cachet, would…

reviews.author: brotherdeacon
reviews.text: Jean-Louis Barrault's Monsieur Opale was a wonder, and led me to consider the transmogrifying of Denis Lavant in Holy Motors (2012) as a rebirth of the same concupiscent Doctor--he who moves with heroic difficulty through two worlds of cinematic duality: truth/illusion and textual/photo-chemical. Although a rather fluttering flame for Renoir, Le Testament groaned with the constrictions of moral evangelicalism and screamed with the excruciation of freedom's Nth degree. It felt at times as if Renoir was shooting for Hammer Films or AIP during their heyday while he managed the constraints of television production within that era--many of the principal sets and lighting setups were perhaps even more of a bargain store amalgamation than that. Fun nevertheless.

reviews.text: A satisfying little mind reading thriller.This guy builds a machine in which he can enter other people's minds, wander around in them and find out if their words agree with their memories. But he gets stuck from the first time, and is obliged to live a vegetative life on his own, but being alive in the other guys memories before finding a possibility of getting succesfully extracted. He realizes that his situation is more complicated, and finds out that the truth is not always reflected in the memories he's witnessing...Small-scale, with decent acting (how come I never heard of Mollen before?) and some nice shifts in color to distinguish between the different conditions, it's easy to follow, and apart from the fact it's never really captivating or tense, there's little negative to say about this resulting in a peculiar scifi thriller drama.

I don’t expect great performances from a low budget scifi story but, science fiction gives you the license to be creative and innovative with philosophy and science. Nothing made sense, the character’s motivations were plain and uninspired. I feel like all the neat ideas were mined from other sources. All in all,…

reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: Probably not the kind of cop movie you’d expect from the director of Commando and Showdown In Little Tokyo. A bitter brutal warning about police violence and the blue wall, wrapped in an ultraviolent action-drama. The mindsets, perspectives, and actions of Exteme Justice’s LAPD death squad remain depressingly relevant, while director Mark Lester makes it daringly clear who the bad guys are and how the system protects them. Even with Yaphet Kotto doing his best gunslinger impression (the character-actor cast is great here), the action feels sickening, like Verhoeven levels of bullet-perforated bodies without the satirical wink. Spiro Razatos as second unit director ensures the gunfights and car chases are intensely staged for a ‘90s DTV thriller.

reviews.text: I’ve been wanting to see this forever since seeing the soundtrack record cover with a shirtless Saxon with gat and it didn’t disappoint. While taking a less explosive, Merli-slapping approach from the usual Italian Eurocrime, this Spanish production is no less satisfying in the end. More a character study of the “good” police inspector (Rabal) and the hardened bank robber (Saxon), it illustrates how similar both men really are at the end, and the beginning of the day. Both kiss their wives the same, who both worry the same, as each kills members of their inner circle and taunts each other with those deaths the same. Both live and (probably) die the same. It’s cool seeing Saxon so dark, especially to killer cuts from the CAM library by Danielle Patucchi and Mario Molino. Never has a combover looked so badass or felt so funky.

reviews.text: I can never speak for the Iraqi people who have endured so much. All I can say with the clarity of my experience is that MOSUL is an excellent modern war film reflecting that reality, framed from the POV of those who fought one of the greatest scourges of our age. I want to be careful in my assumption that this is the first western produced major release modern war film set in Iraq told expressly from the Iraqi perspective, because despite my recent research efforts I may be overlooking something. If that point is indeed the case though, this is an exemplary first outing for something I have been wanting for years, and I hope more films made by artists and/or with direct input from the people who lived through this will follow.

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: Werner Herzog and Cambridge scientist Clive Oppenheimer go around the world to consider meteorites - from the big one 65 million years ago to the smaller ones that make for nifty paperweights. They talk to scientists, artists, hobbyists, and anyone else affected by meteorites - which, in their view, could be anyone. Structureless and thesis-less like so many Late Herzog documentaries, but in a pleasing way, because all of this is interesting. The directors have respect for the knowledge of everyone they meet, while also displaying healthy humility at our sheer smallness and powerlessness before nature and the universe. Herzog's eye for interesting images and brain for new ways of looking at the world have never left him, and here he encourages us to look at the remnants of meteorites as beautiful, mysterious visitors from other worlds.

reviews.author: Ford H
reviews.text: Fireball is another interesting documentary from Werner Herzog, co-directed with Clive Oppenheimer. It explores the fascination with the unknown and the beauty of what is brought to our planet, which is itself almost mythological, as in ancient times meteorites were considered messages. I won’t pretend I understand all the scientific talk, but it’s unmistakably clear that everyone interviewed has a profound passion for meteorites, which feel like more than just rocks, but relics, or perhaps a forgotten history.

He uses the director’s chair less as a glossy soap box, more as an artistic way to root out authenticity — which is understandable when you’re entrenched in a business that’s rife with such inauthentic cretins. Penn is able to tap into this oddly masculine creativity that feels akin to someone like Sam Shepard. With Flag Day, I feel the spirit of Dennis Hopper and Barbara Loden than I do anyone else. reviews.text: Flight of the Phoenix is one of those pure trips down memory lane for me, a film I caught early on through TV that left an imprint less because of its quality and more because of the moment in time it’s tied to. It’s not particularly memorable as a piece of filmmaking, and it goes without saying that it’s leagues inferior to the ’60s original, which I really do need to log soon, but there’s something about this version that always makes me smile while it’s on. It’s comfort viewing in the truest sense, the kind of film that plays well in the moment and then almost immediately evaporates from memory once the credits roll. reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Four Flies on Grey Velvet" is an early 1970's film directed by Dario Argento. Although Argento had been involved within other areas of filmmaking for some time, "Four Flies" marks only his third film (and third inclusion within his early 'Animal' trilogy) directed up to that point. It is absolutely acknowledged that in this early phase, Argento cut his teeth on the highly stylized Italian genre of Giallo. Giallo, meaning "yellow" in Italian (which has etymological leading back to the pages of pulp crime novels paper having a tinge of yellow), specializes within the art of the crime, both from detective-based angle of crime solving, and the maniacal murder's point of view within their insanity laden disposition. The principles of…

reviews.author: Joe Lynch
reviews.text: I am SHOCKED I haven’t seen this early Argento Giallo until now and it may now stand as one of my absolute favorites of his, a taut murder mystery incorporating music, style and exceptional craft. The deaths scenes (esepcially the “down the stairs shot”) are exceptional Gialli stylings, really vicious and visceral. Gorgeously shot, showing Argento even pre-SUSPIRIA breakout, was in complete control of his style and storytelling. That final slo-mo moment is fucking insane. Does the plot make sense? Does it even matter with a movie like this? The Morricone score is jazzy, groovy and ghastly in all the right places. Cannot stop thinking of this and NEED to see it on the big screen someday.I wish more movies had awesome long titles like this.

With an intensely satirical tone and heavily flirting with melodrama, it internalizes this discourse in its form and narrative, and specially on its main character, the semiotic symbol that encapsulates all this. And the film really does a great job on showcasing a very vivid portrait of France…

reviews.text: Neo-neorealism, because what is modern realism if not outwardly acknowledging the process that allows it to claim such a distinction? Like the photo-negative of Rossellini’s Europa ’51, a paragon of status and celebrity only achieves more, following a fairly quotidian accident that leaves Léa Seydoux internally shaken nevertheless. The ubiquitous desire to manufacture and package “the real” drives this entire film, each marvelous smash/match-cut a continued compounding of facilitated distances within spaces that only continue to encroach upon one another: war zones and resorts, the newsroom and the field, the camera and “the camera”.

reviews.text: After talking about a South African production going American in Triggered, here's one that embraces its roots. It's like Starman if Starman were a junky wandering through urban Cape Town. And there was a ton of sleazy, red-lit sex. At its best when it feels like a feature-length Chris Cunningham video, Gareth Place's trippy visuals and Haezer's fantastically crunchy, bass-heavy electronic score do a lot of the heavy lifting (the music and sound design really is MVP). As might be expected from a film shot without a script, it's kinda sketchy and relies more on the weird physicality of Gary Green than his acting ability. It also outstays its welcome. I'd have preferred it to have slashed the runtime and maintained that acerbic surreal tone throughout but it became a little gooey and soft-centred by the end.

reviews.text: 100-word review: A haunting, slow-burn thriller that expertly balances bleakness with a sliver of human connection. Galveston dives deep into themes of survival, redemption, and the crushing weight of past mistakes. Its gritty, nihilistic tone is unflinching, yet never gratuitous, offering a raw portrait of characters on society's fringes. Elle Fanning delivers one of her most transformative performances, shedding her usual ethereal roles to embody Rocky — a damaged yet resilient young woman — with vulnerability and quiet strength. The cinematography is a standout, employing long, lingering shots and inventive camera angles (and changes) that heighten the tension and desolation of the Southern backdrop.

reviews.text: It takes far too long for “Galveston” to emerge from the novocaine of its various clichés and allow us to feel the tender flesh that bleeds across every scene of this seedy road noir, but — in fairness to director Mélanie Laurent — some filmmakers are never able to break the leathered skin of a Nic Pizzolatto story (see: “True Detective” season two. Better yet; don’t). Adapted from a well-received novel of the same name that Pizzolatto wrote prior to his success on premium cable, “Galveston” is draped with all the self-serious despair that looms above the author’s infamous HBO series, but it crucially lacks the same capacity for bullshit. reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: There's a shot in this film that I can't get out of my mind. It's when the little German boy hops onto a crowded midday trolley. Even after the boy has gone out-of-shot aboard the train, instead of cutting to the next scene, the camera lingers for an inordinate amount of time, allowing us to glean the faces of each commuter passing the camera by with stoic solitude. They look hot, sweaty, cramped, annoyed, wistful, blank. Then, the camera slightly pans right to view the empty street as people walk by the ruins of their former office-buildings, apartments, marketplaces. All destroyed by the war. Yet they keep marching on. Not out of some optimism, but out of blind necessity. They don't know what else to do. This, I imagine, is the essence of Rosellini's Neorealist Trilogy. What rawness in just ten fleeting seconds.

reviews.text: Bresson would direct the exact equivalent of Rossellini's last neorealist war installment two decades later, but with a rural setting and a female lead, and it would be called Mouchette (1967). reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: Bleak does not even begin to describe this film. Germany Year Zero is Rossellini’s litmus test for empathy; an examination of post-war Germany and how its citizens dealt with the effects of a crumbled fascist regime. The film traces the life of a 12-year-old boy named Edmund following the conclusion of WWII and subsequent fall of The Third Reich. Edmund is caught between two ideological worlds: the Nazism of his ex-soldier brother and former teacher, and the anti-fascist Resistance of his father. Rossellini portrays the former (un)reformed Nazis as the cowards and deviants they are, never begging sympathy for them. Rather, we are asked to empathize with the young boy, and the other women and children trying to survive amidst the…

reviews.author: Xebeche
reviews.text: I never thought I'd see a horror anthology film where I'd be so disappointed by the ending of every single story. Each segment of Ghost Stories is visually sumptuous, but then they all end in a pitiful fizzle. It's literally two and a half hours of dropping the ball, and they all kind of have the same flavor of failure: heaping loads of intrigue and symbolism that never coalesce, as though every short is about a big reveal that never happens. They are all deliberately vague in a way that is never interesting, and it's a bummer because there is a lot of stellar work on screen. Awesome performances, stellar practical effects and creature design, but alas, they're all undone by the writing.

reviews.text: Abortion, adultery, career, romance, art, independence, friendship, sex, sexual health, rent, space, assertiveness, religion, trust, marriage, and sexuality interact in every day moments, small arguments, disappointments, triumphs, deep conversations, quiet conflicts, and chance meetings. The major dramas are largely eschewed. We don't see the weddings, except still images, black-and-white through the character's lens. Her life is in constant collision with reminders of dependence--not community, not in the film's view--and constraint. She navigates, pushing through narrow tunnels of relationships, jobs, roommates, and responsibilities, holding on dearly to what modicum of freedom she can find. reviews.text: Possibly the most pretentious gentlemen's club since Exotica, but its casual kookiness and oddly avant garde stage acts are a bit more fun. A contrast to most of Abel Ferrara's darker material, this sweetly photographed commedia dell'arte reminded me of Robert Altman's more experimental comic efforts with a shared fondness for overlapping and improvised dialogue, rambling characters--and only the most minimal plot requirements. An odd arthouse ticket that also pleased my voyeuristic side thanks to a stable of lovely naked femmes.

reviews.text: One of the most bizarre ways I’ve ever seen a film shot - this editing is nuts - gave me constant anxiety for the weirdest reason. Like an early 2000’s music video , or a Nine Inch Nails music video too. The music and the flashing colors and lights were really something else. I’m not sure how I felt by the end… it seemed like something the Safdie’s would come up with today for some odd reason. The City tension, the dark humor, the complex angst, and the nonstop commotion. It’s so interesting to see Dafoe in these roles. A film that was barely even shown in the US except NYC. It’s crazy to me because it’s just another Ferrara/Dafoe…

reviews.author: Josiah Morgan
reviews.text: Ferrara pulls together fleeting neon beams obstructed by human bodies to act as a demonstration of freedom, the comedy in Go Go Tales is primarily physical, a relation between body and character that we're trusted to innately understand. The mind of the object and the mind of the owner are one and the same. I wonder, then - is the mind of the viewer and the mind of the viewed symbiotic too? Most Ferrara films seem to crave humanity, but this one craves growth and profit, which is the foundation of all its absurd humor.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: Cohen is one of the few filmmakers after Ford to comprehend and convey the gravitas of violence in America. But, unlike Ford, who approached the essence of violence through the lenses of history, colonialism and expansion, Cohen examines it via religious psychosis as a metaphor for the general sense of paranoia and cruelty that permeates this country—a brutality foundational, inherent in the character of these “United” States. Crises of faith and of nature in a nation always ripe for a reason.

reviews.author: Scott Tobias
reviews.text: Somehow had never seen this until now, despite a longstanding fascination with Cohen and the film's cult reputation. Even knowing Cohen's way with wild genre hooks, I wasn't prepared for how gloriously bugnuts this sci-fi/horror hybrid turned out to be, as a detective investigating a series of strange murders winds up investigating his own supernatural past. Cohen's staging is typically reckless at times, and I don't love Tony Lo Bianco's performance (Robert Forster was originally cast but left a few days into the production; he'd have been perfect), but this is really one-of-a-kind. Cohen's use of real NYC locations is a huge plus, too, when juxtaposed with a story that wouldn't seem to ask for street realism.

reviews.author: Christian Ha
reviews.text: Although Going My Way isn't typically my kind of film, I decided to give it a try given its Best Picture win at the Oscars and because it was a favorite of my dad's when he was younger. The film offered a decent slice of life, with solid performances and production values. While it didn't stand out as exceptional, I found it enjoyable—a whimsical and charming piece. Although it didn't convey anything particularly noteworthy, it did manage to capture some genuine human moments despite its overly sentimental tone. Overall, it's a decent movie, but I definitely wouldn't rank it among the best Oscar winners. It's not a bad film by any means, but it's not outstanding either. Still, I'd recommend it, albeit with some reservations.

reviews.text: At some point in his long and beloved career, Tom Hanks began to transition from America’s sweetheart to America’s serenity. He steeled a troop of soldiers on a veritable suicide mission in “Saving Private Ryan,” remained stoic as Somali pirates hijacked his container ship in “Captain Phillips,” and landed US Airways Flight 1549 in the Hudson without losing a single one of the 155 souls on board in “Sully.” It’s a screen image that has naturally spilled over into real life, as we saw earlier this year when Hanks’ became one of the first major celebrities diagnosed with COVID-19; his fame helped people recognize the reality of the virus, and his composure helped people steel themselves for its imminent arrival…

reviews.author: Sean Fennessey
reviews.text: This was certainly a choice to kick off prep for the Sidney Lumet celebration we’re doing this summer. I’d never seen this one, a very unlikely pairing of Lumet and a script from genremeister Larry Cohen. I’d always assumed it was a typical mid-tier erotic thriller but it’s just a slightly overplayed legal noir melodrama—the movie I kept thinking of while watching was Leave Her to Heaven. It’s not as lush as that, but Don Johnson’s preening, power-suited gigolo is in the same phylum as Gene Tierney’s ghoulish glam gal from hell. So different for Lumet in tone — a slithery little thing, none of the hard bitten, theatrical crime stuff we expect from him. It’s all high rises, high finance, high heat.

reviews.text: Sidney Lumet, the guy known for gritty New York crime thrillers and socially aware dramas, and Larry Cohen, the master of exploitation, seem like a real creative odd couple. Somehow the combination works. Cohen hits on a delightful premise, a sort of reverse Basic Instinct where a female lawyer is drawn to the extremely handsome prime suspect in the murder of his wife, and Lumet mostly plays it straight and follows his actors’ leads. Really, he turns the whole film into a showcase for Don Johnson as the ultimate gigolo, and he’s a total hoot as one of the most punchable movie characters in history. (In one scene, a woman tries to buy him a drink in a bar. He turns her…

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A courtroom drama/erotic thriller hybrid with a very rewarding combination of Sidney Lumet's classier dramatic thrills and Larry Cohen's sillier, raunchier exploitation instincts. It takes the cynical relationship between lawyer and client that crosses lines of power and finance to perversely personal and violent places, the confession stand scene in the empty courtroom + the climactic altercation depicted on the poster are both really good. Also helps that Don Johnson gets to play one of the most obviously guilty, misogynistic murderers to ever grace the screen (a handsome, charming "lady killer" turned literal killer of ladies is how he is described in the text of the movie lmao) and he chews up every damn second of it; just non-stop slimy smirks while relishing in the pure grossness of lines like "killing her with gloves on would be like fucking with a rubber." Jesus Christ, Larry. Hugely underrated in both these filmmakers catalogs.

Harry is a man increasingly displaced by the contemporary world; with his orange cat Tonto, his loyal familiar by his side always., he ventures not so much in search of a place, but in search of significance in a shifting terrain. Through cultural repression, changing values, and the fickle mist of contemporary life, Harry doesn't fit, not into…

reviews.text: There's a scene where John Garfield orders this kid to go get dinner for the family, and he brings back a bag full of Chinese take out boxes along with a giant turkey, but the boxes are stuffed with usual Thanksgiving foods. The boxes, originally known as oyster pails, were designed for fish markets to use as containers to give to customers who bought oysters (you can see the original 1908 patent here). The boxes were designed for the often dirty and smelly molluscs that could be easily thrown out after delivery. Chinese restaurant adapted these boxes as perfect for their often strong smelling and often heavy sauce foods.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: There is order here, not only in the obsessive compositions but in a narrative structure of mirroring symmetry not unlike that of The Deer Hunter. And yet, that arc is subtler here, loosened by the epic scope and refocused elsewhere by its surprising humility. So many moments stick in the mind. Ella stifling a laugh when she sees Nate's mannishly literal idea of wallpaper; her and Jim standing on a lakeshore, arranged right where the sun reflects off the water to backlight them perfectly; the epic ride of the immigrants to war undone before it truly begins by the interlude of a wagon upturning and trapping its riders underwater as the husband tries in vain to save his drowning family. Lines like "It's getting dangerous to be poor in this country" announce the film's themes, yet the depths of Cimino's class commentary, even the basic narrative, are not clear save in retrospect. Fordian ambivalence on a vast scale.

reviews.text: Let's call this a first-time watch, since my only other viewing was the theatrical butchering on VHS. For at least the first third of the film, I thought this was a straight-up masterpiece, an almost impossibly vivid rendering of a conflict that represents so much about American capitalism, tribalism, violence, and injustice. And as thoroughly as Cimino's supposed indulgences have been documented, it's not as if every penny is not up on the screen. But the film *does* feel more and more unwieldy and shapeless as it goes along, particularly in a second half that gives way to chaotic gun battles. Anyway, lots of wonderful stuff here, including one of Christopher Walken's best performances. To include it among the worst films ever — Cimino won a Worst Director Razzie that year, which... fuck off with that— is a travesty, and an example of bad production stories affecting a film's reception.

reviews.text: A lot of people will compare this movie to Jordan Peele’s but let me tell you that not every horror movie involving black people is Get Out. Needless to say that this is a completely different beast in its own league. Not so much scary as it is heartbreaking, His House is one of the very few haunted house movies that provides a good reason why its occupants don’t just leave. It’s a reminder that the ghosts of our homeland follow us wherever we go. They would never leave or abandon us, and neither could we get rid of them. Whether or not these supernatural beings are hostile will depend on how you invite them in.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: We don’t see much of Bol (Sope Dirisu) and Rial’s (Wunmi Mosaku) harrowing journey from war-torn South Sudan to whatever cold pocket of Britain this pair of asylum-seekers hopes to call their new home, just enough to wonder if the various indignities they’re sure to suffer in the country that once colonized their own could possibly be worse or more inhumane than the process of getting there. After escaping from the militias who butchered their families and surviving the perilous sea crossing that claimed their daughter’s young life, Bol and Rial are understandably blank and undaunted by the callousness of the official who conducts their exit interview at the detention center — he’s cold, but death is colder.

reviews.text: Haunting, disturbing, and surprisingly heartbreaking. His House a horror thriller film about a refugee couple who struggles to adjust to their new life, as they are tormented by their traumatic past. Escaping a place, where the threat of being killed is a common occurrence, is commonly regarded as a good thing, but not at the expense of the death of a loved one, and both protagonists, Bol and Rial, experience the haunting of their deceased daughter in a different but shared manner at their new home. Humans process grief in various ways, as some might try to forget and move on, while others cling to the memories of the past, and the movie managed to show this through the characters…

This is a far more commercial effort than director Jun-hee Han's debut, "Coin Locker Girl," but in this case that's hardly a bad thing; and while it takes about an hour to get to the burning rubber you'd expect from a movie called "Hit-and-Run Squad," the increased time spent on developing both the ensemble drama and criminal conspiracy here pays off in a satisfying conclusion in which every character has their role to play.

reviews.author: Nick Dets
reviews.text: It’s not that big of a stretch to call this latter-era entry Lewis’ Bigger Than Life; a dark, even unflinching look at middle-aged suburban malaise and mortality. That it still tries to be a madcap comedy makes it both an entertaining oddity and a frustrating clash of tones. By the midpoint, which introduces Hitchcockian thriller elements, you could be forgiven for checking out entirely. Still, I find Lewis’ work here too fascinating to dismiss. Playing a man so out of touch with himself that his life becomes an absurd farce, he remains dimensional and poignant even when the material is clearly not working. The third act’s blatantly telegraphed twist may be the script’s biggest sin, ultimately sinking this curio entirely.

reviews.author: Sérgio Alpendre
reviews.text: Dos filmes em que Lewis atua para outros diretores após o término de sua rica parceria com Frank Tashlin, que se aposentou após um último filme em 1968, este é sem dúvida o melhor. Não é grande coisa, pois os outros competidores são Boeing Boeing, Way... Way Out e Don't Raise the Bridge, Lower the River. A tentativa de dar um outro direcionamento à sua persona continua. É uma comédia com bem menos burlesco que O Bagunceiro Arrumadinho, por exemplo. Tanto que quando passava na TV, era um dos que eu não gostava muito de ver (mesmo a dublagem era inferior). Na revisão, dá para perceber a boa direção de Marshall e se divertir com os infortúnios do personagem de Lewis em Lisboa.

reviews.author: reener
reviews.text: There's a lot more going on here than anyone will say, it's saturated Jerry, director George Marshall is known for the broader Bob Hope style comedy. The pocket scenes with plot pauses aren't quite done so conventionally, neither is the flashback frame story, though it's at a molecular level. The first hour or so with some occasional spots later it looks closer to a Jacques Tati film than anyone's ever gotten. It's all joy for someone like me but if you're not as staunch the "best" is the introductory scenes, a tunnel of free associative bits, but sight of the God Vestige lies nearly halfway. Jerry is hammered at a Portuguese bar, and after making a version of the Alaskan Polar Bear Heater it turns into an insane, pinpoint sharp vaudeville ballet until he passes out.

Interesting sequence where Jerry is excitedly rushing through his bedtime routine in anticipation to having sex with his wife while the William Tell Overture plays, two years before Clockwork Orange! Anticipates the darkness, despair and emptiness of the later Jerry films.

It never manipulates the emotions nor diverts into criticizing the failing legal system, instead portrays the pain and suffering of the victim and its family straight. The second hour tenderly showcases the mental healing and moments of humanity-compassion among fellow community members, turning spiritually uplifting. The screenplay and the performances from cast were excellent. Love and compassion are the essential tools to overcome the evil in the world. The drama sheds light on the meaningful aspects of life while brimming with hope.

By pure coincidence, Larry Talbot aka The Wolf Man turns up looking fot a cure for his lycanthropy, and then by another coincidental turn of events, the Frankenstein Monster is discovered in a cave near the doctor's house. reviews.author: Digital Press
reviews.text: Immediately following the monster soup that was House of Frankenstein (1944), Universal continued the assembly line with what was originally to be called “Wolf Man vs. Dracula”. Gone are Lugosi and Karloff, but Lon Chaney Jr. returns as the Wolf Man even though he was shot dead with a silver bullet in the last film. Carradine returns as Dracula even though he disintegrated in the sunlight. By this time we are used to these shenanigans! We’re also used to the signatures of these films: there’s a mad doctor (not Frankenstein), the monster, a hunchback assistant, and an angry lynch mob of villagers.
