reviews.text: absolutely brimming with a concrete tenderness, operates as a perfect testament to the endurance of the working class, even in the face of impending adversity. The pioneering spirit of a tight-knit community, placed in the most picturesque setting imaginable, with its flowers, cobbled roads and seemingly-endless woodland vistas, what a delight! As I work my way through Ford's work, it only grows more evident that there haven't been many like him, with the level of empathy and compassion that shines through his films, uncovering each person's potential regardless of their circumstances. Funny that just 5 years ago, I would’ve been so turned off by just how overly-sentimental this all is, but now I completely lap this type of shit up!

reviews.author: Matheus Fiore
reviews.text: Ford foi um dos autores do cinema que melhor entendeu como indivíduo, comunidade e espaço se relacionam e se transformam. Mas, para além disso, conseguiu articular essa dialética na mise-en-scene como pouquíssimos (um punhado, e olhe lá). Em Como Era Verde Meu Vale, a imagem relaciona esses três elementos em histórias sobre infância, família, sociedade, perpassando assuntos como política e economia e analisando como eles afetam e transformam indivíduos e grupos.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: Form as content. The title is not rhetorical nor is it a question at all; it is a statement, and one that we see contradicted as these recollections progress, with Ford’s mise en scène acting as a memorial for the narrative unfolding before us. Compositions at once joyous and mournful, nostalgic yet attentive, anguishing or ecstatic depending on the variation in tone and placement within the story. Images of elegiac delicacy and expanse as seen through the eyes of youth, but filtered retrospectively through reminiscences of a man’s past. And viridescent as the past may have been for him, all colors do fade into black and white but the bittersweet comforts they provide us are as certain as a range is wide. Content as form.

reviews.text: At times, it's almost impossible to believe that Season of the Witch was written and directed by a man, because George Romero's portrayal of the ways in which suburban life was suffocating to women is both thoughtful and remarkably sensitive. Never is Joan Mitchell (Jan White) mocked by the movie for her discontent, or her fears, or even her dabbling in witchcraft. Instead, we see and understand the reasons for her growing desperation — for what, she doesn't know, but if something doesn't change (if she can't cry, or scream, or fuck) we know that might not survive at all.

reviews.text: A drama with feminist leanings directed by the king of zombies, George A. Romero. Hungry Wives (aka The Season of the Witch) is a very interesting movie. It is dialogue-heavy, has surreal flourishes and contains more than a few nightmarish moments. It tells the story of a housewife who dives into witchcraft to escape the monotony of suburban life and an unfulfilling (and abusive) marriage. The movie explores issues as gender roles, the generation gap between parents and children and personal empowerment.

reviews.text: What do you do when your old war buddy is murdered outta the blue? Well, if you're Mike Hammer, you stop at nothing to get revenge. You see, Mike is a PI. He's as smooth with the ladies as Thomas Magnum, and as handy with the steel as Philip Marlowe. Plus, he drives a Z-28, has super sexy secretary named Velda, and dresses like he's John Gotti. He's a macho motherfucker, and he means business. I, the Jury, is an adaptation of a Mickey Spillane novel. It's also a remake of a 1953 movie starring Biff Elliott. The best part? Stepping into Mike's shoes this time around is Armand Assante, and he's lights out.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Very underrated and sleazy neo-noir penned by Larry Cohen that updates Mickey Spillane's mean 1947 revenge novel with lots of lurid 80s detail. CIA conspiracies, seductress psychotherapists, mkultra'd serial killers, etc. Has that goofy paperback private eye charm to it until suddenly it's paranoid, sexual, and gruesomely violent. Great shootouts/squib work. Shot really nicely by Andrew Laszlo (The Warriors, First Blood, Southern Comfort, etc) as well, was glad to see him get the opportunity to flex his skill with boobytraps and sweaty, dirty backwoods chases. Great ending too, how brutally blunt and writerly it is leads me to believe it was taken straight from the book.

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: I've only read a couple of Mickey Spillane's novels at this point, but the appeal of the Mike Hammer character seems to be that he's a brutal thug who just so happens to carry a private dick's license; the reader enjoys seeing him unleashed on the bad guys because, often, he's just as bad. I like Armand Assante well enough as an actor, but in "I, the Jury," he's perhaps a bit too smooth (and small) to portray Spillane's iconic bruiser.

The fact that he spends the movie surrounded by beautiful women while being manipulated by the powers that be in his investigation gives this the affect of wish fulfillment, like he's a guy off a street who won a contest to be a noir hero for a day. What an incredible experience, a film that makes you feel as if you had opened the window of a car on a sun-drenched coastal road and was hit full-on by the wind of time, a very specific time, that smells of cheap gasoline, shared cigarettes, and the illusions of a country running faster than its own dreams can keep up. The year was 1962, and Italy was in the middle of its economic boom, a modernizing miracle that was turning the once agricultural, war-torn country into a nation of brand-new refrigerators, modern televisions, and young people eager to break free from the shadow of their parents. It was in this hurried euphoria that this marvelous film was born, and…

reviews.text: There's a long history of documentary specials in which filmmakers and fans explain the plot of a movie and then describe cool stuff about it. There is also a long history of me digging them. IN SEARCH OF DARKNESS takes that model, chugs a Creatine and cold brew smoothie, and proceeds to roll through some 50+ '80s horror movies over 4.5 hours in chronological fashion. It's marvelous. Most of the discussion is firmly in nostalgia-bound 'if you know you know' territory, but I know, so I was in heaven. Did I need to hear for the seventh or eighth time how fun it was for practical effects and makeup wizard Greg Nicotero to discover Sam Raimi's brilliant Looney Tunes by way of Roger Corman sense of humor during the making of EVIL DEAD II? Well, technically, no. But it never hurts to feel safe.

But leave it to Ben Wheatley — an irrepressible British filmmaker whose best movies (“Kill List,” “High-Rise,” “Sightseers”) have always felt like claustrophobic reactions to the psychic horrors of modern living — to zag where the likes of “Locked Down,” “Coastal Elites,” and “Malcolm & Marie” have zigged, and leverage our suffocating new status quo into an open-air horror movie that will make you never want to go outside again.…

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Incubus" is a 1966 horror film directed by Leslie Stevens. In something that can be described like traditional folk horror meeting "The Twilight Zone" (1959-1964), the film seemingly takes place on a different planet that is not unlike Earth. A good general comparison would be that of "The Wickerman" (1973) but within even further extremes of isolation. Being a film of only a few acting performances, the narrative follows a grouping of otherworldly succubi (female demons) who go about "reaping the harvest" by killing sinners for their dark lord. reviews.text: An interesting film within its gimmick, the one clear thing that is commendable about "Invasion of the Bee Girls" is that it is very much committed to the bit. Any lesser film would take a look at its own absurdity and go full spoof, but "Invasion" relishes in its weirdness and is self-serious about its delivery. In that frame of mind, I found myself appreciating the plot and storyline of the film, really trying to recreate a bit of an atomic era element from the 50's mixed with the late 60's/early 70's exploitation and European wave trends. The plot isn't very expansive but yeah it doesn't really need to be as the embellishment of the kitsch is what is important here. Very much worth a watch if someone comes across this.

reviews.text: One of my favorites. The cynicism and contempt for corporate entertainment in the Donen-Kelly musicals is always cut with a dash of sentiment in the final number. Few movies from the fifties grapple with the encroaching, sponsored fakery that television helped to formalize in American entertainment. These filmmakers are mad about TV, and shoot an urban-set musical in CinemaScope to prove it. Kelly’s roller skates routine is a “Singin’ in the Rain” sequel that has charm and daring, but it’s far from the showstopper. That belongs to Cyd Charisse, one of the more impossible humans to have lived, perhaps never more than during the boxing gym routine here. Plus, Dan Dailey is the greatest tall dancer. Or maybe the tallest great dancer.

reviews.text: I'd always heard this was a downer but nothing this masterful could ever really depress me. The musical numbers are all top-notch, especially Gene Kelly's famous roller-skating solo, which had me unconsciously holding my breath throughout. And the characterizations are SO much better than the usual MGM musical fair - complex, and identifiable in a way that is usually not possible with so much singing and dancing. Throw in some pitch-perfect satire of the TV industry's penchant for cynically maudlin manipulation (something that, alas, has not changed in 60 years), and you've got a musical that hits pretty much all of my buttons. There's even a fight scene at the end!

reviews.text: The kind of "comedy" that could only come out of the 70's: couched in layers of tragic irony and loaded with despicable cretins whose ignorance and selfishness leads to their own (at least moral) downfall. JOE kind of threw me for a loop as I had no idea what direction it was headed and Peter Boyle's titular character is so disgusting that you realize that the movie isn't on anyone's side (except maybe Susan Sarandon's). And boy does Boyle pull out all the stops in his authentic and fairly riveting take on general hateful dumbassery. The tagline "Keep America Beautiful" could easily be swapped out with another famous tagline about America in the remake.

reviews.text: Very crude but ingenuous exploitation of every possible 1970 paranoia generational and class related. A rich text if not much of a movie. Dave Kehr’s capsule written when the movie was probably around a decade old mentions that it had likely dated in a grotesque way and that is probably part of the appeal now as a window into lots of ugly fantasies. It is a shame Avildsen direction lacks more punch. I had forgotten how much Boyle’s casting on Taxi Driver was intended as reference to his work on this one. Screenwriter Norman Weixler also did Serpico, Mandingo and Saturday Night Fever, that must be one of the wildest run of titles from this period of American movies.

reviews.text: After striking at oil, a small community gets suspicious as a stranger rolls into town asking about the rich land’s previous resident. There is a charming routine with Claude Adkin and Lee Van Cleef as a pair of perpetually amused roughnecks, and the duo's ten minutes of screen time is a delight. Even though the subject matter involves murder, the costumes and set design reflect a softer west - closer in tone to Seven Brides for Seven Brothers. Minimal gunplay makes this more of a drama than your traditional western, but those that can keep up with its slower pace are treated to a wild fight in the middle of a gushing oil vein.

reviews.author: arkheia
reviews.text: A subdued B-western that slipped between the cracks underneath comparable films like Bad Day at Black Rock (1955). The film follows Jack Mahoney as a mysterious stranger who rides into an isolated town in search of his friend Joe Dakota but instead uncovers a dark secret behind the citizens and their local oil well. Mahoney saunters around the townsfolk with a calm aloofness. Even as he’s still learning everything, his reserved exterior keeps the villains guessing exactly how much he does know every step of the way. As he eventually finds his worst suspicions confirmed, he’s neither surprised nor outwardly upset but almost expectant of the town’s violent secret. His curious response may be representative of a post-WW2 America, internalizing…

En eso me recordó al plano con que terminaba hace dos días Mies vailla menneisyyttä, de Kaurismäki, en que los protagonistas avanzaban hacia el fondo del plano y se perdían en su paisaje urbano tras cruzar unas vías que, eventualmente, un tren cruzaba perpendicular a la dirección del foco. The wholesome and romanticized American B–western (no better symbolized than in the angelic Luana Patten) starts getting perverted by glimpses of darkness and avarice. Another early secondary appearance in which Lee Van Cleef leaves a strong impression (before the Eyetalians turned him into a bona fide star). And that climactic scene at the exploding oil well becomes almost something expressionistic — not to mention a dramatic inversion of the more comical first time we encounter said location in the movie.

reviews.author: solh
reviews.text: Harmony in a small oil-drilling town is disrupted by a visit from a stranger in search an Amerindian acquaintance in this western starring Jock Mahoney. The film is loaded with tension throughout due to how elusive the stranger is about why he wants to see the Amerindian, as well as how suspiciously unwelcoming the townsfolk are. The mystery of what exactly is amiss is very intriguing. Less successful are some detours towards romance with Luana Patten actually coming off as a bit of an annoying character, especially as her gullibility is pointed out late in the piece. The supporting characters are generally great here though with such hostility quivering only just below their surface and there are several memorable stretches as strong personalities clash, most notably Mahoney subverting a bar game where they knock each other off stools.

reviews.author: Trace Thurman
reviews.text: Johnny Frank Garrett's Last Word (formerly just The Last Word) is a stupid movie. That may seem like shallow criticism but it is in fact a stupid movie that thinks it's a lot smarter than it is, which makes it even worse. Directed by Simon Rumley (Red, White and Blue), the film plays like a Lifetime movie that had a baby with a SyFy movie. While that may sound like good trashy fun, it's actually the exact opposite. Johnny Frank Garrett's Last Word is a dull exercise in pretension whose only true saving grace is the fact that it runs at a mercifully brief 95 minutes.

reviews.author: Travis Lytle
reviews.text: "Johnny Frank Garrett's Last Word" tries very hard to make an impact. Telling the story of a convict who curses the people of Austin, Texas as his life expires on the executioner's table, the horror film boasts some earnest performances, at least one investable character, and a swing at period flair. That story, however, is flimsy at best and generic at worst, offering very little that genre fans will find original or satisfyingly gripping. The production treads the line between capably constructed chiller with a limited budget and artless, digitally shot eyesore that can not crawl out from beneath its faux sepia filter. The work is a case of the solid and not-so-solid, but the not-so wins out.

A particular juror that convicted Johnny is now on a quest to see if Johnny's in fact innocent and tries to stop the curse that seems to be putting his family at risk. If you're familiar with director Simon Rumley then you know this guy doesn't pull any punches on his films. He knows how to upset you, scare you and rattle your nerves. Nice performances and Rumley's camerawork here is excellent. Fluid, frightening, suspenseful. There was a real Johnny Frank Garrett that was wrongly executed in 1992 for the rape and murder of a nun, just like here. Nice possession, devil inside film. Check it.

This movie is no exception either. We have no maps in this film, and no wonder! It ultimately boils down to an amiable juror (Park Hyung-sik) consistently vexing a reasonable…

reviews.text: A house with no base seems to hover above the trampled dirt, rusty wrenches, and scrap metal surrounding it. Dog mask to hide the teardrops. See a man; shake a hand. Minding the gaps and clearing them. Contriving a crooked smile. Holy motor, blocks busted; no use now. Shirtless and slow dancing, she feels my skin, rough as a ram horn; her fingers are a crisp sip of cool water in the dregs of August. Lives like dried dust of this bitter earth, that is, forgotten, stowed away like sheep to the slaughter.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: this cautious ennui of poverty that seeps in through makeshift spaces and broken promises -- "that's the way nature is." the ironic refrain of music emerging from inside docu-drama surfaces aligns burnett's film with both a populist vernacular and the alienated post-war tradition, i felt killer of sheep was quite close to the loose qualities of king vidor's the crowd and susumu hani's she and he, a type of cinema that calculatedly presents the feeling of spontaneous action and rides that tension. the matchcuts that burnett employs are very lively and give definitive formal shape to a seemingly 'plotless' film, and i adore the warmth of this film's black & white off-center compositions, there are several 70s trends in cinematography that i feel were deleterious to cinematic language writ large, but burnett avoids all of them and constructs his own unsteady beauty.

reviews.author: Sean Baker
reviews.text: Larry Cohen is the ultimate guerrilla filmmaker. Driving a cab on to and down a pedestrian filled sidewalk in New York City sans permits or safety measures is quite reckless but Cohen got away with a career full of these stunts. So the stories of stealing shots and scenes are both fascinating and inspiring while being incredibly cringe-inducing. I couldn't help but think of tragedies such as Sarah Jones's death on the set of Midnight Rider and the deaths of Vic Morrow and two child actors, Renee Shinn Chen and Myca Dinh Le on the set of The Twilight Zone. (Btw, Landis was interviewed for this doc).

reviews.text: King of the Rocket Men is an old adventure film from the 1940s about a scientist who becomes a masked hero with a jetpack to stop a mysterious villain. It’s not a very deep movie, but it has a certain charm: the costumes are retro, the special effects are a bit stiff (even funny today), but you can feel the creativity and the desire to make people dream. reviews.text: Even more than it's a movie about male friendship, Kings of the Road is a movie about communication. About the way men have been trained to avoid intimacy with one another; about the fact that they can only connect through humor, and gesture, and shared adventures. About how it's become nearly physically impossible for men to speak about emotions, leaving them so desperate for release that they turn to loops of film, or the printed and written word as refuge. About how they laugh, and clown, and fight, because those are the only emotions they're allowed to share.

reviews.text: I really don’t like to take an artist’s sexuality into consideration when looking at their work, simply because I believe art comes through a person, not from a person, from a place where we’re all one and without an ego. But there’s something to be said about the way Visconti, who was gay, chooses, lights, portrays men. And not in a superficial way—his characters are rarely drop dead gorgeous, nor does he use the camera to make love to them or anything like that. I really don’t quite know how to put it, other than maybe, just maybe, he understands men a little better, he really shows them from the inside out. And there’s something about the way he carries them into my world that moves me—with a raw gentleness, and they always stay.

Lejos de Vittorio de Sica y Roberto Rossellini tiene tanto de neorrealista como de cuento tenebroso a la manera de Tragica notte de Soldati u Ossessione del propio Visconti, pero ampliando el foco de manera gigantesca. Es al mismo tiempo un registro etnográfico de una sociedad minúscula y llamada a las armas de todos los desfavorecidos, de una forma tan sencilla, sin caer en panfletos ni en delirios espectaculares. Es un milagro que esto exista.

reviews.text: "The Blonde Fury" or "The Lady Reporter" (as my Vinegar Syndrome copy has it titled) is a 1989 martial arts film directed by Mang Hoi. As the film centers on Cynthia Rothrock in the central role, her character is an undercover FBI agent who is under the guise of a news reporter in order to investigate a counterfeiting outfit. All the beginnings for cohesive narrative are there, but quickly the film just takes the route of being all over the place, leading most viewers to check out on much of the storyline. It doesn't matter anyways because you get Rothrock doing some quirky martial arts hijinks in this film that has a cartoonish delivery.

reviews.author: BeardofTsu
reviews.text: My first Cynthia Rothrock movie of the year is the 21st film of hers that I've logged. "Lady Reporter" isn’t one of her best. The story is overly convoluted, making it hard to stay focused outside the action sequences. In this film, Cynthia plays an undercover FBI agent sent to Hong Kong to investigate a counterfeiting ring led by the villainous Ronny Dak. She teams up with a group of bumbling characters, and the film takes on a comedic tone with jokes that mostly fall flat, causing me to zone out at times until an acrobatic fight that showcased Cynthia's skills brought me back to life! The fantastically choreographed bamboo scaffold scene is just one example of this. Overall, it’s…

reviews.author: threepenny
reviews.text: Cynthia Rothrock, at the top of her game, in the first of her three-picture deal with Golden Harvest, and even today it is still astonishing to see this blonde gweilo starring - STARRING - in a Hong Kong picture. And you can just feel the love coming off the production for her and presenting her in the best possible light, what with her friend Mang Hoi behind the camera and later, Corey Yuen creating a jaw-dropping action climax. Can you imagine if all three of her Golden Harvest pictures were like this??? But alas, by the time this one hit screens after it got shelved and re-worked, Golden Harvest execs had already moved her to America and China O'Brien 1…

reviews.author: Gregor Kreyca
reviews.text: The action, co-choreographed by Corey Yuen, is really top notch here. On that front, The Blonde Fury aka. Lady Reporter really is one of Cynthia Rothrock better movies. Unfortunately, I did not care much about everything in-between the fight scenes. The plot was a bit boring and the comedy mostly unfunny. Still, for Hong Kong action movie fans and fans of Cynthia Rothrock it is absolutely worth a look. The new Eureka Blue-ray looks great and has some decent extras including a good interview with Cynthia. So, recommended, but only for fans of the star and genre.

reviews.text: Janicza Bravo makes bold choices in her feature debut to varying degrees of success, but they're all fascinating at the least. Co-written by Bravo and her husband/lead actor Brett Gelman, the script itself is pretty damn weird, but it's the direction she takes it in that makes Lemon so compelling. Her blocking of the actors alone is something remarkable–the juxtaposition of characters sitting perfectly still in front of a passionately dancing crowd, having them sit back-to-back in dialogue scenes. Her confidence behind the camera transfers over to the edit, as many of the shots are notably unusual in their sequence. The abstract, self-aware editing by Joi McMillon incorporates the film's surrealism and absurdity into its form. It's effective in creating…

reviews.text: Cursed with a capital C, Lemora is a dreamlike (or nightmarish, honestly) story of a young girl making her way through the unknown at the invitation of a handwritten letter – with gangster daddies, suspicious bus drivers, terrifying old women singing songs, vampires, and diseased monsters once human – with terrors abound, supernatural or not.

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: the incoherence of the style here is actually to its benefit: lemora feels like a film on the verge of collapsing under the weight of the unease and terror that it depicts, as if it can barely contain its own images, the maximalist excess bleeding outside the cobalt lights, vibrating at an unknown frequency. one of those stories that is suffused with too many ideas for its short runtime, everything's coated in thematic and imaginal bombast, a lovecraftian/lesbian fantasy that scares and enchants in equal measure; truly unique!

reviews.author: Hamza
reviews.text: Putting aside the surface layer, the brutality of nature and the characters mentally falling apart, what really got me about this film is how it lowkey flips a propaganda setup into something way more human and conflicted. It looks like it’s playing along with Soviet ideology, but underneath it’s poking holes in it. I love how Mikhail Kalatozov pulls this off while still operating within those constraints. There’s this subtle mockery of officialdom running through the film, on one hand you’ve got these characters in absolutely life or death situations, and on the other, this weirdly cheerful, patriotic tone that is detached & hypocritical. It ends up exposing how blind indifferent the system can be.

reviews.author: Dirk Diggler
reviews.text: Damn. I actually loved this even more than The Cranes Are Flying. It starts out as a melodrama with a rather conventional and straight-forward story and simplistic characters, but it simultaneously has strong realism, humanism and impressionistic qualities which makes it a rather moving and visceral tour de force. Its a tale of man versus nature with a good amount of romance and an intense, tragic and existential survival adventure set in the unforgiving Siberian wilderness. The cinematography is absolutely-fucking breathtaking, surprise surprise its a Kalatozov+Urusevsky collaboration, which is of course THE highlight of the film. Hands down one of the most beautifully and intensely shot films I've ever seen with its gliding wide-angled tracking shots and intimate close-ups. The…

reviews.author: Kenta Suzuki
reviews.text: Letter Never Sent is an underrated film by Mikhail Kalatozov with a basic story about four scientists who find diamonds in Siberia and go through a challenging condition. The film definitely has one of the greatest cinematography of all time. It's a great showcase of how technical prowess and skills in filmmaking can create the perfect atmosphere for a movie. Mikhail Kalatozov masters lighting, shadows, cinematic techniques and camera angles in this film with an absolutely breathtaking cinematography by Sergei Urusevsky.

reviews.text: Lingui, the Sacred Bonds is a powerful and emotional experience, one that deals with tough topics in a matter-of-fact way. These topics, of abortion and rape, need to be discussed and Lingui presents them through circumstances which are not contrived. As the characters live in a strict Islamic world, they are heavily restricted in what they can do. However what most stands out about Lingui is the unity of women and the sisterhood they create to help each other deal with problems they know exist but have no power to prevent. Men get away with everything, while women must keep secret their pains. The lead character is a woman shamed, since she is a single mother and hence an outcast.…

reviews.text: Written and directed by Mahamat Saleh Haroun, Lingui, The Sacred Bonds is an emboldening drama about a Muslim woman who despairingly attempts to assist her daughter get an abortion when it is morally and lawfully prohibited. Haroun shoots the film beautifully with a pleasing aesthetic that gives rise to a clear and pertinent statement about the people of Chad, a country in north-central Africa. Early in the story, 15-year-old Maria is expelled from her school for being pregnant, and it rapidly becomes evident that the girl wants an abortion. Working alongside Haroun, who happens to be the first Chadian full-length film director, is cinematographer Mathieu Giombini. Giombini discovers elegance with the most unexpected angles and spaces, especially in the film's…

reviews.author: clare
reviews.text: The most truly dreamlike of Bava's films. The way it is edited and structured epitomizes dream logic. There are many sudden breaks to different scenes or locations with no explanation. Even the opening scene makes sense only in a dream context: Lisa gets off a bus and a tour guide is immediately waiting to tell them about a fresco of the devil. Lisa then decides to head to an antique shop (which she likely couldn't have known about). But the motivation is pushed along by dream inertia. This is just where it flows. Then suddenly the streets are all empty. Later on, the house flickers, scene to scene, back and forth between full, lush furnishing and ancient rot. Corridors seem…

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Mario Bava GOD of the gory, gothic art deco waking nightmare delivers 95 straight minutes of "what the fuck is even happening?" setpieces. Little bit of Carnival of Souls in here, little bit of Vertigo, all wrapped up in a gruesome, dreamy cycle of death stemming from romantic jealousy, oedipal complexes and guilty memories that then take the shape of artificial statues/dummies? No clue. But incredible colors, reflections, camera movements, music, vibes, etc. Loved it. Probably should’ve expected it of these Italian freaks by now but was still shocked by the creepy sex scene next to the art-designed corpse and the guy getting run over by a car in graphic on screen detail no less than 6 times.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: The perfect Mario Bava movie. It is all beautiful surfaces and mannequins ready to be smashed. A movie about getting trapped in an image that is seductive and violent, about how the attraction to beauty brings with it its own destruction. Bava barely even tries with plot, despite lots of decadent aristocrats' drama, he knows Elke Sommer in great outfits and sets while a series of dolls are arguing and murdering each other is all any movie needs. Plus, there is Telly Savallas having a blast as the butler/emcee/filmmaker stand-in. By the end, Bava has exhausts his cinema. There is nothing left, but Rabid Dogs raw misanthropy.

reviews.text: Neorealism isn't usually this funny or sweet, but maybe if there'd been an actual American school that wasn't tied to film noir and crime stories, it would be. As is this is an easy home run thanks to the admittedly low-hanging fruit of bittersweet childhood, but it plucks it off the tree without any false sentiment. That's not really why I love the movie though - that would be because it's also one of the all-time best time capsules ever put on film, at its best it's an impossibly immersive documentary about Coney Island in the 1950s, focused on the things that documentaries (and home movies) usually capture only marginally.

reviews.text: This was unsettling of a film I have seen in a while. When city couple Peter and Marcia who are having marriage problems decide to go camping over the holiday weekend. After a total disregard for nature and the wildlife including Peter running over a kangaroo in a pretty graphic scene, strange things start to occur. We later learn Marcia had an abortion and she starts to hear what she thinks is a baby crying but Peter laughs it off as just an animal in distress. Both characters are unlikable whose behavior only seems to get worse and further damage the area and cause the wildlife more distress. Nothing is really explained and you are left to speculate if there were supernatural events happening or not. Some beautiful cinematography and excellent performances from John Hargreaves and Briony Behets make this an absolute delight to watch unfold. Atmospheric horror at its very best. Definitely my kinda shit.

reviews.text: The beginning of this film absolutely astounds me. We're given a methodical, subtle, and unsympathetic look into the wordless lives of several teens in St. Petersburg, Florida following the death of Tyron Lewis and subsequent riots of 1996. These opening minutes of Fuller's film offer a startling and unique representation of racial hatred, complete with unsimulated fistfights, before abandoning the topic altogether once Cale (played by the director in a blank, emotionless performance) and Nicole begin talking to each other, shifting the incredibly prevalent theme of racial tension towards an aimless depiction of adolescent loneliness? Keith Morris' narration fails to add any substance to the bored angst of the film's characters, and it doesn't matter how artistic the sound design…

reviews.text: For nearly 20 years, Long Island was home to a serial killer. This still-unidentified devil is believed to have murdered 10-16 sex workers from 1996 to 2013, approximately. These heinous acts went unnoticed by law enforcement for almost two decades, and it’s this dark crime that documentary filmmaker, Liz Garbus, explores in her first narrative feature film, Lost Girls. Specifically, the film follows the disappearance of 24-year-old Shannan Gilbert and the investigation (or lack thereof) into her possible murder that leads to a trail of corpses – the unsolved cases of more than a dozen missing and murdered sex workers.

reviews.text: It works so well, even when you don't expect it to. And it works completely against the odds. reviews.author: Ziglet_mir
reviews.text: Love is an intangible thing and it is therefore fascinating to see it represented by other intangibles, symbolized by endearing hobbies that evoke inward machinations. 1939’s Intermezzo implements a metaphor of music to help interpret the love story. Transitional scenes are used as little reprieves, or decrescendos (at pianissimo), that intermingle with the heavier accented plot moments. Music has the ability to overwhelm the human senses as does love. Music truly, has the power to tap into any or most emotions, to describe the things that are seemingly out of reach. All the pieces to a composition are the idiosyncrasies required to provide such depth, volume, and dynamic.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: My previous viewing of this on DVD on a tiny tube television prevented me from appreciating it as much as I did today. I've always thought of Welles' Othello as Shakespeare Noir, and now I see Macbeth as his Shakespeare Expressionist Horror. It looks more like James Whale's Frankenstein than your average, or even above average, Shakespeare adaptation. As Hannah noted on Twitter, the visual motif in Othello is one of traps and enclosures, while here it is wide open nightmare landscapes, shadows and fog. The rolling mist in the "tomorrow and tomorrow" soliloquy forms a visual rhyme with the smoke from the chimney in Citizen Kane as Rosebud burns. The search for meaning in identity and actions proves elusive,…

reviews.author: comrade_yui
reviews.text: a king anointed by christians but puppeted by druid witchery -- blood marked by a madness inherent to fate, where non-human powers dictate human emotions -- the chiming of bells and thunderclaps hath made him bold, and unwise, and madder still. the use of skyward negative space reminds us of mizoguchi's myths and anticipates late-malick -- low-budget expressionism for republic pictures reveals welles as the most-germanic of the non-german hollywood auteurs, unruly theatricality anchored by an unbearable heaviness of perspective -- the fetish of the voodoo statue makes golems of men, mistakes soldiers for trees, conflates the animal and the mineral worlds -- the animate becomes inanimate, out brief candle, the throne is a stone -- no men of women born.

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Welles goes all in imagining MacBeth as self delusion nightmare full of great gothic touches. reviews.author: Channing Pomeroy
reviews.text: Welles’ experimental B-movie Macbeth is something of a miracle. He cut a deal with Republic Pictures, known best for singing cowboy oaters, for $700,000 to film his recent stage production using some some leftover sets, costumes that are an odd mix of Tartan, Tartar, and Statue of Liberty. For comparison, Olivier’s Hamlet, filmed contemporaneously had a $2.1MM budget. The result is uneven but such a visually powerful film that I think next time I will watch it on mute, perhaps with some favorite music playing.

reviews.author: Geoffrey Broomer
reviews.text: Gathering his future wild bunch, Sam Peckinpah used the studio system to make for the Mexican border - burning bridges along the way. Before the dirty dozen made convict soldiers en vogue, Major Dundee saw a company of Union officers with their Confederate prisoners and makeshift militia chasing a group of Apache renegades. Heston is our title character, hard to like, and a veritable Captain Ahab in his single minded pursuit of the Apache leader. Sam Peckinpah redefines meta, also hard to like as Captain Ahab in his single minded pursuit of self-destruction through the white whale that is Major Dundee. Blue or gray, this wears its troubled production on its sleeve - proudly displaying grizzly war wounds earned in a conflict that never gave it a second thought.

reviews.author: Daniel88
reviews.text: Major Dundee can perhaps best be described as the dress rehearsal for Peckinpah’s magnum opus The Wild Bunch. Thematically and even to some extent stylistically you can see the resemblance with one of the greatest westerns in movie history, but Major Dundee still has the look and feel of a John Ford cavalry epic – not that there’s anything wrong with that. Dundee is a fun movie, but much like Wayne’s The Alamo (1960), it tries to be a long epic whereas it would have worked so much better as just a normal action driven western with a lot more editing (the entire Heston-recovering-from-his-wounds-and-feeling-pity-for-himself-in-Durango sequence could have been cut). reviews.text: Charlton Heston leads a company of Union cavalry and Confederate POWs across the Rio Bravo pursuing an Apache band that has taken into their fold some American children who they captured after killing everyone during a raid at a ranch. It's an uneasy alliance held together by the cool actors in other films by Sam Peckinpah, specifically Warren Oates, Ben Johnson, L.Q. Jones, R.G. Armstrong, plus James Coburn and Richard Harris. The chase across the river into Mexico for the kids isn't too far from John Ford's "Rio Grande" . The shots of men mounted on horseback in twos also kind of looked like Ford's "The Horse Soldiers". But Mexico is pure Peckinpah and there's nothing wrong with borrowing from the classics to make a badass western.

reviews.author: Adam Nayman
reviews.text: There’s a great essay waiting to be written about Bill Pullman as the ur-cuck of 90s American studio cinema; I count three notable neo-noirs (The Last Seduction, Lost Highway and Malice) that depend on his plausibility as a guy who could score a hot girlfriend and then drive her to cheat via his own passivity. Credit Aaron Sorkin for saddling Pullman’s character here with what might be the most emasculating twist in erotic thriller history: my client can’t be a serial sex killer, your honour, because he’s shooting blanks, and by the same logic, he couldn’t have knocked up Nicole Kidman, either. Overall, the laughing-with to laughing-at ratio here is about 50/50, but what matters, I think, is that it’s funny - the final reveal with the neighbor’s kid must have brought the house down in a crowded theater in 1993.

Bava, Bergman, Buñuel, and Has all come to mind as a bunch of Flemish family members collectively lose their minds while stuck in Orson Welles' titular estate (I still can't quite pronounce the name even after hearing it repeated for 2 hours). A little slow to start but it really takes off in the second half with lots of fantastic moments I won't spoil or soon forget. And that house is prime real estate for anyone who's ever wanted to live in the Haunted Mansion or on Ash Tree Lane.

reviews.text: Watching Shinya Tsukamoto carry a camera around, exploring the darkest corners of the world in pursuit of answers regarding fear and death is so satisfying. After a few Ju-on movies, I wasn't on the Takashi Shimizu train, as I found them to be mostly monotonous exercises that failed to sustain a chilling atmosphere. However, Marebito has me interested in continuing to work through his filmography. It's gripping from start to finish, primarily focusing on a flawed and unhinged character that's worth following if you're looking to be unsettled.

reviews.author: Robert Cettl
reviews.text: Andrei Konchalovsky is an intriguing case within American film. An accomplished Russian director he managed to leave the Soviet Union in the early 1980s and work (or worm) his way into Hollywood filmmaking, apparently at the invitation of noted actor Jon Voight. Although there may be many that lamented the eventual dissipation of his directorial talents on such fare as the Sylvester Stallone / Kurt Russell vehicle Tango & Cash, for a while in the 1980s Konchalovsky was one of the most dynamic filmmakers in America, thanks to such stunning initial works as Maria’s Lovers and Runaway Train, the latter finally uniting him with Voight. The delicate analysis of complex human emotions in Maria’s Lovers was all the more unusual in…

reviews.author: José Luis Guarner
reviews.text: Esta es una película claramente fallida, pero también una de las más atractivas que en los últimos tiempos vio el cronista; en cualquier caso, una absoluta curiosidad. La historia es extrañísima, algo en torno a un marido impotente, cuya esposa virginal se hace preñar por un trovador ambulante para recuperar a su consorte —una estrategia cuya verosimilitud terapéutica, dramática o mítica resulta más que discutible. Es, seguramente, la lógica consecuencia de transplantar un cuento de Platonov del siglo XIX a un pueblo industrial de Pensilvania en 1945, y de la notoria incomodidad con que el director —un ruso seguramente pudoroso— aborda un material erótico al que, a todas luces, no está acostumbrado.

reviews.author: ethelred
reviews.text: Over the course of his lengthy career, the Soviet writer/director/special effects wizard Pavel Klushantsev only made one pure narrative film, Planet of Storms. The rest of his filmography consisted of a rather unique blending of science documentary with narrative science fiction film. In Road to the Stars, Klushantsev runs down the history and workings of rocket science before launching into a speculative segment on life on space stations followed by human colonization of the moon and other planets (all featuring some dazzling special effects that clearly inspired Stanley Kubrick's 2001). reviews.text: A movie that much like the experience of its central character/performance asks you to open yourself up to the acoustic and psychological vibrations that connect our bodies to the earth and the earth to the great other. If you're willing to meet it it's a place of ghostly movements, alien sounds, and graceful landscapes; the only place where history, memory, and dreams all coalesce into an organically broadcasted, constantly flowing, echoing stream of ambient sensory (un)consciousness. It feels like an attempt at translating the impossible, or at least coming to some sort of terms with it, an attempt I ultimately found quite scary and moving simultaneously.

There is no other film which feels like this: like the whole world has been hollowed-out and made into a barely convincing deathtrap constructed by death itself for those still alive. The Revolution has failed. The Establishment is entirely discredited. All of Western Civilization is a rudderless ghost ship, a Marie Celeste awaiting its Captain of the Damned, its Nightmare Messiah. The only other film which really captures the spooky isolation of small towns along the California Coast is John Carpenter's 'The Fog', but that is a localized apocalypse. 'Messiah…

reviews.text: The plot, what little there is of one, is very Lovecraftian - endless flight through a seaside town, followers of an obscure sect pursuing you even in your sleep, locked up safe in your motel. But there's an overriding voice that is reminiscent of Shirley Jackson - events taking on intimate, sinister undertones that echo and echo through claustrophobic domesticity just starting to sprawl out into a post-war infinity.

reviews.author: Ian West
reviews.text: An unsung classic of 70's horror, Messiah of Evil is an ultra eerie and unsettling nightmare—a grimly fiendish offbeat art horror masterpiece that oozes the kind of succulent dream dread slathered atmosphere that drives me wild. This is a hazy transmission from another world that’s equal parts Romero's Dead universe and say… Carpenter’s Antonio Bay, both by way of Lovecraft and Carnival of Souls… which is probably one of the most appealing things ever for me. Discovering movies like this is why I watch movies—this is essential 70's horror with unmatched tone and easily one of my favorite films of any genre.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: At first, I was put off by the lack of a reveal (of what, I fittingly won't say! sooo myster--no, I just don't want to spoil it), but as I listened to the closing moments repeat the opening narration, it all clicked. The filmmakers took to heart the fear of the unknown idea and suffused their entire film with it. They're not going for shock (though some moments are shocking) or gross-out (though some moments are gross); they're going for unnerving, creepy, and mysterious. While some explanations are given, there's still lingering questions when it all comes to a close, by design.

reviews.text: A pure atmosphere combination of like 4-5 different genres I already love individually: the Romero-esque societal sickness/breakdown movie, sleepy coastal cosmic horror, surreal gothic Italian set pieces, and religious cannibal cowboys. This thing has got it all and is basically 90 straight minutes of amazing location work/set design, painterly colors, strange music, wandering waking nightmare imagery, and the pervading feeling of overwhelming, inescapable doom.

reviews.author: Matt!
reviews.text: Doom. Gloom. Dread. The stuff of nightmares that begin as daydreams, permeating through your soul like a whisper on the wind, beckoning you towards the beautifully dark ocean waves gently roaring as they crash onto dusk-lit beaches in the dead of night. Desolate downtown streets. Deserted parking lots. Barren supermarkets. Creepy wall art that follows your shadow. Movie theaters whose sinister emptiness echoes until vacant faces begin to quietly inhabit the uninhabited spaces. The spooky atmospheric eeriness of a seaside town where folks stand silent and motionless and watch you from off in the distance, with hints of Romero and sudden cosmic horror that’ll have you bleeding from your eyes. The ending loses me, but the build up to get there is something few films have managed to capture. P.S. If you’re seeking shelter, stay away from anywhere with a sunroof.

reviews.author: ozora
reviews.text: Suprising drama about the existential crisis of a woman that feeling to have past her prime is being pushed by work and love life in an unconfortable corner. And she decides to push back, uncaring about the methods, just urged by the need to feel on the winning side of life again. Under the appearance of a pretty conventional romance drama, the movie develops a great character study, laying its strenght on a solid characterization. Everyone behaves on a relatable, flawed way. Chasing his/her own selfish needs, no matter the stepping stones they pass over. And that doubles for the protagonist, a very complex and layered character that during the movie evolves, fighting to overcome the victimized passive role she feels the world has cut out for her. And building for herself the new aggressive, manipulative role she think is necessary to get the happiness she feels deserving. Until that crashes down with reality in a bold, bitter, shocking epilogue.

reviews.author: Vince The Cinephile
reviews.text: Hong Khaou (Lilting) directs a luminous Henry Golding as a gay man who returns to Vietnam to reconnect with his roots. Khaou’s films are always a joy to watch as he brings a certain lightness and distinct emotional quality to the mundane. His characters are always melancholic, and on a journey of self-discovery. But in this story however, it feels there’s more to unpack, more to be said which are left unexplored. Monsoon lingers too much on Golding’s beautiful, sensitive gaze to express its gaps, but that’s not enough. The film has so many insightful thoughts and ideas but it has no coherent way of exhibiting it on screen. Anyhow, Golding has a star quality that is rare of a leading man: soft masculine gaze with a relatable appeal. Overall, Monsoon has a strong potential that is underdeveloped. It kept me hanging, and thinking of things on how it would make this film better.

The one thing that aged poorly about this documentary is that there are some anti-woke YouTubers in this documentary such as Tyrone Magnus and Chris Gore. reviews.text: Yesterday saw a rare screening of Kevin Brownlow's near-mythic five-and-a-half-hour reconstruction of Abel Gance's silent film Napoleon, a labour of love that has dominated more than 50 years of the historian's life, but has never been available on home video, and maybe never will be, due to ongoing and thorny contract wrangles with Francis Ford Coppola, who has his own version, which is incomplete, runs at the wrong speed and has a score written by his dad.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: There are films that entertain us, films that move us, films that make us think. And then there is Abel Gance’s Napoleon, which goes beyond any of these categorizations, a cinematic storm that sweeps you up and throws you directly into the hurricane of History, into the whirlwind of revolution, and into the unbreakable spirit of a man who shaped his time. Watching this film is an overwhelming experience, a dizzying jump into the essence of cinema as an absolute art. For anyone who considers themselves a cinephile, this will never be a recommendation, but an obligation in the name of art. (if you study cinema theory you will have to watch anyway)

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: In the early 1800s, Ludwig van Beethoven was writing his third symphony in honor of Napoleon Bonaparte. It was a paean to the (as Beethoven perceived him) military genius and liberator from Corsica, and it only became known as Eroica (as opposed to simply being named for Napoleon) in the wake of Napoleon's turn toward "true imperialism" after becoming officially the Emperor of France. Others alive at the time (and later, of course), viewed him as a tyrant, a villain. Before Hitler became a byword for evil, many Europeans used "Napoleon" as the point of comparison for all the evil of humanity. The truth of the matter is, as ever, in between the two, I am sure, but this film…

reviews.text: Trying to be romantic in a world that has reduced human connection to transactions: sex objects, hazy video images, bank account numbers and anonymous cityscapes, hotel rooms, and screens. Ferrara's minimalist, lo-fi vision of cyberpunk is to die for—all mundane spaces abstracted by intense close-ups, lighting, cross-fades, and strange, fragmented compositions on extremely long lenses with the occasional dreamy musical interlude. One of the rawest expressions of horniness, alienation, and despair put to screen. "Falling in love without falling in love."

reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: Desire in a transactional world that has rendered actual physical emotion complete imaterial. A movie made against a world it abhors. It is a thriller that intentionally jettison its entire plot and is pretty much compromised of leftover scenes. Everything movies have trained us to regard as important is off-screen or at best seen in monitors, instead you most get to watch a bunch of scene between three people, a series of smokescreens and emotional manipulations that matter because the movie give us time to understand how the trio acts of each other and makes those actions have weight. It is movie very much concerned with the idea of consumption and spectatorship and one predicted in how lived experience and…

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: I raise you all to name a film which reveals itself more and more upon each repeat viewing! I stand by thinking that probably more than any other film that one viewing is not enough. The first image we see is Dafoe behind a reflection in a door, equally abstracting and obfuscating him. Obfuscation is a clue - this is a film about images but not the meanings behind images or metaphors through images, but rather the falsity and unreliability of images. To my mind it's the greatest film on the subject of representation I have yet seen (well, and Fort Apache). The Gibson is all still there, and I cover most of that in the last thing I wrote…

reviews.text: Every powerful force remains carefully at the borders or just offscreen as the camera focuses on a series of performed gestures and the eyes that consume them. Ferrara remains impressively disciplined into Defoe's POV, at the lowest and most clueless end of the intrigue, not that it matters as much as the multiple impressions the movie can get around its corporate espionage. A movie about a world that is consistently disintegrating while trying to focus on the desire of something of it to be real (Argento’s performance foremost or Defoe/Ferrara perception of it). How it observes the consequences while extending this desire through 90 minutes would already be an achievement. 21st-century cinema did peak in 1998.

reviews.text: Ferrara’s most remarkable film because of its incompleteness, which due to the nature of the medium (in dissolves, cuts, ellipses), is a totality by omission. That Sandii is Pandora armed not with a box but a computer disc is an afterthought. What is truly disconcerting is the fusion between dream, memory, and video recording that permeates throughout the film. X’s recollections during the latter half of the film in particular constitute a cinematic stream of consciousness that I’ve only encountered with similar strength in Edvard Munch (1974).

reviews.text: "Is Playtime cyberpunk?" is a thought that ran through my head revisiting this, which depicts a realm of the future that lacks all of the sleek looks and cool technology of cyberpunk in favor of depicting the quotidian likelihood that our future will likely look like what is now the present, of cities that have lost their personality in favor of landscapes of indistinguishable condo towers and office spaces, all faceless rectangles of steel and glass where identity is so obscured that the credits are listed in German, Japanese and English. Interior spaces are crushed flat and set against negative space that makes damn near each room suffocating if not outright swallowed in darkness. Nothing belongs to anyone, all spaces…

reviews.text: News of the World is a competently made, old-fashioned western road movie. It's predictable, you know where it is going but the subtle & graceful performance of Tom Hanks and the chemistry between him and Helena Zengel is what makes it work. It is Paul Greengrass' most visually striking & heartfelt film without being showy. James Newton Howard’s score was lovely. It's surprisingly timely movie too (the movie opens and ends with mention of meningitis/cholera virus outbreak and the spread of ‘fake news’ being a significant plot point).

reviews.text: This is a movie that seems like it shouldn’t be as entertaining and fun to watch as it is, but Paul Greengrass directed the hell out of it. I love the style he went for, it’s very reminiscent of classic Westerns but adds a lot of extra flare. That, in addition to the really impressive cinematography and production design make this one of the most visually appealing Westerns I have ever seen.

reviews.author: Sam
reviews.text: A gorgeously shot, interestingly directed and fairly intense western, News of the World surprised me. Now, I don’t think this movie is exactly amazing or groundbreaking but it was sweet and did what it was trying to. The cinematography is absolutely stunning providing a clean and organized look on top of its gorgeous and intricate locations. Paul Greengrass really understands how to direct a movie, and especially knows how to utilize lighting perfectly. The sound design and editing are also very immersive and well done. Both Tom Hanks and Helena Zengel deliver fresh and compelling performances that strongly support the narrative. It definitely has some repetitive moments but I enjoyed it quite a bit, it’s a movie that feels really hard to truly hate. Glad to see a film reminiscing over classic westerns work.

reviews.text: Nighthawks is a gritty thriller with a realistic and dark tone that combines crime and suspense with a touch of political intrigue. Performance wise Sylvester Stallone and Billy Dee Williams as New York cops and Rutger Hauer’s chilling portrayal of the ruthless terrorist were solid and rest of them were good. The movie visually is also grounded as the makers were focused on a realistic tone. Action sequences were not over the top but intense and well-grounded. The pacing at times feels uneven, but the tension generally holds throughout. Overall, it’s an engaging thriller that showcases a different and grounded side of Stallone.

Unfortunately it's a little hard to get behind a guy who so frequently makes the dumbest decisions possible in an attempt to save his own ass, and that tends to undermine the script's stabs at social relevance. Still effectively stylish, with some especially sly sound design and a typically killer Riz Ortolani score.

reviews.text: Hitchcock wrongly accused man thriller as cheap Poliziotteschi. Stylish in the few moments it gets to explode into murders and street-level chases and political maneuvering but surprisingly content to dial back the intensity of the situation to instead just casually observe the way Italian institutions are built and manipulated to work for the rich and against the common man. The righteous anger is felt but it'd probably work better as the latter movie if Salerno wasn't forced to change the cynical ending he was clearly builds towards to something so clean. That being said one thing I love about watching movies like this is that it didn't matter whether they had a budget or not every Italian genre movie in the 70s had a sick prog rock score... We have to go back.

reviews.author: ratbastard
reviews.text: Italian crime drama / poliziotteschi from Vittorio Salerno. 'Fabio' is casually fishing while listening to a football game on his radio, his attentions turn when he overhears a woman screaming for help within the reeds. He investigates to discover an older man, who is revealed to be a wealthy Professor named 'Ranieri', bludgeoning a woman with a pipe. While Fabio initially panics and struggles to deal with the events he has witnessed, Raneri goes straight to the authorities to frame Fabio. A neat 'wrong man' style poliziotteschi, boasting stylish visuals, and a solid score from Riz Ortolani. Salerno draws from his giallo background and influences - shaping an uneasy tone, and tension. A solid cat-and-mouse tale for the most part, and while you feel for Fabio, his decisions are poor. The performances are fine, the exchanges are decent, and the set pieces are well executed. Themes of cynicism, classism, injustice and corruption pervades.

reviews.text: Third time. A real “What you give to it, it gives to you” film. If you’ve seen a lot of movies, it’s easy to get bogged down in what this wants to be, what it is aesthetically mining. And if you seek clean social morality, this probably isn’t the one. Too ephemeral, too specific, too hooked into the historical American tradition of liberty in the face of fear and the unknown. One long drive to freedom. There’s no judgment and no plan. The politics aren’t political, they’re social and humanistic. There is an evident philosophy that gets a big platform—a nomadic order of decency and connectedness. It’s sensitive but direct about loss—the amazing regret and What if? that powers life…

reviews.text: High-strung and vociferous Barbara Streisand is a high-priced escort who has killed in self-defense, but at the hearing the prosecution wants to throw her indefinitely into the psychiatric ward (a very gloomy and decayed New York City loony bin). To beat the rap, Streisand would be better off playing mentally unbalanced. But she doesn’t want that, she insists to her lawyer Richard Dreyfuss to prove to the judge that she is mentally competent. Nuts, by director Martin Ritt, is a moralizing courtroom drama with just enough long speeches by everyone involved to remind you that it is based on a play (Tom Topor was the playwright). The movie, with quite a few flashbacks that includes Leslie Nielson as the bad-guy client (wow, it’s weirdly fun to see him be the antagonist!), is kinda watchable for what it is. Low priority, but there are interesting psychological torrents to extract from this.

reviews.text: An unassuming middle-aged couple win a trip to Hawaii, only to have their flight hijacked by North Koreans searching for a former agent. Okay! Madam is Executive Decision (1996) stealth in confined spaces with moments of True Lies (1994) espionage interpersonal relationship humour. The action is always secondary to the comedy, but both chuckles and tension are carried effectively by extremely likeable leads in Uhm Junghwa (Tidal Wave) and Park Sung-woong (Monstrum). The two have beautiful chemistry, and when they aren't playing off each other, they are ably supported by a stacked cast of recognizable character actors (Bae Jeong-nam, Jung Man-sik, Kim Byeong-ok are all on the manifest). A great deal of effort is put into a twist that isn't really a twist, but for this one laboured plot point, Okay! Madam succeeds in making plane hijackings family fun.

reviews.text: Don’t be fooled by the dusky seduction of its wedding night prologue: “On the Rocks” is far and away the least cool thing that Sofia Coppola has ever made. That’s not a criticism so much as a contextualization. If the perfume ad prelude cocoons you inside the same gauzy softness that made “Lost in Translation” so entrancing, “Marie Antoinette” so tactile, and “Somewhere” so tenderly siloed within itself, it only does so in order to cut a sharp contrast into the domesticity that follows. That’s when this fizzy champagne cocktail of a film jumps a few years forward, landing in the kind of marriage where the waters have become just a bit too calm for the people swimming in them…

While I understand the filmmaker’s impulse to resolve the story the way he does (I have no clue how historically accurate the ending is as I unfortunately know nothing about Constitutional reform in late 80s South Korea) the execution is laughable. I cringed through the final 10 minutes and by the time the freeze-frame rolled around I was nearly catatonic. Maybe I’m a cynical asshole and this is powerful for Korean audiences but I’d be willing to bet not. And are we supposed to believe they ate that fucking dog? Outside of its metaphorical qualities, why would they do that?

reviews.text: This is more like material for an art installation that you come and go, in a theater you probably end up snoozing (like I did), though the film itself drives you to that unconscious state with casual black screens of 2-4 minutes and even snore sounds! Org is pure experimental underground, full of jump cuts, found footage, out of sync sounds and some weird and sometimes awesome scenes involving three comic-book characters (Terence Hill as Zohooom, Isaac Twen as Grrrr, and Lidija as Shuuuick) fighting and loving in isolated and apocalyptic landscapes. There's sex, humor, horror, fantasy, anti capitalism, metacinema, documentary (with Godard, Glauber Rocha, Mekas, Espinosa...) and influences from Warhol, Brakhage, Vertov, Makavejev... Like a mad zapping through late…

reviews.author: Rick Burin
reviews.text: In 1948, Orson Welles left Hollywood, the town in which he had arrived with such fanfare eight years earlier. After the success of Kane, he watched - helpless - as his next three projects were taken out of his hands, recut and sometimes even re-shot. His fifth picture, Macbeth, was a travesty that he failed to deliver for two years, apparently disillusioned with movies and burnt out at 33.

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: A downright frightening adaptation, exploiting its troubled production to reduce Shakespeare to a cut-up psychological thriller, one attuned to Othello's paranoia of living in a white world. Though Welles butchers the play into fragments and summaries, he brings out the core of the text, understanding that Iago does not drive Othello to jealous rage so much as give the protagonist's simmering tension an outlet to erupt. Filtered through Eisensteinian montage and Howeian cinematography, it is an utter nightmare of a movie.

reviews.text: Warm acoustic guitar. A helicopter shot of early morning sunlight falling over a river in rural Louisiana. A bearded and clenched Justin Timberlake staring out the window of the prison bus that’s taking him back to his southern-fried hometown after a 12-year stretch behind bars. You can tell exactly what kind of movie “Palmer” is going to be before the title card even appears onscreen: A nice (but hopefully knowing) drama about decent people finding the strength to persevere through difficult circumstances. The kind of thing that you might fire up on a Friday night as you lie down on the couch with one eye looking…

reviews.author: AdamAB
reviews.text: Pelé functions as a brief overview of the icon’s illustrious career and cultural significance, though it lacks the conviction to dig beneath the surface. The documentary is at its most riveting when examining the football star’s apolitical nature, and has the benefit of its subject’s own voice to add context to proceedings. While it is always enjoyable to watch Pelé’s brilliant sporting achievements, he is probably a figure that warrants the mini-series treatment considering his importance.

reviews.author: Joachim Jelle
reviews.text: An unprovocative, somewhat by-the-numbers portrait in the likes of Asif Kapadia’s, Pelé tackles the, quite honestly, unproblematic football star by way of the political pressure in Brazil. The star, himself, pops up for down-to-earth talking-head interviews, but the directors fail to use this opportunity as a means to really get under the skin of one of the most famous players in the century. Be that as it may, the doc benefits from Pelé's good-hearted nature, his grace on the field, and the sublimely restored archive footage that really transports you to the field and the many World Cups he won.

reviews.text: It can be frustrating to watch a film that doesn’t seem to understand its own strengths; it’s downright maddening to watch three of them. With “Peninsula” (stylized for its North American release as “Train to Busan Presents: Peninsula”), director Yeon Sang-ho has now made an entire trilogy of exuberant, maximalist, and ultimately tiresome zombie movies that cannibalize their best ideas in a crazed dash towards mediocrity. This erratic and derivative new chapter is by far the most chewed up of the three, as its outsized ambition (or at least its scale) makes it that much easier to see how Yeon’s latest yarn shrinks away from its own potential like it’s scared of the movie it could’ve been. At the end…

reviews.text: Doesn’t have the emotional core that Train to Busan destroyed me with, but I curbed my expectations and ended up having a decent time with this doofy movie. A more action/more zombies/more cgi kinda sequel and the scale is way bigger than Busan.. with bigger production and numerous atmospheric lighting choices/attention to detail that kinda made me wish this was in the sameballpark as it’s predecessor story wise. I was on board with the fast paced intro and Escape from New York/Land of the Dead/Mad Max/video game influences, but that second act started to drag a bit for me. Luckily the finale lets loose... it’s a certified firing on all cylinders banger and worth the price of admission alone despite the poor CGI’s best intentions. Didn’t love it like I thought I would, but Peninsula was a decent time and a decent addition to its world.

The drama has an intensity entwined within it due to the cross purposes of both characters along with hitman's own sense of morality. He's a capable killer who thinks nothing of murder for money or his own protection, but an innocent child may be…

Set within queer/feminist bohemian enclave of mid-80's NYC where everyone is an artist, whether scraping together to get by or descending to the streets from luxury apartments paid for by blood money, Perfect Strangers is a leather-jacketed suicide mission, a meet-cute crime scene. Every man is lethal, if not by birth then by the breaking that follows, dangerous to themselves and others, intentionally or otherwise. What to do with men? If we cannot make them safe from the world can we make the world safe from them? How do we negotiate our positions in regard to men? Do we let them…

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: Larry Cohen shot this and Special Effects back-to-back, using young, hungry, and presumably non-union talent from the Lower Manhattan art scene. This typically high-concept effort, which appears to be the cheaper of the two films, stars Anne Carlisle (Liquid Sky) as a single mother whose mute toddler son witnesses a stabbing by young punk Brad Rijn (Smithereens). When his underworld boss tells him he needs to take care of the one witness, he seduces the mother.

reviews.author: Edith
reviews.text: What's amazing about this film, besides being made on an incredibly small budget, is its ability to bottle eighties New York in the same self-reflective bitterness of pulpy forties. Working folks who are now looking for love, feminist Karens and single moms, or dads trying to see their kids. Nobody gets what they want and everyone gets what is coming for them. Crime and violence affects everyone here, that line of moral ambiguity heightening your sense of unease. I also really love how much it surprised me in taking the narrative from the adults to that of a child, a cityscape Night of the Hunter. Larry Cohen doesn't force political and sociological themes in flag waving dialogue, but let's the…

reviews.text: Cohen's made an unsurprisingly strange little drama out of his initial premise -- more of a doomed romance than a thriller -- and peppered it with characteristically amazing location photography and enough bonus atmospheric material to maybe count as some subtext, but that can't change the fact that the characters are complete aliens who seem to exhibit no recognizable human or even logical behavior and materially nothing happens between the first and last 5 minutes.

reviews.text: Larry's feminist picture, and as always with a Cohen script, it's filled with obvious disdain for sexists, homophobes, and all manner of bigots. Of course, being a Cohen script, these ideas are handled with the grace and tact of a street fair merry-go-round barreling down a heavily-trafficked street- I'm reminded of the unproduced script of his I read that included several attached letters from members of the LGBT community assuring him that no, his script was not "offensive", just painfully straight. Perfect Strangers is clearly the work of an extremely well meaning ally, and not everything fits- a scene introducing a minor character as the only gay cop on the force seems to only exist as an excuse to show…

reviews.author: Bruno Andrade
reviews.text: On a visual level, Cohen’s films are always alive with a centrifugal near-chaos. By combining multiple points of view, he denies the viewer a single character to identify with. Cohen’s scenes, built up from combinations of hand-held with tripod-filmed images, and static shots with moving shots, are alive with multiple tensions and conflicting perspectives. We see things from all sides, and we are encouraged to think and compare without being led toward any easy conclusions. - Fred Camper, Reel Life: the low-budget genius of American film

It’s rough around the edges, but good shit.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: Pick Me Up could easily have been a pedestrian "girl on the run from serial killer in the middle of nowhere" yarn but it's lifted by two things. First is the idea of there being two serial killers and the pair having a "turf war". The second (and most important) is Michael Moriarty. God bless Michael Moriarty; he lifts up everything he's involved in and Pick Me Up is no exception. Moriarty's maniac truck driver is absolutely delightful and completely owns every scene he's in. Larry Cohen just let's him off the leash and it's great. The story moves briskly and is constantly entertaining. It's horrific and funny but also really dark. The fifty five minute runtime is used really well - the final ten minutes or so are brilliantly put together, including the ending itself which is amazingly ridiculous. This is an absolute blast from start to finish.

reviews.author: nathaxnne [goodbye <3]
reviews.text: In which every hitchhiker, every trucker, is part of a shadow-world of psychopaths who sometimes work against, and sometimes with, each other, really fulfilling the paranoid fantasies of those travellers in remote areas of the Pacific Northwest, at crappy rest-stops, tourist attractions, and fleabag motels. In Pick Me Up, everything you are worried is going on in that tractor trailer, along the side of the road, over in the next room, totally is. This is a great premise for a Masters Of Horror episode, and having Larry Cohen direct, David J Schow adapt his own short story, Michael Moriarty & Fairuza Balk play leads helps to ensure a winning execution, as it were. Moriarty, especially, really runs with this material, and makes one long for a Larry Cohen Citizen's Band Trucking Movie which sadly has not yet come to pass!

He's one of the greatest and most underrated genre actors ever and always outstanding, and again steals the show. His little scene with the grocery store clerk is priceless. But the rest of the cast including Laurene Landon (who has great chemistry with him) is very good, too. The story of two rivaling serial killers on the road - one a hitchhiker and one a truck driver who picks up his victims - is full of tension and dark humor. Also loved the ending with a callback to 'The Ambulance'.

reviews.text: A queasy and intriguing horror-inflected techno-thriller that gets lost somewhere in the Bermuda Triangle between “Mandy,” “Inception,” and “Ghost in the Shell,” Brandon Cronenberg’s “Possessor” is so drunk on its own sick potential that it doesn’t have the time (or the balance) required to realize most of it. On the other hand, 90 minutes of Andrea Riseborough and Christopher Abbott engaging in ultra-gory psychic warfare over control of the latter’s body is more satisfying than what most of the current Best Picture nominees have to offer, so maybe it’s wise not to look a gift horse in the mouth.

reviews.author: Sean Fennessey
reviews.text: Impressive, immersive, and fucked in a way that never pushes the viewer too far away. Reminded me more of Andrzej Żuławski than Cronenberg's father—severe, hysterical, and humorless. None of dad's dark, kitschy humor, and the practical viscera is bold, bright, and psychedelically deployed. Still, the obsession with body invasion, possession, mental disease wrought from technology—a chip off the old block. Can't think of many young filmmakers who work with such precision. Also love the direction Christopher Abbott has taken his career, working with extremist auteurs who want to shatter his beauty by emotionally and physically torturing his characters. Highly recommend if you enjoy films that scoop out your guts by the end.

reviews.text: What do you get when you take the antagonist from the movie Phonebooth, and the action from Speed. You get the South Korean action drama film, Quick. Lee Min Ki plays Han a motorcycle courier that is just trying to escape his motorcycle gang life. When one day someone rigs his helmet to a bomb, from here on out Han has to complete deliveries to keep the bomb from going off on his head. An interesting concept, but I feel this movie gets bogged down by the senseless melodramatic story. At times they knew what kind of film they were making and bought into the unhinged nature of this film, but when they tried to get serious this film screeched to a hault. It’s still a fun film. I would just prefer if it was 30 minutes shorter.

reviews.text: Watched this on a whim because of the welcoming Netflix banner ad, and, boy, would I like those two hours of my life back. In what is quite possibly one of the most inept examples of storytelling in recent history, Rebirth shamelessly apes David Fincher without the requisite thematic grime nor genre knowledge to actually pull off a film of that stature. It's a film where entire scenes consist of secondary characters parroting back questions ("Do you want me to leave?" "Do I want you to leave?") immediately followed up by another scene of another secondary character parroting back questions in one long echo chamber of a plot.

reviews.author: JakubM
reviews.text: Easy to shrug this off as a cursory retread of Fincher's The Game, but there's something fascinating in the way a white-collar drone's disorienting journey through a self-help retreat doubles as a deconstruction of the appeal of cults. Stages in his journey reflect the way these groups dig up and needle at people's deepest desires and anxieties, promising empowerment and a new way of life on the back of genuine therapeutic practices, then suddenly shifting into high-pressure sales tactics, coercion, and outright blackmail. Rebirth’s organization is an acid-trip manifesto corrupted into a national (if not global) wellness brand, a jumble of masculine self-help, new age vibe work, and tech-bro disruptor culture designed to help sell powdered drinks. Fran Kranz is…

Also, a very young Preben Kaas shows up in a brief, early role.
