reviews.author: AWS
reviews.text: A rich girl is disinherited by her family because she refuses to get a job, and she ends up getting one anyway as a repo chick, which she turns out to be incredibly good at. There’s an elusive train she’s trying to repossess, and it all ties in to terrorists with a nuclear weapon who want to put an end to golfing. Shot almost entirely in front of a green screen, every background is cartoonish and surreal, and I found it incredibly endearing. The story and acting take on the same kind of wacky sensibility, and the movie is fucking hilarious. All of the cast is good (it includes people like Rosanna Arquette, Miguel Sandoval, Xander Berkeley, Karen Black, and Frances Bay), and the lead girl (Jaclyn Jonet) is fantastic. I don’t think a lot of people would get this movie, but if you watch it and don’t hate it, then I recommend you watch it. I fucking loved it.

It cemented Steve McQueen, James Coburn, Robert Vaughn, and Charles Bronson on their rise towards the Hollywood A-List. It also gave Yul Brynner a second memorable character to add to King Mongkut of Siam that arguably made him a star. This sequel however, that arrived six years after Sturges' film couldn't be further from the original's star-wattage, with only Brynner returning, and the rest of the seven looking decidedly less than magnificent. reviews.author: Filipe Furtado
reviews.text: One of the great miracles of American film. A wonderful overactor in a fish out of water comedy that somehow becomes a perfectly balanced, subdued ensemble piece. Laughton is great, he has so many perfect reaction shots, but the movie secret involves how the movie finds equal room for everyone else as form ideally follows theme. McCarey's behavioral gifts, his good rapport with actors and eye for improvisation and how to let character disappear into action, pay off often in the late 30s and 40s and this talent really find full expression for the first time on this one. There’s so much great character stuff spread throughout that I always forget before my once every decade visit that it runs a tight 90 minutes.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: O Butler Where Art Thou? This shares with Ninotchka and Sullivan's Travels (amongst others) the idea that there's nothing more funny than watching someone's exaggerated pretensions get stripped away when they find themselves outside of their natural habitat. Charles Laughton as the unflappable English valet does more comedic face and eyeball acting in the first reel than some actors will do in their lives. It's one of those instances in which his very posture and appearance is hilarious, his eyes flicking back and forth like one of those Felix the Cat wall clocks. Also like Ninotchka and Sullivan's Travels, there's a sweet optimism and faith in humanity that make it as moving as it is funny.

The film, which looks like the exact midpoint between Robert Downey Sr and Nick Zedd, shows her and some other hippies trampling on American flags and having sex with a guy in a Nixon mask. Heroically, Ed Harris stands by her, dismissing the film as "a little '60s thing" and reminding the press of Americans' right to free expression. The heartwarming message of the film is that America is a place where artistic expression and political protest are things that everyone can do as long as they distance ourselves from it later and agree that it is bad.

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: Titling this "Salvatore Giuliano" almost feels ironic, because although the film undeniably revolves entirely around the eponymous Sicilian outlaw, he hardly gets any screen time — alive, that is. His death more or less bookends the film, but perhaps more to the point, there's a continuous throughline about how while this is undeniably "about" Salvatore Giuliano in the sense that he's structurally at the center of it and none of it would have come about without him, it's not really about him in the grand scheme of things. He may have started a fire, but then it ignited all of Sicily.

reviews.text: Francesco Rosi's unique and ambitious take on the life of Sicilian bandit-turned-political-terrorist Salvatore Giuliano proceeds in the immediate aftermath of Giuliano's death. From this starting point, the Italian film director oscillates between the past and the present, gradually revealing only one character that appears to have had first-hand knowledge of the double-crossings that led to the killing. It's blessed with the subtlest of touches. Giuliano, while alive, is only briefly glimpsed, and his quasi-presence on the screen nurtures the narrative to have an innuendo type of posturing that never shows anything directly. There are some solid performances, particularly from American actor Frank Wolff, who is perhaps best known for his role of Brett McBain in Sergio Leone's Once Upon a Time…

One of the most radical historical films I've ever seen, and I can't wait to revisit it.

reviews.author: Diogo Serafim
reviews.text: Cinema as a historical investigation. The idea of not showing the film's main character and to organize the entire action around a dedramatized, peripherical narrative where his ghost looms as a sweeping shadow might sound abstract and sterile, but Rosi finds a perceptive device of vast, complex compositions, frequently crammed with actors inside, so crowded they sometimes seem to conjure the idea of an entire country witnessing the action, granting the film a sensation of insurrectional fervor that gives one the impression that the screen itself could explose at any given moment. The film is by no means a biography of Salvatore Giuliano, but rather an expansive portrait of Sicily as a region oppressed by the social, political and economic forces of Italy, told with an impressively raw spatial conscience and some very audacious chronological jumps.

reviews.author: Hutch
reviews.text: A political thriller told by way of swirling reconstruction that jumps perspectives and years to portray the separatist movement in post-WWII Sicily. The film is named after one of its elusive bandit leaders, but he’s a largely absent figurehead around which Rosi constructs an elaborate portrait of the politics that cuts and thrusts between the police, mafia, media, political leaders, rebel militia and ordinary folk, leaving Salvatore Giuliano as little more than a symbolic corpse in the telling. Rosi’s style is energetic, deploying a roving and zooming camera, with great use of contrasting focal lengths, to contrast the human drama with the landscape in which it occurs. The land is such an important character here, from the whitewashed houses of its towns to the rugged volcanic hills that hide the insurgents. Rosi’s film depicts the struggle to possess this hard and sun-scorched land, ending inevitably in betrayal and futility.

We focus on an Irish trawler that gets marooned at sea after being attacked by some kind of previously undiscovered sea creature, which later infects the crew with some kind of parasite. Neasa Hardiman's film does a good job of establishing the situation. The boat provides an effective claustrophic location for the action to take place, while the cast are nicely varied. Haemoo (Sea Fog) features the same social commentary, deeply flawed characters, and based on a true story gut punch as their more celebrated work - for a voyage that frequently dips into horror, while courting the country's popular disaster pictures. Not a long journey, the extent to which the horny sailors are transformed into beasts by the prospect of the fairer sex seems like a parody of nautical superstitions - yet this odd choice aside, Shum has navigated a highly effective debut.

She is best known as the mother in the TV series Good Times, one of the first black comedy sit-coms. Her character had been a maid in Maude and then she got her own show. She played a lot of maids in her career and does so as well here. But interestingly, she is the lead character who solves a murder. It is an interesting idea though hard to imagine how a maid was going to solve murders in future episodes. Sure, we had a mystery writer and a doctor who stumble across a murder in every episode…

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: A womanizing Italian oaf who thinks sex work is the ultimate form humiliating degradation finds himself having to do much worse to survive the rise of fascism in Italy. The style is a really cool mix of barbaric neorealist holocaust drama and a more theatrical, satirical and colorful expressiveness aimed at critiquing institutional cruelty, power/gender dynamics and (in Wertmüller's own words) a "particular petty bourgeois social type.” I could see how some could find some of this troubling and maybe even juvenile (there's a practically slapstick setpiece in this involving a farting corpse) but it's ambition to be funny and uncomfortable and shocking does have a weird power/gravity to it; the climactic scene where he tries to seduce his way out of a concentration camp by having sex with a grotesque Nazi officer is top tier exploitation.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Neat rows of dirt-caked prisoners, crusted pale grey by time and toil, march into the wide auditorium of the concentration camp, and it is breathtaking how that turns them into stunning scenery. That image alone is an effective indictment of the dehumanizing effects of not just the militaristic, controlling formalism of the totalitarian state but also of anything that might do the same--art, for instance. Hanging on this moment are so many cruelties, injustices, ironies, and critiques that it's a testament to the visual power of this moment that this idea rings out so well. Finding the most powerful visuals in this moment almost seems extraneous, considering what is going on (no spoilers, but, well, it is a concentration camp),…

reviews.text: Incredibly good thriller. The story follows a man who hits a little girl in his car, the girl was running from her wealthy abusive father who was probably going to kill her anyway. But, the death enrages the father, pretty much because she died from someone else's hands. The way the filmmakers have made this is beyond anything Hollywood is creating and for me is the future of cinema. The camera angles, use of slow motion to create emotion, the soundtrack, and the performances all equal a great piece of art.

reviews.author: Ziglet_mir
reviews.text: Returning to this film after two years showed me even more subtle comparisons between the Sullivan Matriarchs. Andrei Konchalovsky is incredibly patient filming his intro setting of NYC, where we hear random apartment clatter; the brief under-notes of personal lives living in one urban place but are undoubtedly unconnected. He then segues us to the bayous of the south where the comparison turns poetic, a hazy maze of indecipherable nature where people are apart physically but are somehow connected. There's a masterful two scene combo approximately 40 min in where Martha Plimpton's city girl demands her mother for guidance and leaves unfulfilled, followed by Mare Winningham's pregnant daughter-in-law sobbing for freedom and gets Hershey's grip tighter around her neck. The cherry on top is Tangerine Dream's haunting score.

reviews.text: Initiated as a simple, government-assigned project about the life of oil workers, Siberiade grew into a sprawling, four part, 275-minute epic about love of country, hatred between families, appreciation of home, and the perpetual march of progress. Set in Elan, a small, Siberian town, the film covers nearly a century of history, largely through the mechanism of a father and son: Nikolai Ustyuzhanin (Vitaly Solomin, whose picture on Wikipedia is the stuff of legends, or at least it should be), and his son Aleksei (Nikita Mikhalkov).

reviews.author: ZephSilver
reviews.text: Huge swaths of Russian history represented as a sprawling, moving canvas. The scale of which can't be properly appreciated until you've stepped back to observe the full picture on display. A history of revolution, disillusionment, national pride, and hardship. Men cutting through a dense Siberian forest to build a road with no discernable end in sight. Holding out hope for the unforeseen future of their homeland. With each decade chronicled, a rebellious spirit is continuously fostered, inherited from one generation to the next. Whether it's on the battlefield, in the workforce, or on the political stage, this is no place for the weak-willed.

reviews.text: I never thought I'd get to compare a Ray Dennis Steckler production to Kenneth Anger or Jack Smith, but here we are. This is ostensibly a sex film, but Steckler seems much more interested in experimenting with gels, camera speeds, multiple exposures, and, of all things, experimental theatre. Ray's best films feel like they could change at any moment, mutating from a hardboiled roughie to a Saturday morning kids' cartoon over the span of a single take. This isn't like that, though, as his gender-swapped Oedipal tale stays in the same sordid, psychedelic mode in which it starts for the entire runtime. Can only imagine what the raincoat audience thought at the time.

There's no pretension here at all as the movie is interested only in being a well-crafted and entertaining actioner and in this, it succeeds as it's got a some solid action and is well-directed and photographed. In Tom Berenger and Billy Zane, the film also has two good…

reviews.text: I suspect a lot of action junkies may be bored by the relative lack of incident, but I was engaged by the willingness to bask in the beauty of the jungle. I could see this with a few changes becoming something closer to an arthouse take on the same material. There’s no pretense that the mission is just (“Sitting in an office giving men orders to kill is the same thing as putting a bullet in someone's heart yourself”), which distinguishes this from the jungle actioners of the prior decade. A picture of Rambo in the back of the bus is a nod to the movie’s intentions.

reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: Urgent, high-pitched, low-key, always crazy engrossing, Some Came Running confirms Vincente Minnelli as one of the best directors to ever side-step into Hollywood. His command of the emotional keyboard is unquestionable; he combines moods-rhythms-tones with the know-how of a seasoned mixologist. His musicals play like neorealist dramas (he is as good a cataloger of micro-behaviors as De Sica: the dancing women's feet of Gigi and Mamita, the gangly rubber arms of Astaire in a subway-ish arcade). His dramas and comedies, conversely, fly to the beat of a happy-go-lucky operetta. In Some Came Running, Minnelli reaches for some disturbing neuroses of the human mind. (Move over, Woody Allen. Let a pro show you how it's done. Minnelli can build.) His characters…

reviews.text: Ginny's ever-intensifying masochism and desperation breaks my heart so much. Despite the obvious contempt and disdain with which the other characters view her, she maintains a kind of honor and audaciousness. Unlike everyone else, with their class aspirations and personal infidelities, Ginny has nothing to hide or lie about. Everything she says and does is unbearably earnest, a completely straightforward reflection of how she feels at that moment.

reviews.text: Larry Cohen reworks Vertigo, Peeping Tom and Blow Out into his own low-rent, pervy, self-reflexive movie-within-a-movie reality. Like De Palma he's interested in ideas of voyeurism and illusion and moviemaking but with none of his elegance; this thing is just a bizarro mess of insane set design, strange performances and (despite some of the 80s neon synth slickness of the occasional murder setpiece) a pretty chintzy guerilla shooting style that makes the whole thing feel completely stripped from any sort of actuality and instead like this fake, vulgar dreamworld we've collectively conjured up by allowing sleazy filmmakers to obliterate the cinematic distinction between a real girl and the beautiful ones they do make-believe violence to.

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: An indictment on the megalomania of the artist, exaggerated of course, but like most of Cohen’s films, it is in this exaggeration that the truth lies.A work that, unlike similar experiments by Fellini or Truffaut, which posses no objective principles but are instead haughty, masturbatory examples of a noxious subjectivity, prioritizes sincerity over hubris and is in fact a searing indictment thereof, uncovering the dimensional strata of both fiction and its materializations on film—the archaeology of actuality. Layers of illusion and truth, exposed one by one until the lines separating them totally disintegrate. Cinema is the ultimate simulacrum.

reviews.author: ScreeningNotes
reviews.text: I always struggle reviewing comedies because it's hard to distinguish between jokes I don't personally find funny and jokes which just aren't funny objectively (because of poor setup, execution, etc.). I think Spies Like Us is the former (jokes which are funny but not to me). In objective terms, its story about two people sent on a fake mission to distract from a real operation works well enough, and I know Chevy Chase and Dan Aykroyd are funny guys, but I just didn't find myself laughing at much of it. At the end it takes a Dr. Strangelove-like turn toward critiquing Cold War tension and arms race irrationality which I would have liked to see more of throughout (maybe I just missed it?).

reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: Whilst Steel Rain might be overlong and sloppy in parts, it's a very fine thriller that tackles some important political issues through a fictitious story. Released in South Korea in late 2017, Steel Rain feels very timely after a year of high tension between the North and the South. The fact that the film also prominently features a newly-elected South Korean president and a dodgy incumbent president also seems well timed, as do the various other contemporary issues touched upon. The politicians here play games and get caught in a tangled web of international imperialism, even if the film greatly over-simplifies things. The topic of reunification vs war is one with no easy answers, and Steel Rain seems critical of the leaders…

It run out of gas by act three, but the acting is solid, the male bonding stuff effective and most of the action well-handled.

reviews.text: Steel Rain (2017) is a buddy action picture based on a webtoon by director Yang Woo-suk, in which spies from the North (Jung Woo-sung) and South (Kwak Do-won) put aside their differences to prevent war. Summit is a stand alone sequel, which has more in common with the submarine Under Siege variation Hunter Killer (2018) than with Yang's first entry. The original Rain's main strengths were the chemistry between the leads, and an Olympus Has Fallen level of violence (almost feeling like a response to that jingoistic American film, in its positive images of the North). Sadly Kwak is relegated to villain status, which is a huge step down - and the action doesn't really heat up until the final…

That it’s a French co-production surely accounts for a portion of the film’s structural oddness — several plot points feel lost in translation, even if the whole thing somehow manages to still make sense — but quirks of financing can only go so far to explain a…

More than redemption the movie was about learning to live with your mistakes.Matt Damon gives one of his best performances. He is subdued, and completely disappears into the character. Loved the dynamics between him, Camille Cottin and Lilou Siauvaud.

She’s absolutely correct about everything she says in it, and nobody has the right to tell her she isn’t. Matt Damon’s character is a fish out of water in Marseille, singularly focused on the event that’s shaped the last half-decade of his life. There’s a subplot in the movie about Bill’s inability to give a fuck about his new partner’s career in the performance arts. I believe this is McCarthy attempting to relay a form of self-awareness with his new film in relation to the infamous Knox saga. While Matt Damon and Tom McCarthy…

reviews.text: Straight to Hell is not for everyone. When I was in college, my friend group and I were once accused of "speaking The Language", no doubt owing to our shared loves of the esoteric and specific and our penchant for jargon. On my last day before dropping out, I gathered the group for one last night together and showed them Alex Cox's Repo Man. It was perfect. It's no surprise, then, that as a lover of spaghetti westerns, Cox's scrappy and inaccessible tribute to the genre would be something like comfort food to me. Straight to Hell is by no means a great movie, but if you're on it's manic wavelength, it feels like sharing a laugh with friends. For me, Straight to Hell feels like another chance to speak The Language. For better or for worse (who am I kidding, definitely for worse), watching Straight to Hell feels like coming home.

reviews.text: The contrast between the dry, docudrama narration and Mann's intensely stylized compositions is a delight, but I couldn't help but be lulled at times by just how flat its framing is, however much it was likely not Mann's fault that he had to stop and hector to get treasury approval. The worst is when that voiceover intrudes upon some brilliant silent moments, such as one of the undercover t-men, totally silhouetted, tailing a crook. His precise calculation of space to give his prey, his assured but cautious movement, is somewhat spoiled by the narrator droning on so loud I half-expected the mark to spin on his heels, aware that something was up. But still, goddamn can Mann direct.

reviews.author: sakana1
reviews.text: The combined talents of John Alton and Anthony Mann make T-Men an awfully good looking movie. Its aesthetics are carefully constructed, with the Treasury Department scenes shot with a passive, neutral camera that resembles the blandest of TV set-ups, while those featuring the criminals and undercover agents are often photograph in extreme ways, particularly with tight close-ups, or from unusual angles. It's fantastically effective, as is the way Mann makes every part of the screen interesting, even with something as simple as a man climbing a flight of the stairs in the background of a shot.

reviews.author: noir1946
reviews.text: Anthony Mann’s T-Men is a tough, no-nonsense noir with lots of style. Doc-noir is my least favorite form of the genre because it tends to be stuffy and didactic, but Mann and screenwriter John C. Higgins (Railroaded!, Raw Deal) don’t let the obligatory glorification of federal agents get in their way of telling a good story. Catching the bad guys is less important than the ordeals agents Dennis O’Brien (Dennis O’Keefe) and Tony Genaro (Alfred Ryder) have to go through to survive detection. Each narrow escape is followed immediately by an even greater danger.

reviews.author: HKFanatic
reviews.text: Similar to the following year's "The Naked City" in that there's an omniscient voiceover reporting on the law enforcement-centric plot; normally I don't mind voiceover for these 1940's crime flicks, but the stiff, informational tone of it here really clashes with the more expressionist techniques of director Anthony Mann and his DP John Alton ("The Big Combo")—the way they utilize nervy close-ups or lower quadrant framing to emphasize characters' psychological states. Fortunately, the voiceover is largely absent during the final act, so we can focus on the film's expert blocking and rich use of shadows. Gravely-voiced Charles McGraw, the hero of "The Narrow Margin," makes for a great heavy here too.

reviews.author: nathaxnne [goodbye <3]
reviews.text: A 1970's Amicus/E.C. portmanteau reconstituted in 1990's horrorcore, Tales From The Hood is conceptually and structurally unified to a much greater extent than most anthology horror films, finding real terrors within citizens murdered at the hands of police, domestic violence, white supremacist politicians, the prison system, gang warfare. Tales From The Hood is most notably a classical horror film, directly in keeping with its Dead Of Night/Tales From The Crypt/Creepshow lineage, without throwaway segments or overreliance on comedic relief. Pointedly, the wraparound is set in a funeral home, allowing for the stories of the dead to be retold. Tales From The Hood is agitprop horror, direct in its anger, finely crafted in its effects. One of the great works of 90's horror, my only regret is that there weren't more of these such that Clarence Williams III's Funeral Director could not have had another shot at becoming the masscult horror host/icon as so obviously and desperately required.

reviews.author: Jack Moulton
reviews.text: Tales From The Script is an essential documentary for aspiring screenwriters. It doesn’t break down how to write a script or how to tell a story but it goes over what to expect in a career in screenwriting and what they value. It’s a very basic doc with interviews shot on DV, but it has access to so many top class writers that I didn’t think much about the production of the doc itself. It’s fascinating to pick up on the common behaviour of a writer based on their attitudes. It’s a doc that both confirms my fears and validates what I want out of screenwriting in my life. It finishes with a story from the writer of Ghost talking about a flop he made shortly afterwards where he felt it was finally worth it because it saved the relationship between a mother and son. That’s what it’s all about.

reviews.author: Ronan Doyle
reviews.text: An insightful dive into the world of one of the least appreciated forms of literature, this documentary counts some of Hollywood’s biggest and smallest screenwriting names amongst its interviewees, boasting talents the likes of William Goldman, John Carpenter, Paul Schrader, and Frank Darabont. Structured around several key topics such as relationships with directors and stars, it’s a film bustling with humourous anecdotes and horror stories in equal measure, shedding light on the highs and lows of the movie writing business. Each of its distinct chapters begins with a clip from a film about screenwriting (such as Adaptation and In a Lonely Place), giving an interesting fictional representation of these same issues discussed at length. It may not exactly be an eye-opening experience that probes deeply into the fabric of Hollywood moviemaking, but it does makes for an enjoyable time in the company of some truly talented and entertaining writers.

The plotline itself - which concerns the death of a man's father for financial reasons and subsequent revenge - is pretty standard and therefore predictable, but the film has plenty up its sleeve including a few bizarre detours a couple of solid central performances. reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: "Terror in the Aisles" is a 1984 documentary feature directed by Andrew J. Kuehn. Embracing the historical element of horror films, "Terror in the Aisles" gives its viewers an interesting walk through on the greatest moments of horror up to that given point in time. If specifically does this within the element of topical theme, like for example films that specialize in jump scare shock versus films that specialize in longer drawn-out elements of suspense. It's an entertaining nuance that makes you ponder on how a presented horror film is doing its job within its articulate intentions versus some simple countdown list focused on popularity that tends to often happen.

reviews.author: Ben
reviews.text: Boils down to a well edited clip show. I imagine watching this back in 1984 when it first came out would’ve been different than watching it in 2022. There are so many classics after 1984 that the small sample they used seems a bit lackluster. That’s not the movie’s fault of course. What is the movie’s fault were the inserted scripted audience scenes with Donald Pleasence and Nancy Allen. For how well the clips from movies are edited together, the writing for the two hosts was pretty bad. I love Pleasence as much as the next guy, but his dialogue was a bit too hammy. For walk a down memory lane and a fun celebration of horror, or terror films as they are mostly called here, Terror in the Aisles was cozy. If that’s what your looking then look no further. However, there are many other shows/movies that have this concept that have done it better.

reviews.text: Churchill supposedly screened this in the double-digits for the hortations on besieged empire back when subtext was blunt, serious business. The first twenty-odd minutes betray haste of production—the editing's clumsy and the lighting makes the Hamilton digs look more stagey than luxe. Then everything comes together in sweet flows of draping, silhouette and Maté glow within Alexander Korda’s rather foursquare direction. (There are twenty medium-closeups of Leigh that’d make you turn a ship around and head back to Naples, too.) And in the end, dwelling on the seams and occasional chintziness—see Olivier's terribly low-rent entrance—is uncharitable when faced with Vincent Korda’s evident industry and excellence. But what keeps you in the game is Leigh: for her force and demonic focus…

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: EIGHT DIAGRAM POLE FIGHTER is the kind of movie that is less than 100 minutes long, but has the epic arc of something twice as long. It's the kind of movie that is so overflowing with melodrama and exaggerated expressions of human emotion that it causes some audiences to laugh. Lau Kar Leung's fight choreography is, I'm sure, praised elsewhere by people more succinct and knowledgeable than me, but what I found striking on this most recent rewatch is how well everything else is handled too.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: wow!! deeply brutal and sad revenge picture with some of the best, most physically expressive fight choreography i've ever seen—a 90 minute martial arts melodrama that somehow hits with the intensity and impact of the best war epics. the time allocated to the brothers' trauma and emotional/spiritual experiences as they prepare for vengeance is some of lau kar-leung's finest dramatic work (when gordon liu shaves his head by himself 😭😭) and the final 20 minute pageantry of blood that takes defanging to its most literal conclusion is so ferocious and beautiful that an ending that evokes The Searchers is the only thing that makes sense. and, again, the choreography!! performers in this do things i didn't even know the human body could do, and they're done in perfect rhythm with compositions and movements that are equally unbelievable.

reviews.author: Sean Gilman
reviews.text: Probably Lau Kar-leung's darkest film, bringing an end to the Shaw Brothers era with a bleak, brutal distillation of his most fundamental subject, the impulse to worldly revenge versus the pious imperative for withdrawal in the face of injustice. A palace, an inn, a temple, a cabin in the woods, an abstract, unearthly battlefield: the scene of a nihilist apocalypse. Unable to prevent himself from taking bloody vengeance, the hero walks away. Not into the sunset, but towards the audience and into the world.

reviews.text: A howl of martial arts fuelled rage. Director/Writer Lau Kar-Leung had dealt with gory combat in the past, having choreographed many of Chang Cheh’s masterpiece, but his swan song for the Shaw Bros feels like an outliner to his comedy kung-fu centric filmography. The death of co-star Alexander Fu-Sheng hangs heavily over the proceeding, the coffin imagery a constant reminder, and the viciousness of the final battle is one for the record books. Has there ever been a more painful way of dispatching people? At the same time, this isn’t merely an exercise in darkness, as Lau Kar-Leung masterfully displays the titular pole staff in a way that’s genuinely breathtaking. reviews.text: Kim Ham-min's War of the Arrows (2011) featured nationalism in the face of invading forces, saw Ryu Seung-ryong portray a villainous Manchurian, and bolstered a simple plot with a focus on the differences between military tactics. The Admiral: Roaring Currents is much the same, with waters replacing forests, and an emphasis on ships over bows. Ryu Seung-ryong is now Japanese.

reviews.text: Kim Han-min’s follow-up to his excellent War of the Arrows may not immediately remind one of that propulsive chase thriller. Very clearly divided between dire wartime drama and seaborne carnage, The Admiral: Roaring Currents makes us wait for its titular promise of naval combat and ship maneuvers. But crucially, that wait is never dull. With the overwhelming undaunted Japanese fleet closing in and gutted Korean forces wracked by despair, Choi Min-sik’s legendary admiral their only desperate hope, the bleak mutinous friction delivers engaging set-up while the inevitable clash looms on the horizon. Min-sik can do mentally tormented in his sleep, and he imbues his portrayal of Admiral Yi Sun-sin with a compelling anguish that simmers beneath resolute command. War of…

The cloak-and-dagger adventure is far too sprawling for its own good, and the air only grows thinner as the film propellers towards its underwhelming finale, but you’d be hard-pressed to find a more lavishly staged staged chunk of pulp nonsense.

reviews.text: Tom Ripley takes his Purple Noon self to Germany, and befriends a talented art picture framer. However, all is not what it appears. The art picture framer fella, Mr Zimmermann, has a dire medical condition, and doesn't have long to live. He needs to go all Heisenberg, and make some fast cash to leave for his wife and child. So, what happens when a sinister underworld baddie makes Mr Zimmermann an offer he can't refuse? Well, there's no such thing as easy money, right? The American Friend is another tale in the life of Tom Ripley. This time he's played by Dennis Hopper, under the directorial supervision of Wim Wenders, and damn, this film looks fuckin' beautiful.

The crimes of Chun Doo-hwan's authoritarian administration are a frequent source for the historical dramas of the last decade, and The Attorney is a compelling drama, it just doesn't stack up against subsequent films on that period (A Taxi Driver, 1987, etc). reviews.text: Youn Yuh-jung again proves what an acting legend she is with another challenging role (this was prior to her Oscar-winning performance in Minari). Although the cinematography is bright and colorful, the subject matter could hardly be more depressing. The film focuses on neglected and forgotten people within Korean society who are rarely seen in mainstream films, including elderly prostitutes, a transgender lady, people with physical and mental disabilities, immigrants and mixed-race individuals, and so on. For that, it deserves to be commended. It was also nice to see locations in Seoul that I am quite familiar with such as Tapgol Park, Namsan, Itaewon, etc. But man, I could have used some more levity...this is a bitter pill to swallow.

reviews.text: Before the BBC perfected the nature documentary with Planet Earth, they explored the vast ocean with their 2001 miniseries The Blue Planet. While it's clear that this is one of their beginning efforts, it still holds a lot of value as a documentary series. For one, undersea life was largely a mystery back in 2001. While the knowledge of aquatic animals has slightly improved over time, the venture into the deep seas offers the audience with footage of aquatic life they'd never get to see otherwise. I can only imagine how valuable this information was back when The Blue Planet came out. Or at the very least, what the experience might've been like, viewing sea life that no one knew…

reviews.author: Timcop
reviews.text: I'm not sure how much you can chalk it up to conspiracy, but there seems to have always been a pretty slim list when talking about the great car chases: BULLITT, THE FRENCH CONNECTION, the Bournes more recently, etc. But for whatever reason, there seems to be a myriad of under-seen and little appreciated car chases in the pantheon of cinema that deserve way more recognition. And what we have here is a hell of a doozy. So much so, this might be an all-time great, a top-fiver even, particularly for its realism and almost seemingly accidental in its effortless ability to thrill while also not being too flashy: this is just an amazingly professionally-done scene with superior driving. I know I spent this whole review talking about a car chase, but the rest of the movie is great as well, particularly watching Belmondo actually fall out of a dumptruck down a hill like Buster Keaton.

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: A lesson in suspense and bound up tension from the grear Claude Chabrol. Le Boucher takes place in a provincial French town where a wedding leads to a blossoming friendship between a young headmistress and a local butcher who has recently returned from the army. These events just happen to coincide with a series of grisly murders in the area. This film is a real captivating slow burn, with the friendship between the two central characters played off against outside events. It's a film where everything has a double meaning; not least the "butcher" of the title referring both the man's job and the murderer commiting the crimes...but could they be one and the same? The mystery itself is forsaken…

reviews.author: Dave Jackson
reviews.text: Le Boucher is a deeply unsettling film. It's hard to pinpoint exactly why. Perhaps because it is so nonchalant in its deceptions. It sets itself up as a mystery and an unpacking of a terrible mind. Yet there is no mystery. And its character study is unceremonious. Its final act shook me up quite a bit in its starkness and grim sadness. All of this captured with equally restrained but incredible style. I adored Jean Rabier's cinematography, his camera slowly moving in long beautiful takes, and the performances from Stéphane Audran and Jean Yanne are wonderfully underplayed. An excellent and quietly disturbing film.

reviews.text: LE BOUCHER. An astonishing film, beginning with a loving depiction of a middle-class wedding, and rooted throughout in documentary observation of life in a small French town. Audran is superb as the casual, taking-a-break-from-life teacher, smoking happily, able to rebuff Yanne’s advances without suspending her kindness to him. Yanne is excellent as well, never losing his composed demeanor even when his composure defies genre conventions. (His character Popaul shows no guilt about killing, and even before the plot kicks in we are given his testimony that the death of others doesn't mean that much to him. Only love dents him.) Despite the film’s detailed depiction of the everyday, Chabrol pays scrupulous attention to the suspense mechanism, setting up the revelations…

reviews.author: Sara Clements
reviews.text: “Because you were home” is still a chilling phrase twelve years later. Bryan Bertino burst onto the horror scene with The Strangers, a divisive film but one exploring a real fear: home invasion. Bertino’s latest horror film as writer and director, The Dark and the Wicked, is also about a home invasion. While the intruders aren’t killers wearings marks, a family on a secluded farm is still plagued by someone or something hell-bent on killing them. But unlike the protagonists in The Strangers, this family, no matter how hard they try, cannot hide or defend themselves because what has invaded their home is something they can’t see. It’s not only evil in human form that preys at night.

reviews.author: Blake Bergman "Various Spaghetti"
reviews.text: Constructed within the earlier years of Jesús Franco's constructive efforts, "The Diabolical Dr. Z" is actually a refined piece of quality, building upon his like-styled works of the era. As Franco made an absorbent amount of film that spans multiple decades and themes, his early work has blended balance of noir and studio-based horror efforts. As a result, we often get a mad scientist archetype who has a monstrous styled henchman as a pseudo-Frankenstein but mixed with the noir crime energy of a dark urban underworld and murder within the shadows. I say this is a refinement as earlier Franco pictures within this era such as "The Awful Dr. Orlof" (1962) were not as connectively well done on a technical…

reviews.text: Jess Franco's The Diabolical Dr. Z takes place in a murky world in which no one is good, and life is about power: who holds it, and who can maintain it. Whether the power is political, intellectual, economic, or literal, it renders even mere existence a competition, one that can only be won by those who realize they're playing. (It's a world very much like our own.)

reviews.author: Liz
reviews.text: Crazy to finally watch this after seeing so many of Franco's later variations on it -- and even crazier to realize just how much of this is actually a reworking of elements from The Awful Dr. Orloff and its (name only) sequel. This is only Franco's fourth horror film, but so much of it feels like a deliberate act of one-upmanship: the nudity and eroticism more brazen, the makeup and gore effects more advanced, and the Daniel White score even noisier and more discordant. Most of all, it's even funnier and more referential, with Franco and Carrière dropping Bresson, Irma Vep, and even Dr. Orloff himself into their Woolrich-by-way-of-Al Pereira pulp confection. I'm so jealous of Miss Death's nails.

reviews.author: Branson Reese
reviews.text: Watched the Arrow Video blu-ray with commentary from Abel Ferrara himself, moderated by Brad Stevens. They've got a really nice anti-chemistry where you can tell Stevens is trying to get Ferrara to think critically about his own film while for his own part Ferrara has no interest in doing anything other that remembering what it was like to have sex in 1978. You might think that's a bummer but much like John Ford meeting Kurosawa and summing up his entire filmography by simply telling him "you sure like rain" there's an elegance to Ferrara watching himself drive a power drill into a man's skull and saying "man if you think this is normal you're fucked up." He's his own John Ford.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: It would be completely reasonable to pan this for being incomprehensible, badly paced, strangely acted, and indulgent, but in that confused, slow, awkward mess are a fair few moments of accidental (?) brilliance. Some of these moments are funny (like the pizza eating scene), some of them are visually intriguing (many, many scenes), and some of them are trashy slice-of-life moments that could make a wholly different but incredible film (the pinball moment comes to mind). That last is actually a pretty apt description of much of the first two-thirds of the film; the small fraction of it that that doesn't cover is a sort of avant garde psychological breakdown.

reviews.text: I’ve quickly fallen down the Abel Ferrara rabbit hole. The more I uncover about the New York artist, the more apparent it becomes just what a fascinating filmmaker he is. A director (and lead actor here) that runs ridiculously headfirst into his work (including being an active drug addict while writing and directing a story about one, Bad Lieutenant), and probably a human being I’d much rather spend time talking about than talking to. Nonetheless, that fascination grows with each passing film my jaunt through the Abel Ferrara filmography hits, and The Driller Killer reveals yet another layer of a multifaceted, artistic psyche. That being said, it’s a layer whose grimy, 16mm document of urban decay blurs the lines between…

reviews.text: This is one of those underrated 80’s gems that people forget about or haven’t seen. It came out in 1982 to horrible reviews and was quickly over shadowed by Poltergeist which came out the same year. It’s the true life story of Doris Bither, played expertly by Barbara Hershey as Carla Moran. The movie still holds up mostly with some things not having aged well. The effects by Stan Winston are still pretty cool if not unintentionally funny “The En-Titty”. The soundtrack was also used in the original A Nightmare on Elm st. and in Inglourious Basterds. There are a lot of chauvinistic elements that would not fly in the Me Too era and some disturbing scenes of rape. Also…

reviews.author: Slig001
reviews.text: The Entity is, apparently, loosely based on a true story. It's a ghost story focusing on a woman who is attacked by an unseen entity, and various boffin's attempts to help her. The film runs at over two hours. It's a slow burn for sure but it's highly engrossing. The Entity settles into a good rhythm; the central premise provides the main interest, and there are ancillary plot points, regarding investigations into the cause of the trauma - ie whether it is psychological or paranormal. The film features a real standout performance from Barbara Hershey in the lead role, and she is helped by some very well done special effects and brilliant sound design, which really makes the attack scenes feel intense. It goes a bit overblown for the ending but it works well with what came before and the conclusion feels somewhat satisfying, even though nothing is really resolved!

reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: The shrink sees psychosis, the occultist sees a poltergeist, the theist sees demons, the scholar sees a phenomenon to study. Evil, however you quantify it, is inexorable—it can’t be stopped. It knows no reason, recognizes no dignity. Its sole purpose is to torment. Whether it be the trauma we have suffered that beleaguers our lives like a specter or some supernatural essence we can’t or won’t recognize, there’s no stopping this evil once it manifests itself. To try and diagnose it is meaningless; to try to stop it is an act of futility. When a sinistry this powerful plants its roots in our lives there is no other option but to coexist, to simply live with it. What’s scarier than that?

You must have dreamt it you must have misinterpreted it you must be mistaken. So your kids saw it too? Well it was a mass hallucination and anyway you have all this childhood trauma and don’t you think you could just be doing this to yourself? Maybe you imagined it! You know, for attention.

reviews.text: I believe that when analyzing the history of the West (by West, I mean Europe, North Africa, and the Americas), we should keep the history of Rome in mind. Not because they were the first in everything—the Egyptians, the Incas, the Mexica, the Toltecs, the Mapuche, the Greeks, the Persians, and the Arabs preceded them in many things both before and after Rome's existence as a power—but because it exemplifies how a great empire can fall under its own weight. We can use Alexander the Great and his Macedonian empire as an example, but it doesn't approach the imperial magnificence achieved by Roman institutions: the Senate, the emperor, the consuls, the generals, the proconsuls, the provinces, the roads. Everything Rome…

reviews.text: I didn’t have much patience for the family drama at the heart of Five Pennies when I was young, but this rewatch was such a lovely experience, rocketing the movie much higher on my Danny Kaye rankings list than expected. Kaye plays Red Nichols, a coronet jazz guy of some renown and a peer (and friend) of eventual legends Benny Goodman, Jimmy Dorsey, Gene Krupa, and Glenn Miller— all of whom played in Red’s band. And yet, Red is largely forgotten today (but for this movie, which itself seems to have slipped through the cracks), mainly because he gave up his career— just on the cusp of the big band era— after his young daughter contracted polio.

Light-footed, expressive, and a comedic expert, he's a classic sort of star, a song-and-dance guy who can bring a touch of acting to the table. He's a bit hammy, but mostly within a decent limit, and when he decides to step it back, he can manage well enough. But he's at his best when he's performing, going all out in song, dance (esp. dance), and those silly impressions and facial expressions. See "Choreography" from White Christmas for a fine example.

reviews.author: annewithe
reviews.text: This is one of those films that I remember from my childhood and loved. And although rewatching it made me feel nostalgic more than anything, I still love it. It's a fine combination of biopic (loosely based on Red Nichols' life & career), drama and music film. I just love Danny Kaye, his voice, his funny clowning, but here he also shows his serious and dramatic side. There are scenes that tugged at my heart strings and the (admittedly sentimental) ending had me crying like a baby. But the absolute highlight of this film is the wonderful music. Love the songs Lullaby in Ragtime and The Five Pennies (written by Kaye's wife Sylvia Fine) but the best music scenes are the ones where Kaye pairs with Satchmo. Their joint rendition of When the Saints Go Marching In (with non-traditional lyrics) is pure joy! (By the way, I found the original soundtrack on Spotify!)

reviews.text: Writing about his faith in tormented exile, Dostoevsky penned: “If someone proved to me that Christ were outside the truth, and in reality the truth were outside of Christ, then I should prefer to remain with Christ than with the truth.” At first blush, this statement might disappoint. Is this just another cowardly instance of religion as wish-fulfillment? Perhaps if this was anyone other than Dostoevsky, yes. But the father of existentialism who could’ve easily surrendered his conscience to avoid prison camp was in no way a coward. For Dostoevsky, truth wasn’t merely a rolodex of scientific facts or historical claims. Truth gained greater, more enduring meaning in relation to the quality of being a person made manifest. Só o Rossellini pra fazer um filme sobre a fé tão prático como esse. O místico existe não a partir de uma relação sobrenatural, mas se presentifica através da natureza: as árvores, os pássaros, o sol, a chuva. O mundo é a prova em si do seu maior milagre: a realidade.

reviews.text: Mad genius without a care in the world. Someone gave a popular illustrator from MSX Magazine some money and said "Show me what you got." You can tell this was made by people who were just drawing and putting together whatever they wanted without any coherence. That's the power of DREAMS. The power to ignore all temptations toward tradition and perceived quality. The power that gives you desperate convulsing animation, wince-inducing attempts at humor, and dire voice acting where a clueless English speaker who just happened to be in Tokyo at the time was asked to voice a seahorse professor with his best fake German doctor accent. This is what it takes to be the greatest dreamer.

reviews.author: Kevin Y
reviews.text: A genuinely joyous affair, at one moment uproariously funny and at another quietly poignant. It’s clear from the first frames that Radha Blank is a multitalented star, and even though her film definitely outstays its welcome, she as a performer never does. Her performance is exuberant and moving, one deeply in tune with the struggles of being a person of color making art in a white dominated industry. Because while this film is an uplifting comedy, it’s also a deeply sobering look at how identity and expression is inherently tied to art - and how quickly that can all be taken away.

reviews.author: Wesley Stenzel
reviews.text: An intriguing prototypical anti-war movie with a flawed message. The film effectively illustrates the horrors of war by showing the misfortune of a wealthy family — an intriguing idea, I guess, but these are the people that will ultimately be least impacted by war in the long term. Several technical elements stand out: the battle footage, a ghost, and the horsemen themselves all look great, and there are several gorgeous shots scattered throughout. But there are also way too many characters and superfluous details that make this a disappointingly messy endeavor.

reviews.author: Ben Reiss
reviews.text: A Spaniard goes to Argentina in the years leading up to WW1 and makes a fortune off of cruelty and slave labor. He has two daughters: one marries a Frenchman who he loves and the other marries a German who he despises. The Frenchman has a son who the Spaniard takes in as his heir and raises as a libertine party boy. Eventually the Spaniard dies, but instead of leaving his whole fortune to our part-French grandson he splits his wealth evenly between his daughters. “Wow, what an intriguing film, wish you didn’t spoil the ending though” -you may be saying. Oh not at all. What I described is just the first 10 minutes!

reviews.text: The film that made Rudolph Valentino a household name is an early example of the anti-war film, telling the tragic story of a wealthy Argentine family, one branch half-French and the other half-German, who relocate to those countries respectively after the death of the family patriarch and become bitter enemies when WWI develops. Of course, this being a Hollywood product, a world war and intra-family enmity are not enough, so the old reliable love-triangle is also introduced to cover the romantic aspect. But this is once when that cliché didn't bother me, as it offers the opportunity to see Valentino in action, and he is both beautiful and beautifully emotive. The film, perhaps, promises more than it delivers, what with…

reviews.text: Valentino’s first close ups, smiling and smoking, then cutting into a tango to show how it should be done: actual star is born moment. Intertitles over waves and catherine wheel fireworks take him to Europe and World War 1. At the periphery, moments that wouldn't be allowed in Hollywood in a few years: a monocled lady with her gal pal at a cafe, a white woman flirting with a black soldier, topless models smoking and chatting with each other during a break, cross-dressing German soldiers dancing down a staircase…There’s a love triangle in there somewhere, along with a family split by the war, but it’s less compelling than the scenes of carousing and war, with the Four Horsemen superimposed over it all.

reviews.text: The fourth outing for Universal's Frankenstein series plays out along similar lines to the previous films, though its definitely a case of diminishing returns. Ghost of Frankenstein picks up after the events of the last film. Angry villagers burn down the castle, but the immortal Ygor has survived and finds his friend the Monster trapped in sulphur. With no other choice, the pair set off to find another son of Frankenstein to fix the Monster again. It's a lot of the same things recycled but the film still boasts some good ideas in its favour. Lon Chaney Jr is an able replacement for Boris Karloff as the Monster but it's Bela Lugosi who really steals the show as the scheming…

reviews.text: Weird and haphazard, The Ghost Of Frankenstein feels like it too was assembled from parts left over from the last Universal Frankenstein film, with a new son of Frankenstein swapped out for Basil Rathbone, another incredibly chill child actor to be lofted about by The Monster, here Lon Chaney Jr. who lumbers affably although without the Gothic Menace And Sorrow of Karloff. Bela has returned as Ygor, as sinister and crafty as ever, as has Lionel Atwill, but in a completely different role, here as an embittered mad scientist because this Dr. Frankenstein just isn't mad enough. We do get the pleasure of The Monster fighting bunches of cops and fully 1/2 of the gowns supplied to Elsa Frankenstein, daughter…

reviews.author: Gibbous Potato
reviews.text: The fourth Frankenstein film in the Universal Monsters series, and honestly, it's starting to become a little tiring. This was, in my opinion, a very unnecessary sequel, especially considering how Son of Frankenstein's ending could have been left as a definitive conclusion to the Frankenstein trilogy. The edge is wearing off, and it seems like Universal was more interested in milking this IP, relying increasingly more on the monster's spectacle, than on good storytelling, which happens to be this film's biggest flaw.

The neo-expressionist sets from Son of Frankenstein are gone - everything looks normal now. Everything is very brightly lit. Lugosi’s Ygor is just a weird guy now, he doesn’t act like he’s had his neck broken anymore (even though this is mentioned in the dialogue several times). Lon Chaney Jr’s monster doesn’t have the layers that Karloff’s does; he’s just a big brute. The plot is that they go to another town and find another Son of Frankenstein - funny how they keep finding them.

reviews.text: A swing and a miss for me. Taymor’s approach is so ambitious, but despite the more impressionistic sequences, The Glorias is largely your standard biopic with some confusing editing. The film is linear in that we go from young Gloria to contemporary Gloria, and yet there’s so much jumbling around in the first hour that it weakens the emotional impact of just about everything. It’s such a relief when Moore finally takes the reins from Vikander, but the film still struggles to maintain its tone. I wish all the different ideas at play were more cohesive, and quite frankly, better done. Some of the VFX work is too jarring to have its desired impact.

reviews.author: Matt Neglia
reviews.text: THE GLORIAS is a monumental piece of filmmaking from Julie Taymor. The proper length, emotional weight & respect is given to Gloria Steinmen’s historic life. It could’ve used some better editing at times but Taymor’s artistic eye and attention to detail (especially one bold sequence involving a homage to The Wizard Of Oz) always kept me hooked. Backed by two fantastic performances from Alicia Vikander & Julianne Moore, who both fully embody Steinmen in an uncanny manner, this will go down as one of the most important films of 2020.

Her high, shy delivery slowly shifts into something lower, more purposeful, more confident. The mistreatment of her character is maddening in so many ways, even more so because of the fact that so many viewers see themselves in her, myself included. She’s awkward, imperfect, and her worth is wholly underestimated by everyone, but that makes her eventual transformation all the more gratifying. Olivia’s Academy Award was so well-deserved.

reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: Wow. Went in to the Stanford Theatre expecting nothing more than a classic Hollywood romance starring Olivia De Havilland. Came out, my soul thoroughly licked from the beating William Wyler gave it, my brain dazzled by both the film's sharp critique of the patriarchy and its humane understanding of people's knotty intentions. No one in a Wyler film is a villain; they all have their faults. And yet De Havilland as Henry James’s Catherine may play the most wrongfully wronged woman that classical cinema has ever conjured up, just as Monty Clift may be one of the most ambiguous chestnuts—tough to crack, a mystery unto himself.

reviews.text: The Housemaid is basically only male anxiety. Male anxiety about what would happen if women treated men like how men treat women (systemically not individually). Our main male character is technically in the position of power as a patriarch and a teacher, and when his power goes unchecked, his world is safe and normal. But as soon as a student is inappropriate to him, his grip on male power (specifically sexual dominance) disappears. He is the one being desired inappropriately. He is the one being assaulted. He is the object that one woman can give to another. The Housemaid is terrified of the power being flipped, even ending with the intention to quell its male audience's fears about the film…

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: “The Hunt” begins with a bunch of NPR-addicted neoliberals poaching a wild pack of Trump-worshipping MAGA types for bloodsport. Director Craig Zobel’s ultra-violent satirical update of “The Most Dangerous Game” aspires to be the movie that America needs right now; it’s a giddy slaughterhouse of mirrors that hopes to bring this country together and make it great again by reflecting the absurdity of us vs them resentment. The movie literalizes the rhetoric of a culture war that has divided the United States into “globalist cucks who run the deep state” and “redneck deplorables” with little wiggle room in between. Blumhouse’s latest blast of low-budget social commentary tries to split the difference between centrists and nihilists — between “bothsidesism” and “nosidesism”—…

reviews.text: Watching A Balmy Swami, Famous Studios’ remake of this cartoon, on TCM today prompted me to revisit the original. While it’s not among the very best Fleischer-era cartoons, it’s quite good — overflowing with ideas and possessing more offhanded visual wit than the remake. Olive and Popeye go to the theater to watch Bluto perform a hypnotist act, and they get unwillingly drawn into the performance. Instead of simply incorporating “magic,” as the remake does, this one achieves its effects by contorting the characters’ bodies: Olive becomes a chicken by bending her knees backwards, Popeye becomes a donkey, Bluto becomes a gorilla, etc. It’s surreal to the point of being disturbing, and it’s great use of animation.

Pretty good drama about regular people being crushed by the turning wheels of history.

reviews.text: This is peak ambiguity in cinematic form. Derived from Henry James’ The Turn of the Screw, The Innocents is a psychological horror film revolving around a governess slowly losing her mind as she thinks that the children she is taking care of are being possessed by the dead. The profound music score and the prepossessing cinematography transformed the 1898 novella into, dare I say, the most equivocal film to date, touching subjects like seclusion and sexual repression in a contentious yet terrifying manner. The lingering uncanny shots can drive someone’s claustrophobia to a maximum and the ending posed multiple symbolisms that was left for the audience to comprehend. Deborah Kerr’s performance was incredibly moving and phenomenal, rivaling her prodigious Black Narcissus act. The formidable phantasmal superimpositions can put anyone on the edge of their seat. An underrated must-watch if you’re into enigmatic psychological horror films.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: The film operates with a striking sense of energy and formal ingenuity. From its opening moments, one perceives an urgency both visual and rhythmic, the kind of creative restlessness that defines cinema in transition. Dialogue is not only functional, it's propelled with remarkable speed and wit, contributing to a texture of tension and irony that feels surprisingly very modern (considering the time). The rapid exchanges, often overlapping and elliptical, establish a tone of perpetual motion, where language itself becomes a form of spectacle.

reviews.author: noen
reviews.text: A requiem for a dying world, Luchino Visconti conducts a symphony of fading grandeur, a melancholic hymn to the inevitability of change. Set during Italy’s Resurgimento, a time of rebellion, unity and compromise, the film transforms history into poetic art, not narrating the birth of a nation, but the slow, dignified death of an era. It is a canvas where Visconti, filmmaker, historian and elitist, paints the twilight of the Sicilian aristocracy with traces of light and shadow, majesty and despair.

reviews.author: Jonathan White
reviews.text: I’m rather amazed that there is no comparative analysis of The Leopard and Dr. Zhivago that I could easily find. Within the first 20 minutes what struck me was that this was the Italian Dr. Zhivago. Both are stories of the aristocracy facing revolutionary change in their beloved countries. Another similarity is the sumptuous cinematography, the directors un-afraid to dote on pictorial landscapes to set the mood. Both films clock in at almost the same length .. 195 minutes for the Cannes release of The Leopard, and 197 minutes for Zhivago. Finally, both novels were picked up by the same publisher. Interestingly, both films are rated 8.0 on IMDB.

reviews.text: The Leopard is one of Luchino Visconti’s illustrious masterpieces. It's a gorgeous stanza set during the period of the unification and independence of Italy during the mid-nineteenth century, and it spotlights the crusade between mortality and fading recollections during the shift of political systems. It houses a tremendous central performance from Burt Lancaster embodying the decline of the Italian aristocracy as nationalism begins to rear its head, and both his physical stature and the narrative moves with a magisterial type grace.

reviews.author: AJ
reviews.text: In William Wyler's last film he lends a cold, precise perspective. He methodically shows all the steps the white police officers, lawyers, citizens, and mayor take to try and force L.B. Jones, the richest black man in town, to drop his divorce suit against his wife who was having an affair with a white police officer. Wyler doesn't delve deep into the perspective of the black community or channel the sense of atrocity and fury in the community's heart. Nonetheless, The Liberation of L.B. Jones doesn't shy away from confrontation. It's hard to watch and Wyler plainly shows the horrors of white supremacy - in the end, the viewer is left with an unambiguous, vitriolic diagnosis.

reviews.author: Kevin_Robbins
reviews.text: The Liberation of L.B. Jones (1970) is currently available on Tubi. The story follows a Black couple going through a divorce after the husband discovers his wife is having an affair with a local white police officer. When the wife hires a lawyer and threatens to contest the divorce, the officer learns that their relationship may become public knowledge. In a town where interracial relationships are heavily frowned upon, exposure could cost him his job. Desperate to protect himself, he goes on a violent rampage, brutalizing his lover and doing whatever it takes to cover up the affair.

reviews.text: William Wyler's final film lacks the careful control over narrative and design that he so often brought to his work throughout his career. It's not lacking in subtext or atmosphere though, as the legendary director boldly explores the vile systemic racism of the times. The film is unflinching in its view of white supremacy, and the systems that teach, enable and encourage its insidious practices. It lays bare the lengths to which the police and higher authorities will go to maintain their status quo, and the subsequent mental gymnastics they make to justify their racist behaviour. There is no sympathy to be found; turning the other cheek is not rewarded with fair treatment. The only hope is that those individuals…

reviews.text: Bad people are complicated. There is something dark at the centre of The Lost Daughter, a film which viciously tears apart the idealism we often have about motherhood. It is a film of mothers, but not one of love. Instead we see a rot, mothers who find children a burden. The Lost Daughter is an uncomfortable movie, with a constant unease and sense of dread. We wait to be given answers, for characters to be uncovered and exposed, and yet they aren't. This is a film which asks us to look inside ourselves and see if we can understand why the characters do what they do. Different people will feel differently about the film. Some will relate to it more…

reviews.author: Carlos Valladares
reviews.text: "Anything to Please the Queen" is love. "Anything to Please the Queen" is life. I can't wait to start (re)watching the sound Lubitschs where (a) Ernst Lubitsch is quicker, more inventively rhythmic, and more efficient with the camera, and (b) the sex play is much freer and less hierarchical in favor of the guy. Surprisingly (maybe not so with Ernst Lubitsch), this may be 1929's most sophisticated American film. It may just be the primitive aesthetics of 1928-29 silent movies—but Lubitsch always frames Maurice Chevalier and Jeanette MacDonald in tight medium-close-ups, so that they sing on the same axis. Thus, Lubitsch equalizes the genders—removes hierarchy—delights in the hedonism of this vaguely Viennese fantasy world (Rick Altman calls it "operetta-land")—dreams of a more perfect society where romance dominates all the time, the gal leads the army, the guy mopes around the house, their servants steal the show by tapdancing the night away, and everyone sings. O Ernst!

reviews.text: This stylish swashbuckler shows gothic horror roots as film moves into the grand historical spectacles of the late 1930s and '40s. I’m not sure I agree with his assessment, but I’ve read Dumas’ Man in the Iron Mask twice, and Tarantino is correct about George Bruce’s screenplay being a significant improvement on Dumas’ story so much that it, not Dumas becomes the “source text” for all future Iron Mask iterations. reviews.text: Buckle your swash, powder your wig and strike your fencing pose - it's a dash of Alexandre Dumas in Hollywood's Golden Year. This doesn't match up to the best of 1939 - the competition was ridiculously fierce - but it's still an entertaining romp that looks good and employs nifty special effects to have Louis Hayward acting opposite himself. James Whale's direction doesn't display the style it had at the beginning of the decade but he marshalls proceedings pretty well and if the casting generally disappoints in both charisma and ability (I doubt Hayward and Joan Bennett would have been at the top of the casting director's wishlist), there is a enjoyable turn from villainous Joseph Schildkraut - and Peter Cushing pops up in his blink-and-miss debut bit part.

This one time independently produced hit looks decent enough but does lack a bit of that top shelf set design you’d see in, for example, an MGM film of the period (say, Marie Antoinette). One of the best directors of the thirties…

reviews.text: James Whale takes the task of telling Alexandre Dumas père's legendary story The Man in the Iron Mask (1939)! And it gives Louis Hayward one of his biggest challenges of his career, playing dual roles as the king(s). The good and the bad. And he grabs the role! I had hoped for more swashbuckling action in this one, for it could have needed some to heighten the excitement, but I guess that comes down to Hayward being a much smoother talker then a swordsman. Regardless of the story being more dialogue ridden then hoped, the romance with Joan Bennett was a match, and Joseph Schildkraut an highly effective scum, making this on par with the version a decade earlier, The Iron Mask (1929).

Many in the older and younger generations in the country are *still* largely divided over their perception of him, as well as that of his daughter, another corrupt, ousted President. So, when I saw that we were finally getting one, but that it was coming from the director of The Drug King, I had decidely mixed feelings.

reviews.text: Expands upon Dostoevsky's idea of identity as a social construct (itself, of course, taken from Gogol), vaporous and frail in nature, by transforming existence into a choice apropos adaptation. To be is to resign to the illusion. Formalistically interesting, sets drenched in minimalism and perpendicular tracking shots - a sterility that pervades the screen, often counteracted by the heavy, prolonged exposition of the first act. Movement, during this tyranny, is plentiful, yet empty all the same, almost as if to accentuate the bore at hand. Once it settles, the deed accomplished and consequences in full flow, the film unleashes its hitherto opaque greatness - subjecting us, like the character, to a reticent stroll through the eclipse, no longer in conflict with it, but united.

reviews.text: For much of The Medium’s first act, its faux-documentary verisimilitude is handled masterfully. The authentic docu-editing/pacing grant the gradual eerie intrusions a truly unnatural air. Thai religious lore among rural jungle landscapes acts as a uniquely fascinating backdrop for The Medium’s story of tested faith and generational secrets. If we’re going purely by The Wailing, the script contributions from director Na Hong-jin are certainly felt in the grounding of rituals and invocations…

reviews.text: I am, for reasons anyone following along at home can guess at, not very interested in explorations of masculinity. Defining what a man is or is not often seems to me to be pointless at best and offensively limiting (and triggering) at worst, so even subversions of masculinity tend to lose my interest. It's when these ideas breach the barriers of gender politics or suggest a null definition that I truly find them interesting, and in the case of Fassbinder's early melodrama, it's more the former that seems to come into play. The film bears witness to the agonizing decline of Hans, a fruit-seller, whose value is so defined by the act of doing that it destroys him to be…

reviews.author: Edgar Cochran ✝️🍋
reviews.text: There is something pervasively invasive about Fassbinder's early minimalistic essay that borders on the overtly theatrical flow of events, that it is impossible not to be entranced by it. Thematically and stylistically, it evidently paved the way for his signature scope of placing a conflicted central character in the middle of a small town and make a psychological analysis of the repercussions this conflict can execute over its surrounding society. This signature stamp would reach its height with Ali: Fear Eats the Soul (1974), a masterpiece of double moral from the perspective of opinionated idiots that criticizes human intolerance and ignorance while brilliantly adding the human factor of inconstancy.

reviews.text: One of the films one would like to call the greatest ever: this isn't a film about mythmaking, or Jesus--this is a movie about humility and the possibility of a better future. If we do realize, it is well after that moment. He even goes as far as to omit sections of the Bible: all instances of Jesus performing miracles are omitted, because to keep them in would mythify Jesus, and distract from the ideas which he tried to share. reviews.text: There's this idea, and with good reason, of attacking any religion for offering nothing more than false hope, failing to solve problems in the material world, engaging in strange, sometimes inhuman, rituals, presenting senseless ideas, collaborating with imperialism, and turning a blind eye to injustice. But there are some, quite a few religious people, at least Christians, who have helped their people. There are some who claim to be "Christian," but when someone denounces injustices within the Church, they are labeled a heretic. When someone says, "Humanity is the child of God, not just a chosen people," they are branded a heretic. This is the source of the religious poetry of the master Rossellini.

reviews.text: Most amazing factoid here is that the wealthy benefactor of this was told by the Virgin Mary in a dream that Rossellini (a non-believer) must be the one to direct this. Much like Pasolini’s version of the gospel, it is rendered more moving to me by its implicit conviction that one need not be a believer to be awed by the life of a Jesus. If you’ve spent much time with western visual art, you’ll recognize more or less every scene as an iconic tableau translated to near constant motion.

reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: Given his lifelong thematic obsession with religion and politics, it is fitting that Rossellini’s last major projects were centered on the lives of Jesus Christ and Karl Marx — two paradigm-shattering revolutionaries whose teachings not only became dramatic turning points in history, but also laid the foundation upon which Rossellini’s films are predicated. His film on Marx never got made, which is unfortunate when you consider that his best work often held Christianity and Communism in dynamic tension. Between Christ and Marx, Rossellini found parallels: “All fashionable revolution is old-fashioned. What interests me is not the antithesis between Christ and Marx, but these two ideas, two ethics, around which the world turns today.” A film on Marx coming on the heels of…

reviews.text: Night of the Hunted is a bit of a departure for Jean Rollin - leaving the gothic fairytale world behind in favour of a cold, clinical dystopia. Despite a different aesthetic, the director still manages his trademark world building; a hazy mesmerising atmosphere runs throughout the film, making it easy to get lost in. The film begins with a wayward woman, who is picked up by a stranger. Following a drawn out but intense sex scene, the action relocates to a mysterious clinic inhabited by people that have lost their minds. The film is essentially a mediation on what it means to be human; is it living and breathing that means we are "alive" or identity formed through memory? It's…

As always, it comes down to two girls. They don't know where they're from, where they're going, or who they are, but they somehow just know each other. reviews.author: Jerry
reviews.text: Liminal sterility. Left to wane inside these white rooms, in hallways lined with bodies outside the minds they house, ambling with unsure certainty in the direction of the dark; minds sprinkled with sparse flashes of images that mean nothing other than that which informs the last slivers of purpose they feel they have left. Mortals drained by a crass disdain for something the authorities do not (and cannot, will not) comprehend. And yet, no matter how much is suppressed, clouded, carried off like a lush puddle in the wind, their humanity remains, tucked as time is in the fleshy folds of the empty space that shapes our existence. Hold my hand, familiar stranger.
