reviews.author: Liz
reviews.text: Crazy to rewatch this a year after having worked my way through Rollin’s filmography and realizing just how much of it is being drawn directly from Paris’ pulp lineage. What was once inscrutable now feels intentional, like the pages of a Feuilladian supercrime saga bleeding into those of a Godardian political screed and one of Franco’s atonally perverse novellas. The fact that Rollin’s son is a dead ringer for Jean-Pierre Léaud only makes this come off looking like the lost Antoine Doinel sequel that we never got, but probably should’ve.

reviews.author: Justin LaLiberty
reviews.text: Rollin playing with genre conventions in ways he really hadn't prior, delivering a genre concoction that's as freewheeling as it is decidedly focused with its subjects bopping around from titular nude vampires to devious science experiments, ghoulish cults and criminal elements -- its perhaps a bit messy when trying to contain all of its eccentricities in a meager 85 minutes, but Rollin is narratively and aesthetically on a plane so narrowly, inherently, his own that even its slapdash nature feels wholly by design

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: Shortly before I watched this I was mindlessly scrolling through Twitter and saw some post from a Baby Boomer complaining about Millennial snowflakes. By contrast, this movie sets generational rift as background and injects it with uncut pulp scenarios and a palpable anger still smoldering from the spirit of '68, imagining the conflict as warring cults of elitists and free spirits. Which is not to say that is what this movie is about. It's about whatever image is on screen at any given moment, which is purely cinematic and urgent in a way that more structured and grounded works are not The effect is uniquely Jean Rollin: narcotic, ecstatic, and erotic, but not alienating or obtuse in the way that some surrealist arthouse stuff or exploitation can be. Long story short, I should destroy my phone and read more Gaston Leroux.

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: I admire the mission statement and the aspects of representation this secures, but my God, it's so fucking boring. Immortals wringing their hands over their endless lives? That's a movie idea older than these characters are. Good guy mercenaries in a crisis of conscience running afoul of an airquotes-suddenly immoral establishment? This is the 700th such story. The only thing that could rescue this is some diabolically tight action, and I'm sorry but it's just not here. The setpieces are few and far between, the choreography is shredded in the edit, the hits are obscured by cuts, there's precious little momentum, and the violence is timid. Nothing's worse than an action film that's afraid you'll get off on its grue. And that's setting aside the dead-empty narrative; I'd be hard pressed to tell you what was even at stake here. Sincerely, a disappointment.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Colors in the dark. A splash of red on white. An off-white suit against blue walls. Against green light splayed over jars and plants on shelves. A light green suit in a botanical garden. Yellow light in a dark staircase. Flashing green lights beyond the curtains. Muted tones amidst the bright; bright tones against bright tones. At times, the colors draw your attention to detail; at times, they draw your attention to a person; at times, they draw your attention to a mood; at times, they simply overwhelm. At its finest, giallo is a genre of colors and tones. it is mood and mystery married by the rainbow. It is shadows in impossible hues. It is a visual labyrinth (those mirrors reveal so much). This film reminds of The Seventh Victim, but it steps back from plot and theme and lets mood and style take over. It relishes its palette. It feeds the eyes.

reviews.text: First-time director Kim Gwangtae delivers a fresh take on the “Pied Piper of Hamelin” with his visceral film The Piper. Set in the hinterlands of Korea in the war-torn 1950s, the film begins with a devoted father and son traversing the country in hopes of finding a cure for the boy’s tuberculosis. The pair (played wonderfully by Ryu Seungryong and the absolutely adorable Goo Seunghyeon) stumble upon a hidden village that knows no news of the outside world and eyes their new arrivals with unease. In an effort to ingratiate themselves with the locals, the father offers to rid the town of their rampant rat infestation.

reviews.text: This brings its own brand of weird. Like an awkward low budget psychological-thriller creature-feature comedy. Where either the greatest kid actor or the most naturally creepy kid actor (I cannot tell which), plays a socially awkward and sexually odd boy who gets telepathically convinced by his teddy-bear that it’s okay to shove his enemies into a pit full of hungry people-eating monsters. The whole thing is just off kilter, with its random soundtrack, terribly wooden acting from some of the adults, bargain basement effects and tone that bounces from one thing to another with no consistency. reviews.text: Sometimes all you need to make a decent movie is a lot of food, a brilliant set, and a single metaphor stretched two hours long and several hundred stories tall. Galder Gaztelu-Urrutia’s “The Platform” is not a subtle film. But these are unsubtle times, with unsubtle problems, and the most alarming thing about this grimly affecting Spanish allegory — which literalizes capitalism’s dehumanizing verticality with twice the gross-out terror of “Parasite,” and almost half of that masterpiece’s furious grace — is that it sometimes doesn’t seem like an allegory at all.

Still, Spencer Tracy is quite good as the central character, and the script is incredibly lean.

reviews.text: Uses a gorgeous western backdrop (including a marvelous Jonny Greenwood score) to stage a very subtle duel of shifting power dynamics/gender roles and psychosexual tension. Not the movie I expected going in and it takes quite a while to reveal itself—Campion is very patient with the filmmaking and deals a lot in the gradual building of detail and implication—but I ultimately found it very rewarding once it did. There's something really felt here in how it slowly sheds its ominous atmosphere of destructive repression and morphs into this strangely vulnerable fable about the presentation of strength and control (especially of the performatively masculine variety) vs. the real thing. Very interested in 1) reading the original novel and 2) giving the film another go with the knowledge of its structure and eventual destination in mind.

reviews.author: Will Sloan
reviews.text: Maybe this movie won't look so impressive to some of you younger folks. I see you all tweeting every day like a bunch of little Noam Chomskys. But you have to understand that in 1977, no one but Larry Cohen was making movies that accused the FBI of harassing, blackmailing, and probably even murdering Martin Luther King. Heck, nobody's making that movie now! They're not even making The Parallax View anymore! Mind you, Cohen doesn't exactly come out and say that Hoover killed MLK, but just pay attention to the dialogue and the editing choices. Not hard to read between the lines.

reviews.author: Josh Lewis
reviews.text: Credit to Cohen for such an appropriately angry, deglamorized fictional dramatization of this period of American history and the spectacular casting job (especially loved Michael Parks as Bobby Kennedy) but can't help but feel him just a bit constrained by the dull TV movie re-enactment form he's opted for, I'm assuming in an attempt to be taken more seriously by boring people who don't care for his B-movie credentials. Which is too bad, I think he does a decent job with this but the seeds were here for him to get as unhinged and wacky as Oliver Stone's history as subjective paranoia horror if he wanted to.

reviews.author: Vlademir Lazo
reviews.text: Se The Godfather (o segundo mais que o primeiro) era um painel histórico e romântico dos EUA do século XX, este filme faz o mesmo sem o romantismo e o glamour, em torno dos homens do lado da ordem e da lei, de uma maneira pulp e muitas vezes grandiloquente, aproveitando que Cohen vinha de filmes de terror e blaxplotations (o que torna curioso ele transitar para um filme em que o protagonista se refere a Luther King como o maior mentiroso da América). Para eliminar algumas das mais engenhosas mentes criminosas e quadrilhas na explosão do gangsterismo era preciso alguém igualmente incomum, obsessivo, paranoico, e disposto a também quebrar regras. Em meio a uma sucessão de jogos políticos, Hoover é um monstro a mais na filmografia do diretor, encarregado de liquidar com monstros ainda maiores, um sujeito que metia medo em meio mundo, mas era suspeito de ser homossexual. Filme brilhante.

reviews.author: Julius
reviews.text: I still have a lot of wrestling to do with Larry Cohen's chosen modus operandi, but Private Files comes from astonishing wells of anger, fire, and curiosity, which seems to set him along a direction of rocket-fueled aesthetic focus (that is, for the master Outsider filmmaker renowned for a lack of refinement). This film has an astonishing clearness of purpose. It feels history sealing, rather than more fuel to the fire of myth, whether it is (or whether there can be such a thing) or not, and its anger seems to alternatively steady his hand and eye as he pushes through production to collate history from a perspective of uncanny hindsight, measuring off select doses of the official and the private, from a position of "the outside looking in." Cohen's poetry of the matter-of-fact is much more successful than Oliver Stone's fantasia in showing us history through a frosted and selective glass.

reviews.author: Diego Quaglia
reviews.text: Radiografia e jornada de um monstro perturbado, o que dá luz para os horrores ocultos na política de um país e o painel dos seus poderosos. Filme seco aonde a emulação documental, crua e contida numa ambientação de época que é prática e barata, mas precisa, dá espaço para um épico histórico tanto visualmente quanto narrativamente sombrio, sujo e soturno da nação estadunidense. Uma aula não só nesse sentido, de cinebiografia e da sua pesquisa atenta, mas de como filmes sobre figuras desprezíveis podem ser feitos para além tanto da obviedade do apontamento ou da abordagem palatável, encontrando de fato a extensão da dimensão delas para além do simplório de qualquer abordagem.

reviews.text: Clocking in at over 230 minutes, divided into ten episodes, Koji Fukada's The Real Thing is a romantic odyssey that defies expectations. It shouldn't work, yet somehow profoundly does. Based on Mochiru Hoshisato's original graphic novel Honki no shirushi and written for the screen by Shintaro Mitani and Fukada, the film unfolds as a sweet, frustrating, and endlessly tangled narrative. It follows Ukiyo, a woman who doesn't just attract chaos but seems to inhabit it, as she jumps from one disaster to another. Her unpredictable presence disrupts everything around her, yet there's something deeply human in her endless cycle of missteps.

reviews.text: The Restless is a fantastic dramatisation of the effect bipolar disorder mood swings have on a family. It launches straight into one of Damien’s rising manic episodes. He’s got irrepressible energy, determined to do a hundred things at once, feeling capable of anything, but more than a little bit scary. He’s a painter, and a husband to Leila and a father to his young son, Amine, but all they can do is watch on in concern. However, what goes up, must come down, and so Damien starts becoming more aggressive, agitated and paranoid, before inevitably crashing, having been awake for days. He ends up in hospital, back on medication, and a fraction of the man we’ve just witnessed.

reviews.author: Alistair Ryder
reviews.text: Big-screen depictions of mental health often lose nuance in favor of exaggerated tropes, inaccurately representing many experiences living with specific conditions. This is certainly the case with bipolar disorder, filmmakers usually showing individuals with the condition in a sustained state of mania rather than the more common occasional episodes. In its earliest stages, Joachim Lafosse’s The Restless, the final film to screen in competition at this year’s Cannes, feels like it’s going to offer a refreshing corrective to some of the more harmful film narratives about bipolar. Unfortunately, this unsensationalised portrait only sustains the drama fit so long.

reviews.author: Julian (Seeking Film)
reviews.text: Four years before the release of Jean Renoir's The River, Michael Powell and Emeric Pressburger released their own Western European, Indian-set drama in the critically lauded Black Narcissus. Wildly acclaimed in its day, the Archers' psychological drama eventually succumbed somewhat to the harsh winds of change, as some of its more dated cultural depictions rightfully came under fire. Renoir would not make that same mistake, filming his production entirely in India with particular attention paid to the country's population and customs. Admirable as this approach may have been, any brownie points The River would gain from its clear interest in its subject matter are offset by an inability to concretely translate that interest to the viewer.

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Shot entirely in India by French director Jean Renoir, The River is a coming of age story with an outstanding sincerity to it. It was the winner of the International Award at the 12th annual Venice Film Festival as well as being one of the first films that brought India to the western world; it furthermore liberated the director from the limits and platitudes imposed by Hollywood studios which he had been labouring under throughout the forties. It is essentially a romance aromatised with the meditation of Hinduism and promotes a multiple of nonprofessional actors in pivotal roles which Renoir establishes to add to the prevailing perception of authenticity. It generates an outgrowth of empathy and sympathy through its unusual blending of poetic dialogue and subdued tensions; its guilelessness is its central quality, and this emphasised a crucial career turn for Jean Renoir.

reviews.text: Ripped from the headlines of the turbulent era between the Great War and the Great Depression, this dynamic, nostalgia-tinged crime drama balances tommy-gun action with epic historical sweep. Legends James Cagney and Humphrey Bogart star as army buddies whose fortunes rise and fall as their fates intersect, first in a foxhole on the front lines of World War I, then in Manhattan’s Prohibition-era underworld. Directed by Hollywood master Raoul Walsh, and based on a story by prolific journalist turned screenwriter and producer Mark Hellinger, The Roaring Twenties brought to a close the celebrated Warner Bros. gangster cycle of the 1930s, and it remains one of the greatest and most influential crime films of all time.

Just the best! Bogart had appeared in a number of the Warner gangster films as a side character by this point but this is the one to finally…

reviews.text: This is a broad generalization, but one that feels rooted in truth: whether because of the pressure of heteronormativity, simple convention, or something else entirely, male actors, typically, engage with their female costars with an attentiveness and intensity that is not present in their interactions with other men on screen. This reality means that, when men bring that same attention to platonic relationships with same-sex screen partners, it's deeply unusual and catches the eye, even if we're not initially sure what we're noticing. The fact that James Cagney does this by default is, I think, one of the main elements that makes his screen presence as powerful as it is.

reviews.author: Joe Lynch
reviews.text: WOW. I had no clue this movie existed and it may be my discovery of the year now. Early Curtis Hansen script (who also ghost-directed) is a taut, tense and something absolutely BRUTAL Canadian thriller about a bank terrier who messes with the WRONG sadistic mall Santa.Elliot Gould goes from Geek to Cool Gould in a fantastic role of a regular guy who should have just kept his nose clean (and didn’t know it was his birthday too, what a coincidence!) Chritopher Plummer is fucking TERRIFYING as the criminal who will do anything for the money. The way the film covers scenes is so dynamic and keeps the action and suspense engaging, no wonder Hitchcock loved it. The aquarium scene is unbelievable…if you’ve seen it…you know…HOLY SHIT. Early John Candy role too! I LOVE L.A. Confidential but now I need to rewatch as much Curtis Hansen as possible ASAP.

reviews.text: I wish I could say I loved this doc as much as I normally love Edgar Wright films, let alone as much as Edgar Wright loves Sparks. This is clearly a work of passionate fandom and full commitment. But I honestly found it kind of dull — 135 minutes of famous people enthusing over how fantastic Sparks is, but without any of the insight I was hoping for into how they do what they do, or what they get out of it. The observations all felt pretty surface-level, and when the band members directly address questions, largely tongue-in-cheek and performative. Par for the course, sure, but I think this could have been 100 minutes long and I would have maintained a lot more enthusiasm for being told to be enthusiastic.

Whatever idealism the hero starts with is slowly whittled down to raw survival, as even the most useful spies tend to become liabilities for the agencies that assigned them to their mission. reviews.author: More_Badass
reviews.text: The Suspect isn’t merely Korean Bourne; it’s the entire Bourne trilogy packed into one frenetic action film. The (unfortunately hyper-edited) fights, the pursuits, the rival agents, Identity’s inadvertent woman partner and suspension-rattling car chase down stairs, Supremacy’s cold vengeance and accidental involvement in a larger plot, Ultimatum’s cat-&-mouse hunt and race across rooftops. Actually, given how Park Hee-soon‘s relentless agent manhunter/ostensible antagonist is introduced via a mid-air skydive save, The Suspect is Jason Bourne versus Ethan Hunt in spirit. (There’s even a brief free-climbing scene and later a Benji-type ally secretly providing agency intel.)

reviews.author: Paul Schrader
reviews.text: Roberto Rossellini's The Rise of Louis XIV was made in 1966 and first shown in the United States at the 1967 New York Film Festival. It was an unpropitious premiere. The theme of the festival was “The Social Film in Cinema” and there was a special seminar on the subject “Reality Cinema: Whose Truth?” These were the halcyon (some would say corrupt) days of cinéma-vérité; four of the many documentary films shown at the festival went on to obtain general release and a hitherto unknown degree of box-office success: Titicut Follies, Don't Look Back, Warrendale, Portrait of Jason, as did a documentary reconstruction film making free use of cinéma-verité techniques, Battle of Algiers. Lost in this rush for cinema-truth was…

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: A world where the nobility festers in unwashed clothes, sweat and unemptied chamber pots even as a king plots to consolidate power through a prison of vanity. The background for this chapter of Louis XIV ascension from the babying shadows of his advisers and regents was a series of civil wars brought on by a chafing aristocracy. Yet Rossellini, armed with a zoom-lens and unpretentious non-actors, slowly casts the Sun King's devious use of fashion and favors to centralize power as the equal of the most complex military strategy. The nervousness of the office clerk who plays a monarch translates as cool aloofness, and his monotone reading of lines held off-camera for his aid gives Louis' words the power of…

reviews.author: Neil Bahadur
reviews.text: Profound - the practically impossible balance between relentless plotting and scheming, and stark simplicity. The young King Louis lives in a horror film of neverending palace intrigue, surrounded by nobles and aristocrats who think because of his youth that he can easily be taken advantage of - even by his own mother. If Louis becomes cold and ruthless it's because he doesn't have any other choice in this rigid society where even a King is powerless in the system he's supposed to be ruling. His cunning allows him to reorganize the courts and in turn reorganize society - the irony of course being that by stripping the nobles and aristocrats of their power and/or making them financially reliant on him…

reviews.author: BrandonHabes
reviews.text: This might be the film Kubrick wanted you to watch before BARRY LYNDON. If you can get yourself into the headspace of watching sumptuous, elaborately staged pageantry in which ridiculous rituals and crass ceremonies reveal a politics of spectacle leading to one king’s ascension of power, this film will offer more to you than some emotionally wrought drama. Kubrick no doubt borrowed from Rossellini’s stately, contemplative style to tell his own story of power conquests and performative politics, even liberally adopting Roberto’s use of stoic zoom lenses to create ironic juxtaposition between a manipulation of spectacle and a complex mis-en-scene. If you can shift your frame of reference away from conventional dramatization to a process in which courtly ceremony disguises…

reviews.author: Diogo Serafim
reviews.text: Power and politics are just a matter of appearances. The film’s clear headed discourse on the domestication of a population through the death of feudalism and the advent of absolutism is a magnificent showcase of Rossellini’s unparalleled ability to synthesize ideas through mise en scène without losing the dialectic nature of the medium. The first half of the film, where mostly chiaroscuro compositions prevail, progress with the main character’s reserved acting towards the second half, very illuminated and following a more dominant presence from our anti hero, only for us to see him undressing himself from his power in the melancholic last sequence to contemplate his own deciduousness in the image of the sun - nothing is perennial.

reviews.text: ¿Recuerdan el sketch de Rossellini en Siamo donne? Pues imagínense ahora aquella obra maestra de intimismo, aquella mirada cotidiana dirigida no hacia las aventuras de Ingrid Bergman y una gallina intrusa, sino hacia un rey francés del siglo XVII, y empezarán a comprender la importancia de La Prise de pouvoir par Louis XIV. Jamás nadie, tal vez ni el mismo Rossellini, había logrado instalarnos en el pasado de forma tan natural, sin producirnos la menor extrañeza. Asistimos así, comprendiendo verdaderamente, a la ejecución metódica y rigurosa de un sutil golpe de estado, como si presenciáramos una retransmisión en directo desde el pasado. La lógica del proceder de Luis XIV se ve potenciada por la de la forma rosselliniana de hacer…

A TV francesa disse sim, com a condição de que fosse feito com o equivalente hoje a 20.000 dólares. Então o filme tinha de ser rodado em 16mm, meu pai nunca tinha filmado em 16mm, a cores, e tipo, em 20 dias. Um filme de época, de reconstrução histórica, um filme estruturalmente complicado. reviews.text: From the guy who wrote I Saw The Devil comes a film about a group of men trying to kill a fake a** CGI tiger. Aside from the obvious threat posed by the enraged tiger, who is evidently also out for his own personal revenge against Min-sik's character, there is also the interpersonal tension and consequent potential for backstabbing that it creates. The film's camerawork and…

Set in 1925 during the Japanese occupation, an official obsessed with trophies (Ren Osugi) is hunting Joseon tigers to the point of extinction. With only one of the cats remaining, the beast takes on mythic dimensions. The film uses the hunt as a backdrop for a character study of a retired hunter (one of Choi Min-sik's finest hours), and his strained relationship with a son looking towards the better prospects of the urban world. Ryoo Seung-Wan shows is apt at keeping things zipping along with a Scorsese like verve without ever letting anyone off the hook or giving any clear signifiers on who we should be rooting for. There's a reason this one won best director and screenplay at South Korea's academy awards.

reviews.author: jrhovind
reviews.text: The police thriller rendered as a practically Danteseque journey through so much sin and moral rot, Ryoo digging around in the engine that keeps Korean society going and finding so many interlocking networks of open corruption and well-heeled cruelty (it’s probably no accident that the film is very much a boy’s club). “Forget the process. We need results.” If Detective Choi starts off as the leader of a merry band of good men hanging on in a world gone bad, his collisions with those running the prosecutor’s office and Seoul’s high-finance wheelers-and-dealers only make him realize just how far clean hands get you in this world; a pure soul and a belief in truth and a knife plunged miserably in the gut. Relentlessly bleak, as Ryoo resists the live-wire set pieces that mostly characterize his thrill-machines, favoring instead a slickly propulsive headlong dive into the heart of late-capitalist darkness.

reviews.text: A remake of Spanish insane mystery-thriller The Body by Oriol Paulo that is surprisingly good and more easily-digested than the original version. But remaking movies is not an easy task and somehow this one proves it. The thrills and mystery; both elements are uneven. While adding some freshness to the story, some parts become draggy and unnecessary, until it leads to the payoff that felt less impactful and shocking than what I've seen in the Spanish version. South Koreans really stick with their style, I guess. Nonetheless, some flaws are not that serious and the entertainment value is still there.

reviews.text: Providing further proof that women always make better exploitation films, this feels almost like the Rothman flipside to AIP's okay Count Yorga series, eschewing the stuffy LA manors for the endless sprawl of the California desert. It’s not perfect, but I'm totally willing to overlook all of its problems (wonky plotting and some not-great performances from Blodgett and Miles) just because of ALL of Denise’s looks and Rothman’s use of eye-popping color. This straddles the lines between art film, horror, and exploitation, and it’s at its best when all three come together, not veering too far out into outright shock or sex. More lady vampire movies need dune buggies.

Lemmon is a dyspeptic cartoonist based on James Thurber whose work mostly consists of tell-it-like-it-is tableaus of gender politics, but it creaks with outdated morality and humor. reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Modern Hollywood’s messiest comeback artist is finally ready to show his work on screen, and there isn’t a moment to waste. You can tell from the first minutes of “The Way Back” that construction worker Jack Cunningham is unlike any character Ben Affleck has ever played before — he’s not trying to impress anyone. There’s no twinkle in his eye, no swagger in his step, no “smartest guy in the room” energy to the way he carries himself. He murmurs when he talks, drinks a beer in the shower every morning, and sparks to the salesman at his neighborhood liquor store as if that’s the only stable relationship he still has left in his life.

This is the sequel to Fast Times at Ridgemont High and does a good job being different but my attention waned and it isn’t a coming of age movie unless the characters, well, come of age. That this also features multiple song and magic routines by a rubber-clad Veronica Lake, a weasely Laird Cregar, and a pen-gun-toting evil chairman of the board has me convinced that it was pulled straight from the most feverishly fun depths of the wartime pulp consciousness. reviews.author: Lara Pop
reviews.text: A noir which says no to virtually every - otherwise cool - noir trope to captivate with innovative storytelling and clever perspective-shifting instead. This Gun For Hire works with multiple storylines and works with them well, tying each fully fleshed out character's story together on a fast-moving train of events. Veronica Lake stuns with her killer trio of beauty & wit & modesty in her inverted femme fatale role. Alan Ladd is the king of playing stoical characters. Rumor has it that he was often paired with Veronica Lake because she was the only actress in Hollywood shorter than him. I don't know about the truth value of this tale, but at any rate, I'll be damned if the guy didn't have the most badass endings in movies, so there's compensation for you. The set design was crisp, the stunts during the action scenes were cool, and the ending really did pack a punch. Absolutely perfect for a cozy evening.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: Angry at God, in love with himself, and callous to the humanity of women, Coffin Joe is the perfect villain, an encapsulation of toxic masculinity and entitlement, believing himself to be the superman while showing no sign of anything more than a penchant for cruelty. He is also lapsed Catholic guilt and clinging to fairytales of immortality (via bloodline) in order to escape his own mortality, and all of this is depicted in the low-rent but stylish shadows and mists of B-movie Brazil, complete with a colorful excursion into the Inferno that shows us the face of the Devil matches Joe's. He is either his own punishment, or he is evil incarnate, or both.

Mojica faz um filme mais maduro, com mais cuidado nas cenas e nas imagens, mostrando um trabalho mais confiante e criativo. reviews.text: One of the best anthologies there are, genuinely not a single weak link among itself which I attribute heavily to the directors of each being already-established directors who are familiar with genre film-making. It would honestly be a misnomer to say this is a collection of horror films insomuch as they are a triptych of fleshed-out dramas with strong horror to them; a bit of a pedantic distinction but what I feel makes these have a longevity that many horror anthologies do not. There's a strong sense that each of these segments would work well on their own as a fully-fleshed film (already true of Dumplings) given how they fit within their respective director's filmographies, which is probably the strongest compliment I can give to a short.

reviews.author: reibureibu
reviews.text: What it means to be good vs the justification of evil, our inescapable fate to the whims of dramaturgy, the folly of man yet his divine right to anyways, vengeance. Everything Park Chan-wook has dedicated himself to, distilled down to its barest essentials so as to be a blueprint laid clear while also a self-winding contraption in and of itself; Cut acts as a simulacra of both its reality (the director, the film, the film-making process, the oeuvre) and its fiction (the themes, the archetypes, the audience, the spectacle) in what is essentially a neat little game of men playing god and their inevitable fate. The road to hell is paved with such pretenders; the fate of their victims perhaps even worse.

reviews.text: In some ways it is a self-conscious reversal of The Son's Room. It is about Italian family as this suffocating thing, only it observes it from a removed distance as it reffuses to come to a fixed position. People simple follow roles set up for them in often chilling ways. The movie humanism as embracing as it terrifying. It is uneven for sure, some of situations feel a bit sketched, some of the ironies to easy, I assume the novel this is based unless it has wonderful writing isn't very good, but I can understand why it spoke deeply to Moretti. At its very best the movie does access some strong places about family commitiment and how that plays against large society. The plotting piles up ludicrous excessive situations, but Moretti's direction drains them. It is melodrama done with artificial amount of restrain, but somehow quite mad.

reviews.text: I appreciate this one more than I like it. It’s for the most part decently acted, shot, and scored, and it definitely is not without its moments - but ultimately, it’s too self serious and outwardly *reflective* for its own good. You can tell the story of estrangement and distance while still projecting warmth, humor, and heart in your storytelling, but the story and characters here feel a bit too removed. Instead, it’s in large part somber shots of characters staring forlornly into the distance and scenes that try too hard to manufacture emotion. It almost feels like the aesthetic of what we expect from a “poignant immigrant story” is superseding all else. Its intentions are pure, but this falls…

reviews.text: On its surface, Garrett Bradley’s “Time” asks a simple question: How can you convey the full length of 21 years in the span of a single film, let alone a documentary that runs just 81 minutes? And from its degraded opening images — borrowed from the first of a thousand video messages that a black Louisiana woman named Sibil Fox Richardson (aka “Fox Rich”) recorded for her husband as she waited for him to be released from the State Penitentiary — offers a similarly simple answer: You don’t measure it in length, but rather in loss.

Delon channels his career making performance in Le Samurai; here again playing a cold, calculating and precise killer; only this time with a family. The familiarity of the plot lends the film…

The style here is deliberate, sometimes pretentious but man did it make the film move with its curious coverage choices and kinetic, brutal violence….and those car chases are fucking GREAT; no CG bullshit here!Feels like at the time some of these set pieces were original and shocking (the car bomb set up; the junkyard kill)And MAN does it literally punch you (and most women in the film) in the FACE at times. reviews.text: Vincente Minnelli's ultimate statement as an auteur. A film that blows you away once you realize where it stands in the history of classical Hollywood. It's Classic Hollywood's documentation on its own destruction, a snuff film of its demise. Two Weeks' "failure" as a film compared to previous Minnelli efforts is completely the point; Minnelli ingrains the turgidness into the film's thematic (hence, aesthetic) design. Every one of his obsessions—trinketized décors and the feeling that they will passively-aggressively swallow the protagonists whole, the lack of privacy in bourgeois interiors, wild melodramatics (garish overacting courtesy of Claire Trevor as a put-on director's wife), hand-slaps, doors that refuse to close, swirling musical licks that burst from a flame-like nowhere, precious objects that…

reviews.author: Jake Cole
reviews.text: Minnelli bridges his own ornate classicism with the modernist new waves, resulting in a film in which his florid melodrama becomes self-reflexive and autocritical, the art of the filmmaker as much assuaging backstage ego trips as jockeying with actors and producers to assert one's visions. The jagged structure of the plot, which takes Minnelli's longstanding mastery of abrupt intrusions of drama and blows them up into colliding internecine battles for any kind of domestic and professional supremacy. Not sure about the timing of its distribution in France since Godard put it on his 10 best list of 1963 but if this movie did not profoundly influence JLG in making Contempt then there must have been something in the air.

reviews.text: Weep. Ugetsu is Mizoguchi's horror film, a nightmare across this life and the next. A man, dirtied and shirtless, wanders across a burnt landscape. Ugetsu draws on folklore and classic Japanese literature to produce quintessential jidaigeki cinema. It is a departure from Mizoguchi's earlier work, being more expansive and complete, beyond just the humiliation and pain of women. The Life of Oharu represented his previous style perfected. But this is beyond, travelling to the abstract.

reviews.author: Barmilliv
reviews.text: Se você procurar hoje em dia, vai achar uma infinidade de filmes de horror japonês. No entanto, assim como houve o primeiro filme de terror da história, o Japão também teve seu ponto de partida. Antes mesmo do terror começar a andar, elementos sobrenaturais já vagavam pelo cinema oriental. Em 1953, surgiu "Contos da Lua Vaga", considerado o filme que deu o grande empurrão ao gênero, com uma atmosfera capaz de causar calafrios e que, na época, deve ter sido extremamente tensa. O filme se passa no Japão do século XVI, durante um período de guerras civis conhecido como Período Sengoku, marcado pela violência e pelo caos.

reviews.author: Diogo Serafim
reviews.text: Fog of greed. Like watching a curve become a straight line through the cruelest of moral lessons: only the material exists, dreams are purely devoted to idealism. This film feels like a fever dream one cannot wake up from until it’s too late, depicting a world of delirious harshness, of raving temptation and sinful desire, a tale of morality, the moon and the rain and the spirit and all the violence in the world. Life is work, humility and pain, dreams of ambition are vicarious veils of deception. The most unsettling thing is how Mizoguchi’s materialism and objectivity mesh with such a maddening matter. A film so deeply haunted that even reality seems to end up irredeemably cursed by its destructive spell.

reviews.author: St. Sebastian
reviews.text: Uncle Vanya is a bittersweet symphony of devotion and melancholy, a character left adrift by those he cherished. I often find myself mulling over my two cherished cinematic interpretations of this poignant Chekhovian tale, and the verdict remains unchanged: Smoktunovskiy eclipses even Redgrave. Both are titans in portraying minds teetering on the brink of collapse, yet here we have THE ensemble. The delicate Sonya (Irina Kupchenko) holds her own against the ethereal Elena (Irina Miroshnichenko) in Konchalovskiy's adaptation—by the way, the only one of his works I truly admire. Meanwhile, the splendid doctor Astrov (Sergei Bondarchuk) sometimes seems to fade into the background compared to Voinitsky's fervent longing for Professor Serebryakov's new bride. It’s a decaying aristocratic haven, resplendent in its decay. I can’t help but weep alongside Innokentiy Mikhailovich’s character every time I revisit that heart-wrenching moment when he pilfers a vial of morphine from the doctor. What a remarkable film, brimming with my favourite actors.

Miller was still vaguely cast-able (i.e. before he became so toxic that Mucinex fired him as the company’s spokes-snot). For another, it’s an expensive, original, multiplex-ready B-movie in an era when virtually anything with an $80 million budget has to be about superheroes or new subscribers. It's an art gallery movie, something which exists only to showcase its art, yet it stands out as one of the watchable films of its kind. It is a film constructed from leftovers, shot alongside Jesús Franco's Count Dracula, and made from disconnected moments and behind-the-scenes footage. This is a work of filmmaking voyeurism, a film that encroaches upon another. Yet it ends up more cinematic and potent than the film it leeches off. It is highly atmospheric, told silently but accompanied by sparse yet often booming music. It's shot in the shadows, observing the action as something to artistically cannibalise. reviews.text: This is surprisingly class conscious for a film about kids fighting vampires. To tackle gentrification through this lens requires a willingness to embrace absurdity and to find an appropriately serious tone at the same time, and somehow, miraculously, this film manages it far better than horror-comedy could be expected to. Presenting this kind of racism as a horror is probably, however, the only accurate way to present it. to present gentrifiers as parasites, to show their relationship to the police (even if the police are black), to show that their power is not just supernatural but political and economic, to show that the only way to defeat them is with a community uprising? That is a sharp, meaningful political message, especially in the current atmosphere. My only complaint is that Rita didn't have a bigger role.

reviews.author: Dan Santelli
reviews.text: A droll, sardonic ethnographic mock-newsreel about vampires lurking amid the shadows and bowels of Paris. Vampirism is framed as social liberation, a bite on the neck is tantamount to becoming radicalized, and yet the joke is ultimately on that distinctly French breed of Cartesian rationalism that balks at consideration of the supernatural. The opening credits devilishly juxtapose the sacred and the sacrilegious, signaling both the sarcastic edge and an incendiary polemic. As if that’s not enough, Chaouat and Duvic have the gall to climactically repurpose the final line from Resnais’ Night and Fog, an admittedly edgelordish provocation that condemns the Establishment and invokes memories of the Holocaust and the national self-deception that marked the Régime de Vichy. A jazzy prank that’s as sour as a Warhead.

reviews.text: you know that moment where you just wake up? and the realities of life haven’t quite sunk in, you’re immersed in the memories of what it was like to be asleep, whatever dreams roamed around in your mind. you’re conscious of your awake self but numb to the world around you, not sure what exactly is real and what is a consequence of the dreams lingering with you. anyway, that’s Vitalina Varela for the entirety of the runtime. watch this movie tired and lose your entire grasp on reality. ghosts coated in shadows, confusion over lies and loss reflected as literal urban decay, the spaces representative of all the grief haunting her existence. she’s caught between the realm of the awake and the asleep, the alive and the dead. and we’re trapped for the ride through the underworld besides her until she finds the light, wherever that may be. staggering work.
Slow moving in dirty slums.Abandoned all the emotions I had.Emptiness, and absence —They occupy everything now.

reviews.text: Based on the horror novella by Ukrainian writer Nikolai Gogol, which was initially published in the first volume of his anthology of tales in 1835, Viy is a colourful movie concerning witches, with a hidden political subtext. Produced by Mosfilm studios, which is one of the oldest in Europe, it features an exciting variety of practical effects and set designs by Aleksandr Ptusjko which perfectly captures the tone of Gogol’s adapted folktale. Viy’s significance as the first Soviet-era horror film released in the USSR is merely the beginning of what makes this so extraordinary.

It loses a step when it has to start focusing more on the young co-leads romance, in part because while Hutton is alright he isn't the most dynamic romantic hero. reviews.author: Michael Shawn
reviews.text: A super neo-noir with an amazing all-star cast, I can't figure why this one isn't more celebrated. The always reliable, handsome and stoically charismatic David Janssen headlines as a cop who is charged with manslaughter after shooting an "innocent" man, a respected doctor, who pulls a gun on him. But his claims of self-defense don't wash when the man's gun can't be found. With hardly anything to go on, Janssen has to piece the doctor's life together and find something, anything to hang on him to avoid prison. He works his way through a who's who of top talent of the 1960s, portraying his colleagues and friends and family of the doctor, including Lillian Gish, Eleanor Parker, Ed Begley, Carroll…

Janssen plays a Joe Friday type (he even drinks buttermilk) and while the story resides on a lot of flimsy logic, it’s almost gritty enough to work. Unfortunately, like many Paramount films of the day, it’s shot like an episode of Mannix, and maybe the stacked undercard of name actors (even Carroll O’Connor, for some reason playing a Latino judge) was there to give audiences a little of what TV could offer them (and I’m now learning that it…

reviews.author: Isa Bul.
reviews.text: Un thriller neo-noir efficace.Même si Warning Shot fait téléfilm (il surfe sur le succès télé de David Janssen dans Le Fugitif), il est bien écrit, réalisé sérieusement et avec intelligence. Le scénario est prenant et les dialogues teintés d'ironie font mouche ; le scénariste Whit Masterson glisse même ça et là quelques petits pics bien sentis sur la violence policière, le problème de l'avortement et le racisme du système judiciaire.David Janssen est charismatique, tout en retenu et crédible. La musique jazz de Jerry Goldsmith est assez exceptionnelle, raison pour laquelle je voulais voir ce film à la base.La toute fin laisse un goût amer tant elle est désabusée.Très bonne surprise.

reviews.author: Marty McKee
reviews.text: David Janssen, in 1967 one of America’s biggest television stars in the fourth and final season of THE FUGITIVE, plays — what else — an honest man trying to clear himself of a murder charge in WARNING SHOT. He isn’t Dr. Richard Kimble, but Los Angeles police detective Tom Valens, who guns down a prominent physician in the courtyard of an apartment complex. Valens claims the victim pulled a gun, but no weapon is found at the crime scene. When embittered district attorney Sam Wanamaker (DEATH ON THE NILE) charges him with manslaughter, Valens picks through a menu of cameos and guest stars in search of clues to the missing gun.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Even Wayne Gretzky missed the net a couple of times over the course of his career. An overstuffed espionage thriller that bites off more than it can chew and never manages to find its footing, Olivier Assayas’ “Wasp Network” is an exceedingly rare gaffe from one of the greatest filmmakers of the last 30 years. Even so, his restless genius can still be felt percolating below the surface and struggling to come up for air. While this scattered, staccato dramatization of Cuba’s most infamous spy ring struggles to dramatize its tangled web of defections and double-crosses, the movie’s underlying strengths are the stuff of vintage Assayas; its best moments allow the French auteur to explore some of his oldest infatuations…

reviews.author: matt lynch
reviews.text: It's not really fair to say this lacks the jangly anxiety and urgency of CARLOS, because the project here is not a rockstar spy movie. Instead it functions very well as a flip on Assayas' epic, still a story of shifting loyalties and commitment to revolution (real or perceived), but with a radically different point of view of the sacrifices of the boots on the ground. This is what the struggle looks like now.

reviews.author: MJsays
reviews.text: It’s no surprise that even Assayas’ weakest efforts are stronger than most Hollywood productions these days. Can you imagine if big budget studios got ahold of this idea? It would be riddled with nothing but unnecessary car chases and explosions. The French auteur’s approach towards exploring Cuban history is not concerned with the action or dramatic events that once put the disgruntled country in the public eye, but rather, the interpersonal mechanics fuelling their socio-political unrest. Admittedly it’s all a bit cut and paste, yes, but with an exceptional cast and powerful underlying message, it’s far from bottom-of-the-barrel educational entertainment.

reviews.text: Bob Hope plays Michael Valentine, a radio personality who plans to end his womanizing ways and get married. Her rough cop brother (William Bendix) doesn’t trust him. Suddenly he is informed that the ruler of a small country has been killed and named Valentine as his sole heir. He is kidnapped, escapes, attempts to get others to believe his story, and is continually beset by close calls, murders and foiled attempts at his life. Being in the company of beautiful Signe Hasso further raises the ire of his fiancée’s cop brother. This was a pretty standard premise for Bob Hope comedy, and Where There’s Life was released when Hope was at the absolute height of his powers at the box office and also had a popular radio show. It is typically breezy, funny and worthwhile.

reviews.author: laird
reviews.text: Hard to tell whether this is conservative pearl clutching or mocking conservative pearl clutching, but either way the gawking shots of 1965 pornography (gosh, how quaint magazines like "Rubber" and "Teenage Nudists" seem now) and the vaseline lens lingering on Sal Mineo's body suggest either director Phoebe Cates' dad or someone else behind the camera was more interested in those subjects than the script required. The vaseline on the edges gives the movie a dreamy affectation, turning NYC into a bifracted fantasy land of dance clubs and sparkling spas full of beautiful people and a sin city of vice markets and crime scenes full of perverts. The year in which this made finds it smack dab in the middle of huge shifts in acting styles and censorship, creating an odd mix of "gee golly whiz" and actual grime and menace. It's unlike anything else!

It’s like a fever dream from someone who’s day drinking very dry martinis. REBEL WITHOUT A CAUSE’s Sal Mineo plays a very disturbed busboy with a sinister streak amongst a cast who seems both confused over what’s going on and game enough to play along with the trippy vibes. Also, like SNAPSHOT, all men (and most of the women) are CRAZY. The final moments in Times Square are batshit haunting. Classic “Horny Noir” (“Hornoir”?) that won’t be soon forgotten. This movie is a friggin TRIP.

Filmed on location in New York City, it has both a swinging 60s vibe with lots of frenetic go-go dancing and the seamy side of Times Square with sex shows and porn palaces. Low budget with a script that doesn't always make sense, it's nonetheless fascinating in its combination of creepiness and campiness. And I loved it.

reviews.text: "Who Killed Teddy Bear?" is a 1965 crime film directed by Joseph Cates. Playing on the elements of taboo novelty in a pulp noir fashion, the film held a cult following back within its release era. Since that time, the film didn't really surface to any recognition outside of certain circles, being something of a lost gem of sorts. Only getting its first blu ray (which was an extremely small release at that) in 2009, it once again has been given some life in 2024 by being released in 4k by boutique sub-label Cinématographe.

It's a haunting film, more avant-garde in its intentions than even the other Hungarians kicking around the arthouse at the time. reviews.author: Darren Carver-Balsiger
reviews.text: God is going. Winter Light is a very personal film for Ingmar Bergman, whose father was a priest. It's a very small scale film, even for Bergman, but about the largest of all things: God and creation itself. Made in the 1960s, Winter Light slots into an era when Bergman spent years making thematically connected films, as opposed to the somewhat unpredictable genre jumping of his late 50s output (religious - The Seventh Seal, social realist - Brink of Life, historical - The Magician, sentimental drama - Wild Strawberries). Winter Light is the middle and best of Bergman's Silent God Trilogy (or Faith Trilogy), and grapples with faith on a very powerful individual level.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Irish animation studio Cartoon Saloon may not be able to match the impact or consistency of Japan’s Studio Ghibli (who can?), but the Kilkenny-based outfit has gradually emerged as one of the world’s last and most valuable bulwarks against the crude and craven soullessness that has defined the post-“Shrek” era of mainstream animated movies. Rooted in Celtic mythology and drawn to look like a moving stained glass window, 2009’s Oscar-nominated “The Secret of Kells” stood apart from its computer-generated 3D contemporaries for its warmth and its beauty. While the likes of “Bolt” and “Kung Fu Panda” offered all the magic of a trip to the mall, Cartoon Saloon’s breakout almost seemed holy by comparison.

reviews.text: Wrath of Man is not your typical Guy Ritchie gangster movie but oh so good, anyone wanting more than it says on the tin will be pleasantly surprised. Familiar plot elevated by a wonderfully solid piece of genre filmmaking. This is a stripped down, hard knuckled heist/revenge thriller, enjoyable in it's own brooding, muscular way with flashes of violence and high body count. Christopher Benstead's score was fantastic. It's Jason Statam's best film & performance in a long, long time. Scott Eastwood is so good in this. How is he not a bigger star? This guy should be headlining big action movies.

reviews.author: Sally Jane Black
reviews.text: It struck me while watching this that the homophobic nature of Hollywood/the explicit homophobia of the Hays Code that forced directors to turn queer characters into mere subtext had the unintended effect of turning every close male friendship into a gay relationship in hiding, thus in the modern era, erasing male camaraderie (to those who look for this sort of thing) instead of erasing homosexuality, as they had done in the past. This is just an extension of the patriarchal/heterosexist power, which extinguishes masculine vulnerability, emotional honesty, and, of course, LGBT all at once, but it stood out to me as a notable side effect in pop culture.

reviews.author: Criterion
reviews.text: Douglas Sirk’s Technicolor expressionism reached a fever pitch with this operatic tragedy, which finds the director pushing his florid visuals and his critiques of American culture to their subversive extremes. Alcoholism, nymphomania, impotence, and deadly jealousy—these are just some of the toxins coursing through a massively wealthy, degenerate Texan oil family. When a sensible secretary (Lauren Bacall) has the misfortune of marrying the clan’s neurotic scion (Robert Stack), it drives a wedge between him and his lifelong best friend (Rock Hudson) that unleashes a maelstrom of psychosexual angst and fury.

reviews.text: Odd to see a portrait-of-an-artist doc without any heroics - the guy’s sad, isolated and with a generally negative outlook on.. everything. Interesting considering that designers, more than other creative heroes, are tied so directly to commerce. An independent like yohji needs to have a sustaining business underneath them. (He mentions this at some point, says keeping his staff employed is the only reason he sticks around). In fashion, it all depends on brand, and shouldn’t this be a mythological marketing opportunity? But it’s just generally a flat and unflattering picture of him. His operation must be as lean as it seems in the film because there was clearly no publicist running interference here. I mean just allowing that scene in his art studio with that truly, truly horrible painting in the background to happen...

reviews.text: A whole hell of a lot. Snyder fully commits to big, sappy emotions and weird grandiose gestures, and the result is that this is bizarrely most interesting in its first half with all the shoe leather of bringing these now much more fleshed out characters together. Unfortunately a lot of the reconstituted footage is riddled with shoddy VFX and the action beats remain mostly unchanged crummy digital smears, only now they go on much, much longer. Still it's a ridiculous miracle of sorts that this even exists at all, so unwieldy and sincere that it frankly transcends good and bad and becomes purely artifactual, and I never thought I'd say this but I'm mildly bummed he's not going to get to do more of these.

reviews.author: davidehrlich
reviews.text: Sooner or later, any commercially viable documentary about the life and work of avant-garde musician Frank Zappa — outsider art’s ultimate inside man — has to grapple with the same headache from which Zappa suffered for the length of his career: the hostile relationship between commerce and creation. The biologically improbable love child of a time-bending orgy between Igor Stravinsky, Weird Al Yankovic, Jacob Collier, and Led Zeppelin (or maybe it would be easier to just call him a true original), the self-appointed Mother of Invention was a composer by nature, and a rock star by necessity.

reviews.author: SkaneNoise
reviews.text: I believe that Zappa (this doc) is unique in a big way that has nothing to do with Zappa. It felt like an appetizer that fills you up. Like a summary with an arch. It touches spots and moves on without dramatizing them but you totally understand the complexities that are natural to any relationship. Not dramatizing everything out was ingenious because that would have made the doc a bit cliched. I became aware of this when they started talking about Moon Zappa and Valley Girl, I started thinking ‘oh shit here’s where they force in the dramatic element about a daughter who wants to reach out and a father who is too involved in his own career to see…

reviews.author: Paul Elliott
reviews.text: Directed by Alex Winter, Bill in the Bill & Ted film series, Zappa is a biographical documentary that beholds the actor and filmmaker having unrestricted access to the Zappa vault. Winter performs a deep dive into the rich cache of archival footage, and the final creation is a two-hour joyride into the mind of the self-taught musician who was both brilliant and contrary. It's as weird and irreverent as his music but still functions as a substantial biography and examination that doesn't ignore the sexism in a few of his lyrics.
